items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Ycrystal keeps scientific data separate from presentation and rendering backends. The Python interfaces are still evolving; inspect their source and tests when extending them.

Layer Responsibility and dependency direction core/structure.py Scientific cell, positions, elements, labels, occupancy, movable flags, provenance. Lattice rows and positions are Cartesian Å. Array inputs are copied and stored read-only; metadata remains mutable. core/scene.py SceneSettings and Environment describe presentation. build_geometry resolves repetitions, boundary images, hidden IDs, periodic bonds, radii, colours, and cell edges into the shared DisplayGeometry. No Qt or VTK. core/camera.py, core/picking.py Immutable orthographic camera and analytic picking. Projection uses top-left continuous pixel coordinates. Navigation returns new cameras. No GUI dependency. io/readers.py, io/qe_lattice.py, io/project.py File detection, ASE-backed readers (QE lattices with ibrav other than 0, which ASE does not read, are built by qe_lattice with pw.x's conventions), provenance, and versioned JSON projects. Questions are exceptions that the caller can answer and retry; no GUI dependency. gui/main_window.py, gui/commands.py Qt actions, dialogs, project state, selection, and display-setting undo stack. Coordinates are never edited by navigation or hiding. core/background.py, io/images.py, io/package.py Background pictures: the framing reference stored in an Environment and the shared placement arithmetic (no Qt/VTK); checked, content-addressed picture storage (Pillow); and the defensive ZIP container that projects and styles use when they carry a picture. presets/custom.py, gui/material_editor.py Custom material variants: typed parameter schemas for Ycrystal's own recipes, content-derived ids, generated POV-Ray recipe text; and the Customize Material… dialog with the personal list in QSettings. core/vectors.py, gui/vector_dialog.py Atom-attached vectors: typed records (Cartesian components, meaning), source defaults and image overrides, arrow appearance, and the single resolver that turns them into arrow geometry for DisplayGeometry (drawn by both renderers; no Qt/VTK); and the Vectors window and editor. core/measure.py Distances and bond angles between displayed instances (AtomId), computed from the structure's coordinates and cell only, plus the session state of the measurement modes. No Qt or VTK; nothing is saved in projects. core/lighting.py resolve_lighting turns an environment's relative light values into a world-space LightingRig (key, fill, reflection panel) for an output camera and a displayed geometry. Shared by the POV writer, the live view, and the Lighting Setup window; nothing is stored. No Qt or VTK. viewport/qt_viewport.py The VTK/PyVistaQt adapter. It consumes shared geometry, exchanges Camera objects, draws overlays, and reports clicks. VTK objects stay here. Its two scene lights come from the resolved rig. viewport/interactor.py The PyVistaQt interactor used by both views. Its render() draws before it returns on every platform (PyVistaQt alone defers the drawing to the event loop on macOS), which the start-of-render bookkeeping (output camera, lights, frame overlay) relies on. viewport/lighting_view.py The Lighting Setup overview: a second VTK window with its own camera that draws the rig and reports main-light handle drags as angles. Its graphics never reach the main view, picking, fitting, or exports. render/pov_writer.py Pure text export of shared geometry/camera into POV-Ray 3.7 and INI output. No renderer process or display needed. render/jobs.py, render/povray.py Isolated job directories, discovery, synchronous execution, results, and image copying. The caller owns cleanup. POV-Ray is found through the saved setting, YCRYSTAL_POVRAY, PATH, and on Windows the installation of POV-Ray for Windows (registry, Program Files); its standard include files are located from the executable's installation, never from a fixed system path alone. render/povray.py holds every renderer platform difference: POV-Ray for Windows (pvengine64.exe) is a window program that gets /EXIT /NR +GAscene.log, starts minimised, writes its messages to a log file, is kept from taking the keyboard focus, and is not started while another copy of it that keeps a single instance is open, or while it would ask at start-up whether to download its missing editor. gui/native.py, desktop.py The platform-dependent choices of the interface, kept in one place: modifier-key names in help texts, the folder for personal-material thumbnails, the taskbar identity and the program file filter on Windows, and the menu entry of --install-desktop (Linux: freedesktop launcher; Windows: Start-menu shortcut and .ycrystal file type under HKEY_CURRENT_USER; none on macOS). Each takes the platform as a parameter, so every branch is tested on any system. windows_shortcut.py, scripts/install-windows.ps1 Windows only. Shortcuts (.lnk) with the application id that the window sets, so that its taskbar button belongs to the Start-menu entry, written through the shell's COM interfaces with ctypes (no extra package). The PowerShell installation script (the developer installation) installs Python and POV-Ray for Windows with winget where missing, .venv, the Start-menu entry Ycrystal (development), and runs the renderer check; Windows CI runs it. packaging/windows/ The graphical Windows installer (recommended for users): a PyInstaller specification that freezes ycrystal.app.main into Ycrystal.exe (window) and ycrystal-cli.exe (command line) sharing one folder, an Inno Setup script, the build script, and a coexistence check. The packaged program runs the same code; desktop.is_packaged() (sys.frozen) gives it its own application id and refuses --install-desktop. Its shortcut, application id, and file type differ from the developer installation's, and each side removes only its own (see Windows installer). core/export.py, render/formats.py, gui/export_dialog.py Image export (FR-EXPORT-01): formats, publication sizes, and mm/px/dpi arithmetic without Qt; writing the POV-Ray PNG as PNG (resolution chunk added, pixels untouched), JPEG, or PDF (QPdfWriter, lossless) through a checked .part file; and the Render Image dialog. All formats share one POV-Ray job; only the last step differs. core/legend.py, render/legend.py, gui/panels/legend_panel.py Element legend (FR-LEGEND-01): LegendSettings (in SceneSettings.legend) and the entries, read from DisplayGeometry so the markers have the drawn colours (no Qt); one QPainter layout and painter (QtGui only, no window) that draws the legend onto the rendered PNG in finish_job, draws the live view's overlay, and gives the frame region it leaves free for fitting; and the Legend tab. The legend is a 2D layer: the POV-Ray scene and the geometry never contain it. render/process.py Asynchronous QProcess adapter. Needs a running Qt event loop (QCoreApplication is enough), not a window. POV-Ray for Windows runs instead as a subprocess.Popen checked by a timer (PySide6's QProcess cannot start a program minimised), and the program's own runs of it take turns, since only one copy can render at a time. render/selftest.py, render/imagecheck.py Small renderer diagnostic and analytic/image alignment measurements. Runs without a display, but the diagnostic invokes POV-Ray.

items.title: Shared contracts
items.text:
Both VTK and POV-Ray consume the same resolved geometry. A displayed atom is identified by (source_index, (na, nb, nc)), with position equal to the input position plus the offset multiplied by the row-vector lattice. Hiding removes that ID from the shared geometry; it leaves all scientific data intact. Selection holds IDs rather than array row indices because rows change when atoms disappear.

The camera reference defines direction, handedness, half-height scale, and pixels. Two cameras exist in the GUI: VTK's camera for the whole view, and the output camera for the image inside the output frame (same orientation and centre, parallel scale multiplied by the frame-to-view height ratio). Export, preview, render, and projects use the output camera with the explicit output size; resizing the window keeps it, so a resize is not a change of the figure (no new scene revision, and a preview stays current). POV-Ray export writes explicit camera vectors and may move the orthographic eye backward to put all geometry in front of it without changing projection. VTK uses the key and fill lights of the shared lighting rig and a material's live approximation; axes, the frame, and selection are overlays only.

Materials, environments, and lighting are presets (ycrystal.presets: JSON manifests in presets/materials/ and presets/environments/, and presets/lighting.json). A material manifest names its declaration kind (finish, pigment, texture, or material), the native POV-Ray identifiers and the include files that declare them, whether it keeps the element colour, its texture space, and a live approximation. Scene settings store material ids at three levels (default, element, displayed atom); build_geometry resolves them per atom (DisplayGeometry.materials) together with the colours, so the POV writer and the viewport draw the same choice. The environment is a plain dataclass that a preset initialises; the writer turns it into a background, a frame-aligned backdrop (gradient or sky, unlit through an empty light_group), a tilted floor, camera-relative lights, and an optional no_image reflection panel. Gallery thumbnails are genuine POV-Ray renders of fixed scenes (ycrystal.render.thumbnails), shipped with the package; index.json records a digest of each thumbnail scene, and a test fails when a recipe changes without re-rendering (scripts/render_thumbnails.py). Previews and final renders run as QProcess jobs; previews go through a RenderQueue (one process, newest request wins) and are tagged with the window's scene revision so that stale results are discarded.

Projects embed the structure and provenance, plus camera and presentation state. They do not store the machine's renderer path or last-used directory; those belong to QSettings (as do gallery favourites, the handle visibility, and nothing else). Schema 5 stores repetitions, cell mode, bond rules, atom size and element radii, the default material with element and atom overrides, element colours, the full environment (background, floor, lighting), and the explicit output size; the saved camera is the output camera for that size (as it already was for schemas 1–4). Schema-1 projects load with bonds off, schema-1/2 projects with the satin material, and schema-1–3 projects without floor, backdrop, overrides, or new lighting, to preserve their appearance.

Styles (ycrystal.io.style) are the presentation part of a project in the same JSON layout, plus the source's element sequence. apply_style is a pure function from (style, target structure, current settings) to new settings and user notes; the window applies the result as one undo command. Element-keyed settings transfer to elements the target contains; atom-keyed settings (per-atom materials, hidden IDs) transfer only when the element sequence is identical.

All figure changes go through SceneSettingsCommand, which carries scene settings and, optionally, the environment and the output size, so a style import, a handle drag, or a size change is one undo step; consecutive commands with the same merge key (spin boxes) merge. Camera navigation stays outside the undo stack.

Supercell handles and axis-constrained rotation live in the viewport. The input filter routes left drags that start on a handle, or any left drag while a rotation axis is set, to the viewport instead of VTK's trackball; clicks are still detected on release. Handles are 2D overlays recomputed before every render from the camera, the cell, and the (preview) repetitions; the drag emits preview and final repetitions, and the window builds the geometry once on release. Axis rotation uses Camera.rotate_about, so the scene turns about a fixed world axis while the structure's coordinates stay unchanged.

items.title: Extension points
items.text:
• Add future readers in io/readers.py, producing Structure and provenance. Keep questions/errors GUI-free, wire the format into GUI/CLI detection, and add equivalence/rejection fixtures. Do not put parsing logic in the viewport.
  • Add material or environment presets as JSON manifests in src/ycrystal/presets/ (declaration kind, recipe or native identifier, includes, live approximation, provenance), render their thumbnails with scripts/render_thumbnails.py, inspect them, and commit manifest, PNG, and index.json together. tests/test_presets.py renders every entry individually; native identifiers must exist in POV-Ray 3.7's standard include files. Assignment selects presets and never modifies coordinates.
  • Extend rendering options in render/pov_writer.py and their scene/output models; extend job lifecycle in render/jobs.py / render/process.py. Keep GUI orchestration in the interface. The output frame is the shared aspect contract: keep exported, previewed, and rendered images defined by the output camera and output size.
  • Keep scientific editing separate from the existing display repetitions and bonds. Display expansion always starts from the original structure, and is undoable. Future scientific editing needs explicit data-layer operations and provenance. core.compare.supercell currently exists for reader comparisons and discards labels, flags, and metadata.
  • New presentation settings belong in SceneSettings or Environment (so that undo, projects, and styles pick them up), with a schema bump in io/project.py, a transfer rule in io/style.py, and a line in the undo-coverage test.

Read the curated reference and documentation convention before extending an interface. The repository's contributor guide covers application tests and maintenance tooling.

items.title: Feature comparison with VESTA, OVITO, and CView
items.text: A factual comparison for the software paper (FR-VALIDATION-01). Read the method first: the Ycrystal column was tested in this repository, while the other three columns come only from documentation and nothing in them was tested.

items.title: Method
items.text:
• Sources. The official documentation of each program, read on 17 November 2026. Every entry below has a quotation and a link in the sources.
  • VESTA: the online manual (title page dated 10 August 2022) and download page (stable 3.5.8; development 3.90.9a).
  • OVITO: user manual and Python reference of version 3.17.2 (released 2 November 2026).
  • CView: documentation of version 1.3.1, the project repository, and the abstract of the 2026 J. Appl. Cryst. article. The article's full text could not be retrieved, so only its abstract was read.
  • Nothing was installed or tested for VESTA, OVITO, or CView. Entries mean:
  • documented: the documentation describes the feature;
  • not found: the consulted documentation does not mention it. This does not mean the program lacks it;
  • planned: the project lists it as future work;
  • removed: the change log says so.
  • Ycrystal entries were verified by the tests named, on the version in this repository at the time (0.4.0.dev0, 17 November 2026; released as 0.4.0).
  • Features change between versions. This table describes the versions listed above and must be checked again before publication.

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
Feature Ycrystal (tested) VESTA (documented) OVITO (documented) CView (documented) Ray-traced rendering Yes: POV-Ray 3.7, an external program that must be installed (Y1) Not found; uses OpenGL (V1) Yes: built-in Tachyon, OSPRay, VisRTX (Pro in the desktop program). The POV-Ray renderer was removed in 3.0.0, the POV-Ray scene exporter in 3.16.0 (O1) Not found; Cairo and OpenGL (C1) Vector graphics export of the 3D scene No: PDF export holds a raster image (Y2) Yes: EPS, PDF, PS, SVG, with stated limits (V2) Not found; image output is PNG, JPEG, TIFF (O2) Yes: PDF, SVG (C2) High-resolution raster images Yes: a chosen pixel size (16–8000 px on the command line, PNG); PNG, JPEG, PDF from the window, with physical size and dpi (Y3) Yes: scale factor beyond the screen size (V3) Yes: output size in pixels (O3) Yes: PNG (2000 × 1500 default), TIFF with dpi (C3) Reusable style or template for other structures Yes: .ycstyle files, in the window and from the command line (Y4) Yes: .vesta file with linked structure as template; style.ini (V4) Yes: session states as templates, "Pick new file", colour and radius themes (O4) Not found; display preferences are saved (C4) Explicit mapping of one element's appearance to another element Yes (Y5) Not found Not found; themes match type names (O5) Not found Images without a window, and batch processing Yes: --render, --export-pov, --batch manifests, no display needed (Y6) Command-line image export (-export_img), listed among commands that work only with the GUI window; batch not found (V5) Yes: Python module and ovitos, headless on Linux, batch processing (O6) Planned (C5) CIF input Yes, without partial occupancy or overlapping sites (Y7) Yes, fractional coordinates only (V6) Yes, one data block, fractional coordinates (O7) Yes (C6) VASP POSCAR/CONTCAR input Yes, VASP 5 and 4 (elements asked for VASP 4) (Y7) Yes; needs OUTCAR for element symbols (V6) POSCAR yes; CONTCAR not named (O7) Yes (C6) Quantum ESPRESSO pw.x input Yes, every ibrav of pw.x (Y7) Not found (XSF written by QE is read) (V6) Yes, ibrav = 1, 2, 3, −3 only (O7) Yes (C6) Atom-attached vectors (magnetic moments) Yes, entered in the window; no import from calculation output (Y8) Yes (V7) Yes, arrow glyphs, centred option (O8) Planned (C7) One file with structure and all view settings Yes: .ycrystal, self-contained (structure, pictures, custom materials) (Y9) Yes: .vesta holds structure and graphic settings; volumetric data stay external (V8) Session state with pipeline, viewport, render settings; whether atom data are inside is not stated (O9) Only for charge-density figures (.cview.json) (C8) Provenance record of a rendered image (versions, checksums) Yes (Y10) Not found Not found Not found Licence; systems MIT; Linux, macOS (Apple silicon), and Windows 11 from source (Windows tested on one computer); public repository (Y11) Free for academic and non-commercial use, closed source; Windows, macOS, Linux (V9) OVITO Basic and the Python module MIT, OVITO Pro proprietary; Windows, Linux, macOS (Apple silicon) (O10) MIT; Windows, macOS, Linux (Flatpak) (C9)

Things Ycrystal does not do, in contrast to at least one of the others according to their documentation: vector graphics, polyhedra, volumetric data and isosurfaces (VESTA (V2); CView (C1)), and analysis pipelines or trajectories (OVITO (O4); CView (C1)). Ycrystal is a figure tool for periodic crystal structures. The case for it rests on the integrated workflow: a style designed in the window, transferred with an explicit element mapping, deterministic views, batch rendering, and self-contained snapshots with provenance. It does not rest on any single feature being unique.

items.title: Ycrystal (tested in this repository)
items.text:
• (Y1) POV-Ray 3.7 is found and checked by ycrystal --check-renderer. Rendering tests: tests/test_render_alignment.py, tests/test_validation.py.
  • (Y2) FR-EXPORT-01: the PDF holds the POV-Ray raster image (rendering guide). Tests: tests/test_export.py, tests/test_gui_export.py.
  • (Y3) --width/--height 16–8000 px; Render Image… in the window. Tests: tests/test_release.py, tests/test_export.py.
  • (Y4) FR-STYLE-CLI-01, File ▸ Import Style…. Tests: tests/test_style.py, tests/test_validation.py::test_styles_never_change_the_scientific_data.
  • (Y5) FR-STYLE-MAP-01, --element-map. Tests: tests/test_style.py, tests/test_gui_style_map.py.
  • (Y6) FR-BATCH-01. Tests: tests/test_batch_manifest.py; tests in CI that load no window toolkit and need no display.
  • (Y7) Supported file formats and Quantum ESPRESSO lattices (every ibrav of pw.x, compared with pw.x's output). Tests: tests/test_readers.py, tests/test_qe_lattice.py.
  • (Y8) FR-VECTOR-01. Tests: tests/test_vectors.py, tests/test_validation.py.
  • (Y9) Project schema 8 with ZIP packages. Tests: tests/test_project.py, tests/test_background_image.py, tests/test_reproducibility.py.
  • (Y10) FR-REPRO-01 (reproducible figures). Tests: tests/test_reproducibility.py.
  • (Y11) LICENSE; support matrix; handoff for the verified platforms.

items.title: VESTA (documentation only)
items.text:
• (V1) "Because VESTA utilizes OpenGL technology, the use of an OpenGL-capable graphics processing unit (GPU) is highly recommended but not always mandatory." POV-Ray, ray tracing, Tachyon, and OSPRay are not mentioned anywhere in the manual. Chapter 3
  • (V2) "Images of structural and volumetric data displayed in the Graphics Area of the Main Window can be saved as vector images." The formats are EPS, PDF, PS, and SVG. "Colors of isosurfaces and sections colored according to volumetric data cannot be represented with vector image formats. Translucent polygons of polyhedra, lattice planes, and isosurfaces become opaque in all the formats except for PDF." 18.5.3 Graphic images
  • (V3) "The image size of the exported graphics files is scaled up as a multiple of the size of the Graphics Area … VESTA can export huge images that exceed the maximum width and height of the viewport." (same section); -export_img … scale=n (chapter 17).
  • (V4) "This option is useful in preparing a file, *.vesta, with the VESTA format as a template file for setting objects and overall appearances." 6.3.6; "style.ini — Default file for styles of the graphic scene" (18.1).
  • (V5) "-export_img options file … Export an image to file. Image format will be automatically recognized by file extension." Chapter 17. The command appears under "17.4 Commands that only work with GUI window"; the section "17.2 Commands that only work with -nogui mode" lists no command (checked on 17 November 2026).
  • (V6) "Crystallographic Information File (CIF; *.cif)"; "Cartesian coordinates included in CIFs cannot be input with VESTA". VASP files including POSCAR and CONTCAR "must accompany another file, OUTCAR, to display structural models". Quantum ESPRESSO is mentioned only as a program that writes XSF. 18.5.1 Input
  • (V7) "These arrows serve to represent magnetic moments or directions of static and dynamic displacements of atoms." 9.1 Vectors on Atoms
  • (V8) "Files with the VESTA format contains all the structural data and graphic settings whereas volumetric data are not directly recorded in *.vesta but imported from external files." 18.5.2
  • (V9) "This software is distributed free of charge for academic, scientific, educational, and non-commercial users"; its source code is "not open to the public" (licence). "VESTA runs on Microsoft Windows …, macOS, and Linux." (chapter 2)

items.title: OVITO 3.17.2 (documentation only)
items.text:
• (O1) Rendering engines: Tachyon, OSPRay, and VisRTX ("pro" in the desktop program) (rendering). Change log (new features):
  • 2.8.0: "Added the POV-Ray rendering backend and the POV-Ray scene file exporter."
  • 3.0.0: "Removed the POV-Ray rendering engine (POV-Ray scene file export is still available)."
  • 3.16.0: "Removed POV-Ray scene exporter."
  • (O2) Viewport.render_image: "Supported output formats are: .png, .jpeg, and .tiff." (ovito.vis) Data plots can be saved as PDF; no vector export of the 3D scene was found.
  • (O3) "Output image size — Sets the width and height of the rendered image or movie in pixels." (render settings)
  • (O4) "Create a template to apply the same data analysis pipeline and camera setup to multiple simulations." (miscellaneous); "Pick new file — Selects a different file as input for the pipeline while preserving existing modifiers." (external file); theme files .ovito-theme (particle settings).
  • (O5) "Only types present in the imported file will be updated…" (particle settings).
  • (O6) "OVITO's rendering engine works headless on Linux: it requires no desktop session, display server, or X11/Wayland connection" (installation); "ideal for batch-processing large numbers of simulation files" (Python introduction).
  • (O7) CIF: one data block, fractional coordinates (CIF); POSCAR, standard and direct format (POSCAR); Quantum ESPRESSO pw.x input, "Bravais lattice types other than ibrav=1, 2, 3, and -3 are not supported" (Quantum ESPRESSO).
  • (O8) "This visual element shows arrow glyphs to visualize a local vectorial property associated with each particle" (vectors).
  • (O9) "You can save your current session, including the data pipeline, viewport settings, render settings, and other configurations, to a .ovito state file" (miscellaneous).
  • (O10) "OVITO Basic is published … under the terms of the MIT License. OVITO Pro is proprietary software"; the Python module is MIT-licensed (licences). Windows, Linux, and "macOS 14.4+, Apple Silicon" (installation).

items.title: CView 1.3.1 (documentation and article abstract only)
items.text:
• (C1) "The main viewer uses CPU-based Cairo rendering … Two optional windows — the 3D CHGCAR isosurface view and the MD/relaxation Trajectory Player — use OpenGL 3.3" (README).
  • (C2) "All three-dimensional content is rendered through Cairo as resolution-independent vector graphics, so that figures exported as PDF or SVG from the interactive viewer drop directly into a publication without rasterization artefacts." (abstract, doi:10.1107/S1600576726009003)
  • (C3) "PNG Image: Renders a high-resolution raster image (default resolution: 2000×1500 pixels)." (documentation)
  • (C4) "How polyhedra are drawn is a saved preference" (documentation); no style or template file was found.
  • (C5) To Do, Automation: "Command-line conversion, standardization, k-path and figure export without opening the window." (documentation, listed as planned)
  • (C6) "It reads and writes … CIF, VASP POSCAR and CHGCAR, Quantum ESPRESSO input files, extended XYZ" (abstract); file table with POSCAR, CONTCAR, and pw.x input (documentation).
  • (C7) To Do, Visualization: "Magnetic moments as arrows, read from VASP (MAGMOM, OUTCAR), Quantum Espresso and magnetic CIF." (documentation, listed as planned)
  • (C8) "A scene file (.cview.json) is saved next to every figure" (charge-density figures); "The Atom Instances tab provides session-only cosmetic overrides" (documentation).
  • (C9) "CView is open-source software licensed under the MIT Licence"; Windows 10/11, macOS (Intel and Apple silicon), Linux as Flatpak (documentation). The abstract lists .deb and .rpm packages; release 1.3.1 provides .exe, .dmg, and .flatpak.

items.title: Documentation workflow
items.text: Ycrystal uses a small Zensical + mkdocstrings-python site. Navigation separates user guides, developer guides, and a curated source reference, inspired by quacc's documentation. Signatures and parameter descriptions come from source rather than duplicate Markdown tables. NumPy parsing is explicit, allow_inspection = false disables runtime import fallback, and members are listed explicitly to avoid inherited Qt/VTK interfaces.

items.title: Install, preview, and build
items.text:
From the checkout root, add documentation tools to a development environment:

.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[dev,docs]" -c constraints.txt -c docs/requirements.txt
.venv/bin/zensical serve

Open the local address printed by serve (normally http://127.0.0.1:8000). To build the checked HTML into site/:

.venv/bin/zensical build --clean --strict

For a lightweight documentation-only environment, the application and its Qt/VTK/ASE dependencies are unnecessary. Use the tested documentation lock:

/usr/bin/python3 -m venv .venv-docs
.venv-docs/bin/python -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
.venv-docs/bin/zensical serve
.venv-docs/bin/zensical build --clean --strict

uv venv --python /usr/bin/python3.12 .venv-docs and uv pip install --python .venv-docs/bin/python -r docs/requirements.txt are equivalent. Zensical statically reads src/ through Griffe. A build must not create a QApplication, window, OpenGL context, or renderer process. site/, .cache/, and .venv-docs/ are ignored. Do not commit generated HTML to source branches.

Strict builds reject warnings, broken local links/anchors, and unresolved reference links. Use --clean in verification to avoid cached results. A dedicated docs CI job uses this same build in a docs-only environment, alongside the existing lint and application-test jobs. To update the documentation lock, resolve the two requirements in the docs extra in a fresh docs-only Python 3.12 environment, freeze its packages into docs/requirements.txt, and repeat the build and broken-reference probes.

items.title: Writing docstrings
items.text:
Use NumPy-style sections for meaningful public interfaces. Type annotations remain the source of types: describe meaning, units, shape, defaults, valid values, copying, and side effects in prose. Include only useful sections: summary, Parameters, Returns/Yields, Raises, Attributes, Notes, Examples, and See Also. A one-line summary is enough for a trivial method; do not add empty sections to callbacks or tests.

For a real example, read Camera.project: its docstring explains Å inputs reshaped to (K, 3), pixel dimensions, an output of shape (K, 2), the top-left origin, and the absence of clipping. The signature supplies the annotations. Its class example projects the origin and unit x/y offsets to exact pixels, demonstrating the contract rather than restating parameter names.

Use Attributes for data models and explain immutability precisely: Structure copies arrays into read-only storage, but its metadata dictionary is mutable. Describe failure results separately from exceptions and say who owns temporary files. Keep scientific data changes distinct from presentation changes.

The NumPy convention and explicitly enabled Ruff D rules live in pyproject.toml. Tests are exempt; GUI methods are exempt from mandatory method docstrings, while their substantive interfaces are documented. Existing pre-commit hooks run Ruff.

For every interface or GUI behavior change, update its docstrings, relevant user instructions, and executable examples in the same change. Verify against the implementation and tests, and record discrepancies in PROGRESS.md; do not change behavior just to fit the prose. Curate new API entries in docs/reference/ and zensical.toml. Do not expose private helpers or inherited Qt/VTK methods.

items.title: Check examples
items.text:
Display-independent docstring examples (requires the application dependencies, not a display or POV-Ray):

.venv/bin/python -m doctest src/ycrystal/core/structure.py src/ycrystal/core/scene.py src/ycrystal/core/camera.py src/ycrystal/core/picking.py src/ycrystal/io/readers.py src/ycrystal/io/project.py src/ycrystal/presets/__init__.py src/ycrystal/render/jobs.py
.venv/bin/python scripts/docs_examples.py
.venv/bin/ruff check .
.venv/bin/ruff format --check .

Run these at the checkout root because the reader examples use tests/fixtures/. The second command exercises scientific/display identities, projection, structure import, project save/reopen, and POV text export; outputs use a temporary directory. The Python examples page separates these from renderer/GUI examples. Run the existing application tests as documented in the contributor guide.

items.title: Visual assets
items.text:
docs/assets/perovskite.png is an actual POV-Ray render of the built-in sample, not a UI mockup. It is intentionally tracked as a small documentation asset. From the checkout root, regenerate it with application dependencies and POV-Ray installed:

.venv/bin/python scripts/docs_render_example.py

The script prepares the default 15-ball SrTiO3 geometry and default camera fitted to 640 × 400, renders synchronously, copies the PNG to docs/assets/perovskite.png, and removes its temporary job directory in finally. It replaces the asset without asking. Use --output artifacts/docs/perovskite.png to inspect a candidate first; --povray /usr/bin/povray overrides discovery. PNG bytes can vary with renderer versions; inspect framing and appearance before committing. No display is needed.

For full-window screenshots and camera-alignment evidence, use the existing scripts/m0_evidence.py on an X11/OpenGL desktop with POV-Ray. Those outputs stay under ignored artifacts/. Do not present them as the tutorial's default view: that script uses the triclinic sample and mouse navigation.

items.title: Publication
items.text:
The documentation is hosted at https://ymatterlab.github.io/ycrystal/. site_url in zensical.toml includes the repository's /ycrystal/ base path. Source Markdown and configuration stay on main; the gh-pages branch contains only the generated site and a .nojekyll file, with its own history.

The publishing workflow in .github/workflows/documentation.yml runs on pushes to main and can also be run manually from the Actions tab. It installs the documentation lock, builds with zensical build --clean --strict, and uses the locked ghp-import to update gh-pages without force-pushing. The job has contents: write and pages: write permissions. Because pushes using GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger a Pages build, the final step explicitly requests one through the GitHub Pages API. Pull requests continue to run the existing read-only strict documentation check in ci.yml.

In repository Settings → Pages, the source is Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). Generated HTML belongs on that branch only; edit the Markdown or source docstrings on main and let the workflow rebuild. Check navigation, API anchors, search, and assets at the deployed URL after changing the publishing configuration.

For a manual update from a clean checkout of main with documentation tools installed and GitHub write access:

git fetch origin gh-pages
.venv-docs/bin/zensical build --clean --strict
.venv-docs/bin/ghp-import --no-jekyll --branch gh-pages --push site

These commands update the publication branch without switching the working tree.

items.title: Python examples
items.text: These are evolving developer interfaces. Run from a source checkout with the application dependencies installed; see the generated reference for detailed parameter contracts. The documentation build itself executes none of these examples.

items.title: Without a display or renderer
items.text:
This is a short interactive example from the scene reference:

>>> from ycrystal.core.samples import perovskite_srtio3
>>> from ycrystal.core.scene import SceneSettings, build_geometry
>>> structure = perovskite_srtio3()
>>> geometry = build_geometry(structure)
>>> len(structure), len(geometry)
(5, 15)
>>> corner = (0, (1, 1, 1))
>>> hidden = build_geometry(structure, SceneSettings(hidden=frozenset({corner})))
>>> len(hidden), hidden.hidden_count, hidden.index_of(corner)
(14, 1, None)

Display repetitions and periodic bonds are available through the same model:

>>> expanded = build_geometry(structure, SceneSettings(repetitions=(2, 2, 2)))
>>> len(expanded), len(expanded.bonds)
(71, 192)

Scientific coordinates are unchanged. The arrays produced by build_geometry are read-only, and the image offset is relative to input positions rather than wrapped positions. See scene and geometry.

Materials and environments are chosen by preset id. Scene settings carry the default material and per-element or per-atom overrides; the geometry resolves one material per displayed atom, and the environment carries background, floor, and lighting:

>>> from ycrystal.presets import environment_from_preset
>>> styled = SceneSettings(material="glass").with_element_material("Ti", "gold")
>>> geometry = build_geometry(structure, styled)
>>> sorted(set(geometry.materials))
['glass', 'gold']
>>> studio = environment_from_preset("studio_white")
>>> studio.floor, studio.lighting
(True, 'studio')

See material, environment, and lighting presets and the appearance guide.

Execute the complete lightweight example with:

.venv/bin/python scripts/docs_examples.py

The script also projects the focal point, imports tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif, saves/reopens a project, and exports .pov/.ini text in a temporary directory, including a glass scene on a transparent background and a white-studio scene with element and atom material overrides, and applies that scene's style to MgB2. It checks the expected outcomes and cleans its files. It does not import the viewport or run POV-Ray. Source docstrings contain further runnable examples; see the doctest command.

items.title: With POV-Ray, without a display
items.text:
.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer --povray /usr/bin/povray
.venv/bin/python scripts/docs_render_example.py --output artifacts/docs/perovskite.png

The second command demonstrates the synchronous job lifecycle: prepare_job → run_job → inspect RenderResult.ok/message → copy_result → job.cleanup() in finally. The result's image_path is inside the temporary job directory and becomes invalid on cleanup. Keep the copied destination instead. Discovery and filesystem setup can raise; ordinary renderer failures return a result. See rendering reference.

items.title: With a display and OpenGL
items.text:
.venv/bin/ycrystal --sample perovskite

Follow the first-figure tutorial. Creating MainWindow or StructureViewport needs QApplication, a display, and OpenGL. Asynchronous RenderProcess needs a running Qt event loop but no window; it leaves job cleanup to the caller. Its finished signal delivers one RenderResult for success or failure. The GUI copies a successful result and then cleans the job.

items.title: Independent evaluation checklist
items.text:
For Computer Programs articles, the Journal of Applied Crystallography expects the program's usefulness and the adequacy of its documentation to be shown by at least two independent users: users who are not colleagues or close collaborators of the authors. The submission asks for brief reports from them, which are used in the review and not published. The journal also expects a web page with documentation and downloads, and anonymous access for referees. Sources: the notes for authors and the submission instructions, as summarised by a search on 17 November 2026; the pages themselves refused automated access, so check the current wording before submitting.

This checklist is what the authors send to each evaluator. It is a set of tasks and questions, not code.

The answers must be the evaluators' own: record them as received, and do not edit, summarise, or complete them on an evaluator's behalf. Nothing in this repository is an evaluation result until an evaluator has written it.

items.title: For the authors, before sending
items.text:
• [ ] Choose two evaluators who did not take part in developing Ycrystal and are not close collaborators of the authors, ideally on different systems (Linux, macOS).
  • [ ] Give access to the repository at a tagged version, and write that version here: ________.
  • [ ] Send this page and nothing else as instructions. Do not demonstrate the program beforehand; how the documentation alone works is part of the evaluation.
  • [ ] Agree how the answers will be returned (a signed document or an e-mail) and that they will be given to the journal for the review with the evaluator's name.
  • [ ] Referees need anonymous access to the program: the repository is public, so they can clone it without an account; confirm that this still holds before submitting.

items.title: For the evaluator
items.text:
Please work alone, with the documentation of the repository (README.md and docs/), and note where you got stuck, even if you found a way around it. Expect about two to three hours. Use your own structures where you can; the repository's tests/fixtures/ and examples/ folders have some to start with.

About you and your computer.

  • [ ] Your field and how you usually make crystal-structure figures (programs used): ________
  • [ ] Operating system and version, processor: ________
  • [ ] ycrystal --version and ycrystal --check-renderer output: ________

Tasks. For each task note the time it took, whether it worked, and any problem.

  • [ ] 1. Install Ycrystal and POV-Ray following the installation guide (docs/guide/install.md).
  • [ ] 2. Make a figure in the window. Open a structure file (CIF, POSCAR, or Quantum ESPRESSO input), choose the repetitions, materials, a background, and a view, then render a PNG (Render ▸ Render Image…). Follow docs/guide/first-figure.md if you like.
  • [ ] 3. Reuse the look. Save the look as a style (File ▸ Export Style…) and apply it to a second structure with File ▸ Import Style…. Then apply the supplied style examples/publication/styles/paper.ycstyle to a material of your own. If a structure has other elements than the style, try the element mapping in that dialog.
  • [ ] 4. From the command line. Apply the same style to a third structure with ycrystal FILE --style STYLE.ycstyle --render OUT.png, with a view such as --view c (docs/guide/examples.md).
  • [ ] 5. A series. Copy examples/publication/gallery.json (or examples/batch-series.json), change it to render three of your own structures with your style, and run it with --batch … --output-dir ….
  • [ ] 6. Reproduce a figure. Render one figure with --save-project FIGURE.ycrystal, move or delete its structure file and style, and render the snapshot again (docs/guide/reproducibility.md). Compare the two images. Then re-open the snapshot in the window (File ▸ Open…) and check that it looks as rendered.
  • [ ] 7. Optional. Send the snapshot to the other evaluator or a colleague and ask them to render it on their computer.

Questions. Please answer in your own words.

  1. Which tasks worked without help from anyone? Where did the documentation not answer your question, or answer it wrongly?
  2. Which messages (warnings, errors) were unclear?
  3. Did the images look as you expected? Did anything look wrong (positions, colours, cut-off figures, lighting)?
  4. For your own research, what would you use Ycrystal for, if anything? What is missing for you?
  5. Compared with the programs you use now, what is easier, harder, or impossible?
  6. Any bugs, crashes, or data that would not open (please attach the file if you may share it).
  7. Would you recommend Ycrystal to a colleague, and for what?

Signature. Name, affiliation, date, and a statement that you have no close collaboration with the authors: ________

items.title: Proposed manuscript figures
items.text:
A proposal for the four figures of a Journal of Applied Crystallography Computer Programs article (FR-GALLERY-01). It says which images exist, where they come from, and which still have to be made.

  • Rendered images are produced by Ycrystal and POV-Ray with python scripts/make_gallery.py, from the inputs in examples/publication/. See the gallery, which also has the figure-methods table.
  • Other panels are explicitly marked as illustrations, screenshots, or plots of recorded data.
  • No mock-ups. No image here is a mock-up of a render.

Each caption separates what is implemented and verified from what is a limitation.

items.title: Figure 1: from a structure file to a ray-traced figure
items.text:
Panel Content Source Status a Schematic of the workflow (below) Illustration, to be drawn by the authors To do b The Ycrystal window with srtio3.ycrystal from the gallery open Screenshot of the real program on a desktop To do (needs a display; scripts/m0_evidence.py shows how the M0 screenshots were taken) c The POV-Ray image of the same project srtio3.png from the gallery Available

Schematic content, from the architecture:

  1. A structure file (CIF, POSCAR/CONTCAR, or Quantum ESPRESSO input) is read with ASE and checked: partial occupancy and unsupported settings are refused.
  2. One shared geometry (atoms, periodic images, bonds, cell edges, vector arrows) is drawn by both the interactive OpenGL view (VTK) and the POV-Ray scene writer.
  3. POV-Ray 3.7 renders the final image.
  4. Around this core sit the reusable parts:
  5. styles (.ycstyle) with optional element mapping;
  6. view policies;
  7. batch manifests;
  8. snapshots with provenance records.

Draft caption. Ycrystal's workflow. (a) A structure is read and checked once. The interactive view and the POV-Ray writer draw the same geometry, so the framing chosen on screen is the framing of the ray-traced figure. A look designed in the window can be saved as a style and reused for other structures, also from the command line and in batch series. Every figure can be saved as a self-contained project with a provenance record. (b) The window. (c) The POV-Ray image of the project shown in (b).

Limitations to state. - The interactive view approximates POV-Ray's materials and lighting; only the POV-Ray image is final. Background pictures appear in the live view as their average colour only. - Rendering needs a separately installed POV-Ray 3.7.

items.title: Figure 2: lighting and materials, with geometry and camera fixed
items.text:
Panel Image What changes a srtio3.png Paper style: satin, white background, soft lighting b srtio3-cover-light.png Only the environment: dark studio, reflective floor, brighter point key light with hard shadows c srtio3-cover.png Environment and materials: ceramic Sr, chrome Ti, ruby-glass O

How (b) and (c) are made. They are rendered from the snapshot of (a) with --style styles/cover.ycstyle, applying the environment part for (b) and the appearance and environment parts for (c). A snapshot keeps its camera and image size. The structure, the camera, and the image size are therefore identical in all three panels. tests/test_gallery.py checks this from the snapshots.

Draft caption. The same SrTiO3 cell, camera, and image size rendered with POV-Ray 3.7 in three looks. (a) A restrained style for a journal page. (b) The same materials in a dark studio with a reflective floor; the reflections in the floor and the cast shadows are ray-traced. (c) As (b), with chrome Ti, ruby-glass O, and ceramic Sr: reflection and refraction are computed by POV-Ray, not painted on.

Limitations to state. - Materials are a presentation choice. Chrome Ti or glassy O says nothing about the physical properties of the atoms. - Glass and reflections raise the render time a lot: in the benchmark, glass in a studio took about 30 times as long as the same scene in satin.

items.title: Figure 3: one style, several compositions, one command
items.text:
Panel Image Note a srtio3.png Source composition of the style b bazro3-mapped.png Element mapping Sr → Ba, Ti → Zr; the same physical scale as (a) c mgb2.png No element settings for Mg or B: background, lighting, size, and default material transfer; a warning records the rest d kyanite.png A real triclinic (P-1) structure, COD 1008755 (de Rango et al., 1966) e afm-synthetic.png Synthetic two-site cell with hand-assigned moments of ±2.2 μB; not a real material

How they are made. All five figures are rendered by one command, ycrystal --batch examples/publication/gallery.json. Each is saved as a snapshot with a provenance record, and the gallery script renders every snapshot again after the inputs are deleted.

Draft caption. One style applied with one command to five structures. (a) SrTiO3, for which the style was designed. (b) BaZrO3 with an explicit element mapping, Sr → Ba and Ti → Zr, so that the A and B sites keep their colours; (a) and (b) share a visible height of 9 Å, so the larger BaZrO3 cell appears larger. (c) MgB2 receives the style's environment, size, and default material; its elements keep their default colours. (d) Kyanite, Al₂SiO₅ (P-1; COD 1008755), drawn with its Al–O (1.81–1.99 Å) and Si–O (1.62–1.64 Å) bonds; polyhedra are not drawn by Ycrystal. (e) A synthetic antiferromagnetic arrangement (not a real material) with atom-attached moment arrows.

Limitations to state. - The element mapping is a presentation choice. It is not a statement of chemical equivalence or site correspondence, and nothing is inferred. - Per-atom settings transfer only to the same structure. - The command line writes PNG only (PDF and JPEG from the window). The PDF holds a raster image, not vector graphics.

items.title: Figure 4: evidence for correctness, cost, and reproducibility
items.text:
Panel Content Data Status a A rendered test image with the projected atom centres marked tests/test_validation.py: largest centre error 0.19 px over five structures Plot to be made from the test; values in validation b Render time against displayed atoms and against materials validation-results/benchmark-linux-2026-11-17.json Plot to be made from the JSON c Replay of snapshots: pixel differences validation-results/replay-check-linux-2026-11-17.json, the gallery's replay check Table available (same machine)

Draft caption. (a) Atom centres found in a POV-Ray image agree with the camera model to 0.19 px at most, including periodic images, for cubic, hexagonal, and triclinic cells. (b) The time per figure on a laptop (Intel Core Ultra 5 135U, POV-Ray 3.7.0.10) grows slowly with the number of atoms but strongly with refractive materials. (c) Snapshots rendered again in a new process, after the original structure and style files were deleted, gave identical pixels.

Limitations to state. - All measurements come from one Linux laptop. - Pixel identity between different machines or POV-Ray builds has not been measured. scripts/replay_check.py is the method. - The PNG files of two renders are never byte-identical: POV-Ray stores the render time in them.

items.title: Before submission
items.text:
• Rerun python scripts/make_gallery.py with the released version and record the version, the commands, and the renderer in the figure-methods table.
  • Draw panel 1a and take screenshot 1b. Make plots 4a and 4b from the recorded data and state the tool used.
  • Measure replays between Linux and macOS with scripts/replay_check.py. If they differ, report the differences instead of claiming identity.
  • Have the independent evaluation done by two real evaluators.
  • Check the comparison with other programs against their current versions.

items.title: Next tests on the Mac and other computers
items.text: An audit, on 17 November 2026, of what has been verified where, and which tests should run next on the Mac mini, on the Linux laptop by hand, and on a computer that has never had Ycrystal. Test counts updated on 18 November 2026, after the Windows work (PRs #35 and #36) added tests. It is a plan, not a record: results go to PROGRESS.md, HANDOFF.md, and validation results once a test has actually run.

items.title: What is already established
items.text: Evidence Where Covers CI, Ubuntu 24.04 (every pull request) Hosted runner, real POV-Ray 3.7 (apt), virtual display (Xvfb) All 901 tests, GUI tests included, with YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1: 900 passed, 1 skipped (the test of an installed POV-Ray for Windows; PR #36's run, 18 Nov 2026) CI, Windows Server 2022 (every pull request, since PR #36) Hosted runner, POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 Tests without windows: 727 passed, 2 skipped (POSIX-only) Windows 11 laptop (18 Nov 2026) PROGRESS.md, docs/development/windows-port.md Full suite with real windows, 898 passed, 3 skipped by design; the user's hand test CI, macOS 15 arm64 (every pull request) Hosted runner, real POV-Ray 3.7 (Homebrew) Tests without windows (728 passed, 1 skipped on 18 Nov 2026; 709 when this audit was written), among them 95 of the 104 POV-Ray tests: validation images, snapshot replays on the same runner, the gallery script at small size. The other 9 POV-Ray tests (preview and release workflow) need a window and run only on Ubuntu and on the Mac by hand Linux laptop runs (Linux Mint 22.1) docs/development/validation.md, PROGRESS.md Full suite without GUI tests (709 passed); benchmark quick set; same-machine replay check (9 of 9 identical); full-size gallery (7 of 7 identical) Mac mini runs (macOS 15.8, Apple silicon) PROGRESS.md, up to FR-BATCH-01 (PR #31) Full suite with real windows, 790 passed at that time The user's hand tests HANDOFF.md FR-VECTOR-01, FR-EXPORT-01, FR-REPRO-01 reported working

items.title: What is not established
items.text:
1. The window on a real Mac since PR #31. Hosted Macs have no GPU for Qt's OpenGL widget, so CI never opens a window there. FR-REPRO-01, FR-VALIDATION-01, and FR-GALLERY-01 changed no GUI code. Still, the full suite has not run on the Mac since they were added: 91 tests are new.
  2. Pixels across machines. Every replay so far compared renders from one computer. Whether a snapshot made on Linux gives the same pixels on the Mac is unknown: POV-Ray 3.7.0.10 from apt on x86_64 against Homebrew's on arm64. The paper must not claim it before this is measured.
  3. Cost on the Mac. The benchmark has run only on the laptop. Two checks are missing:
  4. whether its memory figure is correct on macOS (verified on Linux only);
  5. the full benchmark set, which is too heavy for the laptop.
  6. The gallery on the Mac, at full size, inspected by eye.
  7. Hands-on use of the window. Most post-0.2.0 features have only scripted GUI checks. The Mac checklist in HANDOFF.md is entirely open, and a Retina display has never been tried.
  8. A clean installation by someone following the documentation alone, on a computer that never had Ycrystal. This is also the first task of the independent evaluators; the authors should do a dry run first.
  9. Windows was added after this audit (PR #35, 18 November 2026): the full suite passes on one Windows 11 laptop with POV-Ray for Windows, and the user tested it by hand. Not done there: the benchmark, the full-size gallery, and replays between machines; see docs/development/windows-port.md.
  10. Quantum ESPRESSO lattices on the Mac and Windows (FR-QE-IBRAV-01, 21 November 2026): the comparison of every ibrav with pw.x's output ran on Linux only. It needs no window and no POV-Ray (step 1f).

items.title: 1. Mac mini, automated (Claude Code or a terminal)
items.text:
Start from an up-to-date main in the existing checkout. The .venv stays, but its editable install must be refreshed.

git pull
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[dev]" -c constraints.txt
.venv/bin/ycrystal --version            # ycrystal 0.5.0
.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer     # PASS: POV-Ray 3.7… passed

1a. Full suite with real windows. Leave the machine alone: windows take the focus for a few minutes.

YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -rf

Expected (18 November 2026): 900 passed, 1 skipped — the skipped one checks an installed POV-Ray for Windows and runs only on Windows. Record the count, the time, and any failure by name. An intermittent failure seen once in PR #30 was never captured, so note the test name if one appears and does not reproduce.

1b. Is the benchmark's memory figure right on macOS? On macOS ru_maxrss is in bytes, and whether wait4 includes grandchildren there is unverified. Run this check before trusting any memory column:

.venv/bin/python - <<'EOF'
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "scripts")
import benchmark_render as b
ballast = bytearray(300_000_000); ballast[::4096] = b"1" * len(ballast[::4096])
print("small command, big parent:", b.run_once([sys.executable, "-c", "pass"])["peak_rss_mib"])
big = "x = bytearray(200_000_000); x[::4096] = b'1' * len(x[::4096])"
code = f"import subprocess, sys; subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', {big!r}])"
print("command with 200 MB grandchild:", b.run_once([sys.executable, "-c", code])["peak_rss_mib"])
EOF
  • Expected (as on Linux): about 10–20 MiB for the first line, about 200 MiB for the second.
  • If the second line is small, macOS does not count grandchildren: report memory as "not measured on macOS" and do not publish that column.
  • If the first line is large, the parent leaks into the figure: report it the same way.

1c. Benchmark. Run the same set as on the laptop, for a direct comparison, then the full set, which the Mac mini can afford:

.venv/bin/python scripts/benchmark_render.py --quick --scale 0.5 --repeats 3 --out artifacts/validation/bench-macos
.venv/bin/python scripts/benchmark_render.py --out artifacts/validation/bench-macos-full

The full set has the 12 × 12 × 12 case and 1600 × 1200 images, with 1 + 5 runs per case. Expect tens of minutes, mostly glass. Copy each benchmark.json unedited to docs/development/validation-results/benchmark-macos-<date>.json (and …-full-…), and add the tables to validation.

1d. Replays across machines, Linux → Mac. Copy these two folders from the laptop, byte for byte (rsync -a, or a USB drive; not through a program that recompresses PNGs):

  • artifacts/gallery/figures/ (2.6 MB, 7 figures at 1600 × 1200);
  • artifacts/validation/bench-linux/snapshots/ (0.9 MB, 9 benchmark cases at half size).

Then on the Mac:

.venv/bin/python scripts/replay_check.py PATH/TO/gallery-figures-from-linux --out artifacts/replay-gallery-linux-on-mac
.venv/bin/python scripts/replay_check.py PATH/TO/bench-snapshots-from-linux --out artifacts/replay-bench-linux-on-mac

What the results mean:

  • modified means a file changed in the copy; copy it again.
  • same (largest difference ≤ 1 of 255) means the pixels agree across the two installations for that figure.
  • different is a result, not an error. Keep the numbers (largest and mean difference, fraction of pixels beyond 1) and look at both images side by side. Differences are most likely in glass, chrome, area-light shadows, and anti-aliased edges.

Copy each replay-check.json to docs/development/validation-results/replay-check-linux-to-macos-<date>.json.

1e. Gallery on the Mac, and replays Mac → Linux.

.venv/bin/python scripts/make_gallery.py --out artifacts/gallery-macos

Expected: 7 figures, and 7 of 7 replays the same on the Mac itself. Look at all seven in artifacts/gallery-macos/figures/ next to the thumbnails of the gallery. Then copy artifacts/gallery-macos/figures/ to the laptop and run there:

.venv/bin/python scripts/replay_check.py PATH/TO/gallery-macos-figures --out artifacts/replay-gallery-macos-on-linux

Both directions together answer question C of the validation report for these two installations.

1f. Quantum ESPRESSO lattices against pw.x's output. Needs network access; no QE installation. Also worth running once on Windows.

.venv/bin/python scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py      # expected: 17 of 17 lattices agree
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/QEF/q-e.git ../q-e
git -C ../q-e sparse-checkout set test-suite
.venv/bin/python scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py --qe-checkout ../q-e   # expected: all agree

Expected on Linux (21 November 2026, QE development branch): 295 of 295 inputs agree. Record the count and any input reported as different.

items.title: 4. A computer that never had Ycrystal
items.text:
A dry run of the independent evaluation by the authors, before real evaluators get it. Use a new user account or a fresh virtual machine running Ubuntu 24.04 or macOS, with no ~/.config/Y-Matter Lab and no earlier checkout.

  1. Follow README.md and docs/guide/install.md literally. Note every step that is missing, wrong, or needs knowledge the page does not give.
  2. Run ycrystal --check-renderer, the commands of the examples guide, and python scripts/make_gallery.py --scale 0.25 --out gallery-check.
  3. Replay a copied reference set (step 1d) with scripts/replay_check.py. This also gives a third installation for the cross-machine question.
  4. Work through the independent evaluation checklist yourself, and fix the documentation where it failed before sending it out.

The repository is public, so the fresh computer (and a referee) can clone it without a GitHub account.

items.title: What each result allows us to say
items.text:
Result Then the documents may say 1a passes "All tests pass on macOS 15 (Apple silicon) with real windows" for this version 1b as expected The benchmark's memory column is valid on macOS too 1d/1e same for a figure That figure's snapshot gives the same pixels on both installations (name both POV-Ray builds) 1d/1e different The size of the difference, per figure; never "identical across platforms" Section 2 or 3 ticked by a person The hands-on item works on that system, as reported by that person Section 4 done The installation guide was followed successfully on a clean system, or what was fixed

Possible next step (a recommendation, not authorised): run replay_check.py in the macOS CI job against a small reference set committed to the repository. Every pull request would then measure Linux → macOS pixel differences automatically. That needs a decision about storing reference images (about 0.5 MB at quarter size) in Git.

items.title: Release procedure and checklist
items.text:
How a Ycrystal release is prepared, and the checklists of released versions. The maintainer decides when to publish a Git tag or GitHub release.

The GitHub release page contains the Windows installers and tagged source archives. The checklists below record verification for each release. See the current feature table for the release containing each feature.

items.title: Procedure
items.text:
1. Update __version__ in src/ycrystal/__init__.py and CHANGELOG.md.

  2. Run the checks on the reference machine (Linux Mint, X11, POV-Ray 3.7 package):

    .venv/bin/pre-commit run --all-files
YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q -rs
.venv/bin/python scripts/docs_examples.py
.venv-docs/bin/zensical build --clean --strict

    tests/test_release.py includes the end-to-end workflow (open a CIF, rotate and pan, expand to 2 × 2 × 2, change an element's finish, choose a studio, render, save, close, reopen without the source file, render again, then POSCAR and QE imports (ibrav = 0 and ibrav = 1) and the rejection of a QE file whose lattice pw.x would refuse), the command line, the desktop launcher, and the examples. 3. Clean install: in a new directory, follow Install and launch exactly (clone, venv, pip install -e . -c constraints.txt), then run ycrystal --version, --check-renderer, an example --render, a short GUI launch, and --install-desktop into a temporary XDG_DATA_HOME checked with desktop-file-validate. 4. Build the artifacts and install the wheel into another fresh environment:

    uv build -o dist        # dist/ycrystal-X.Y.Z.tar.gz and -py3-none-any.whl
/usr/bin/python3 -m venv /tmp/yc-wheel
/tmp/yc-wheel/bin/python -m pip install dist/ycrystal-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl -c constraints.txt
/tmp/yc-wheel/bin/ycrystal examples/SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render /tmp/check.png

    The wheel contains the presets, thumbnails, and icon; the source distribution adds constraints.txt, the examples, the test fixtures, and the notices. 5. The Windows installer (on a Windows computer, or the ycrystal-windows-installer artifact of the Windows installer workflow run of the release commit): build it with packaging\windows\build.ps1, run packaging\windows\coexistence-check.ps1, install it once by hand (wizard, Start menu, a preview), and attach Ycrystal-X.Y.Z-windows-x64-setup.exe to the GitHub release. It is not signed; see Windows installer. 6. Record the results in docs/PROGRESS.md and in the checklist below, marking each item passed, failed, or unverified.
