items.title: Scientific validation and benchmarks
items.text:
Evidence for the claims a paper about Ycrystal would make (FR-VALIDATION-01): what was tested, how, with which tolerance, and what was observed. Everything here was measured by running the named tests and scripts; anything not run is marked unverified, with the command that would run it. A reading of the source code is not counted as validation.

All measurements below were made on 17 November 2026 on one machine: a Linux Mint 22.1 laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 135U (14 logical CPUs, 7.2 GiB of memory), Python 3.12.3, and POV-Ray 3.7.0.10 from the distribution package. They were not repeated on macOS, on Windows, or with another POV-Ray build.

items.title: Questions and status
items.text: Question Answer from the evidence Status A. Does the POV-Ray scene, and the ray-traced image, show the structure where it is (atoms, periodic images, bonds, cell, vectors, projection, handedness), with nothing cut off? Yes, within the tolerances below, for every fixture tested Verified on Linux; macOS unverified B. Can one style be applied to different materials without changing their scientific data? Yes: no coordinate, cell, element, label, occupancy, flag, or vector changed, for 8 inputs × 2 sets of style parts Verified (no renderer involved) C. Do snapshots give the same figure again, in a new session and on other installations? Same machine: the same scene exactly and identical pixels (tests, and 9 of 9 benchmark figures), also in a new process with the sources deleted. Other installations: not yet measured Same machine verified; other machines unverified D. How much time and memory do modest, medium, and large figures take? See render cost for this laptop Measured on Linux only; macOS unverified E. Are the ray-traced effects real: shadows, soft shadows, reflection, refraction? Yes, each measured as a property of the image Verified on Linux

items.title: Test structures
items.text:
Small input files written for this project (MIT licence); see tests/fixtures/README.md.

Structure Kind Used for SrTiO3, Pm-3m, tests/fixtures/SrTiO3.cif (also .vasp, .pw.in) Real compound, rounded textbook constant (a = 3.905 Å) Cubic cell with boundary images, styles, effects BaZrO3, Pm-3m, tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif Real compound, rounded constant (a = 4.19 Å), for demonstration Second perovskite for element mapping (Ti → Zr) MgB2, P6/mmm, tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif (also .vasp, .pw.in) Real compound, rounded constants Hexagonal cell Triclinic P1, tests/fixtures/triclinic.cif Synthetic: invented cell and atoms Low symmetry, skewed axes Antiferromagnet, examples/vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal Synthetic: not a real material; ±2.2 μB assigned by hand Atom-attached vectors Si, diamond, tests/fixtures/Si_conventional.cif Real compound, rounded constant Style transfer

items.title: A. Geometry, from the scene file to the image
items.text:
The live view and the POV-Ray writer draw one shared geometry (DisplayGeometry). The checks go in three steps:

  1. The geometry is right.
  2. The scene file for POV-Ray holds exactly that geometry.
  3. POV-Ray draws it where the camera model says.
Check Test (tests/…) Tolerance Observed Periodic images are exact lattice translations of their source atoms and lie inside the displayed cells test_validation.py::test_periodic_images_are_exact_lattice_translations (5 structures) 1e-9 Å Pass The scene file has one sphere per displayed atom with its position, radius, element, and image; each bond as one cylinder or two halves between the atom centres; cell edges between lattice points along a lattice vector test_validation.py::test_pov_scene_holds_exactly_the_shared_geometry (5) 5e-7 Å (the file has 6 decimals) Pass Looking down a, b, or c, the other two lattice vectors turn counter-clockwise on screen (no mirror image), and the named axis faces the viewer test_validation.py::test_lattice_views_keep_the_cell_right_handed_on_screen (3 cells × 3 axes) Exact sign Pass Every displayed image of an atom carries its source's vector: parallel, same sign, centred, of the set length test_validation.py::test_vectors_keep_attachment_direction_and_sign_in_every_image 1e-9 Pass (2 × 2 × 2 cells, 35 arrows) Rendered atoms and periodic images: every sphere found, at the projected centre, of the projected size, with the right colour; the mirror image does not match test_validation.py::test_rendered_atoms_and_periodic_images_follow_the_camera_model (SrTiO3, SrTiO3 2 × 2 × 1, MgB2 2 × 2 × 1, triclinic 2 × 1 × 1, BaZrO3) Centre 0.5 px; area 8 %; mirror > 5 px Largest centre error 0.19 px (others 0.08–0.16); largest area error 3.5 %; mirror errors 51–119 px; 10 to 42 spheres each Rendered bonds: at ¼ and ¾ of each bond the pixel is opaque and has the colour of the atom of that half test_validation.py::test_rendered_half_bonds_join_their_own_atoms (3) Dominant colour channel All samples not hidden by an atom: 16 (SrTiO3, 30 bonds), 16 (MgB2, 8 bonds), 4 (triclinic, 2 bonds) Rendered vector arrows: arrow colour near each projected head; no arrow colour outside the projected arrows test_validation.py::test_rendered_vector_arrows_follow_the_shared_geometry ±2 px around the head point 22 of 22 heads Rendered fitted views are never cut off: transparent border on all four sides, drawn extent inside the projected framing bounds (equal to them without arrows), landscape and portrait test_validation.py::test_fitted_views_are_not_clipped_in_the_render (4 scenes × 2 shapes) 1.5 px Border pixels transparent in all 8; drawn extent within 0.76 px of the bounds without arrows; with arrows up to 4.5 px inside them (the arrow bounds are conservative); nearest border 8 px Synthetic arrangement, rotated, rolled, panned view; mirrored and shifted controls test_render_alignment.py (existing) 1 px Pass Camera model equal to VTK's matrices; fitted views never clip; arrows included in the framing test_camera.py (existing) 1e-9 Pass

Why these tolerances. - Sphere centres, 0.5 px. The centroid of a disc found in the image is its centre to well below a pixel, even with anti-aliasing. Half a pixel is far smaller than any visible misplacement, and twice the largest error observed. - Disc areas, 8 %. An edge pixel counts as inside when its alpha is ≥ 128. For the smallest discs (radius about 4 px) that changes the area by several per cent. - Bounds, 1.5 px. The drawn extent is quantised to whole pixels (up to 1 px), and anti-aliasing may leave a barely covered edge pixel transparent. - Analytic checks. These use the precision of the numbers involved: 1e-9 Å in memory, 5e-7 Å in the scene file.

Views for the image checks are chosen from the camera model alone. The test searches a fixed 10° grid of orientations for the one where projected atoms are farthest apart, then requires every atom to be visible (a gap of more than 4 px between discs). The render then shows whether POV-Ray agrees.

items.title: B. Styles do not change the science
items.text:
test_validation.py::test_styles_never_change_the_scientific_data applies examples/grey-studio.ycstyle to 8 inputs:

  • SrTiO3 as CIF and as POSCAR with selective dynamics;
  • BaZrO3 with the element mapping Ti → Zr;
  • MgB2 as CIF and as Quantum ESPRESSO input;
  • the triclinic cell;
  • silicon;
  • the vector project.

It does this with the default command-line parts and with all four parts. The test then checks:

  • Data unchanged. Cell, positions, atomic numbers, labels, periodicity, occupancy, movable flags, import record (except the time of reading), and vectors are identical to a separately read copy.
  • Input object untouched. The input object itself is unchanged.
  • Same atoms drawn. Without the display part, the same atoms are drawn at the same positions.
  • Files untouched. Neither the input nor the style file is written.

All 16 cases pass.

Related existing tests: - test_style.py: transfer rules, element mapping, packaged styles; - test_release.py: command line; - test_batch_manifest.py: a real POV-Ray series with inputs unchanged byte for byte; - test_camera.py: view policies.

items.title: C. Snapshots give the same figure again
items.text:
Same machine, verified (tests/test_reproducibility.py, FR-REPRO-01):

  • Same scene. The replayed scene file is identical except for its date line, for:
  • styles with element mapping;
  • fixed, fitted, and saved cameras;
  • vectors;
  • a background picture;
  • a custom material.
  • Identical pixels. Real POV-Ray replays had identical pixels: the tests allow 1 of 255 per channel, and every replay had a difference of 0. This held:
  • after the structure, style, and picture were deleted;
  • in a new process with an empty home folder;
  • for three batch jobs.
  • PNG bytes always differ. POV-Ray writes the render time into the file, so a replay never has the original's SHA-256.

Other installations: unverified. To measure them:

# On machine A: renders the benchmark cases once and saves their snapshots.
python scripts/benchmark_render.py --quick --scale 0.5 --repeats 3 --out bench-A
# Copy bench-A/snapshots to machine B, then on machine B:
python scripts/replay_check.py bench-A/snapshots --out replay-on-B

replay_check.py first checks the recorded SHA-256 of every reference image and snapshot. It then renders each snapshot with the production command line and reports per figure: - the largest and the mean difference per 8-bit channel; - the fraction of pixels beyond the tolerance; - both systems and POV-Ray versions.

The result is written to replay-check.json. As a control, the check was run on the same laptop with the snapshots of the benchmark run below. All 9 figures had identical pixels (largest difference 0), including glass, chrome, and the studio's area-light shadows; see results.

items.title: D. Render cost
items.text:
scripts/benchmark_render.py times the production command (ycrystal INPUT --render OUT.png --width W --height H), each run in a new process.

  • Warm-up. One untimed run per case, which also saves the snapshot for question C.
  • Timed runs. Then the timed repeats.
  • Reported. The median, minimum, and maximum of:
  • the wall time of the whole command;
  • the render time that ycrystal prints (0.1 s resolution);
  • the peak resident memory of the largest process, the Python process or POV-Ray, from wait4, read by a small launcher process. On Linux, a child's peak memory also counts the size of the process that started it, so measuring from the benchmark process itself would report that process's size. The first recorded attempt did exactly that and was discarded. On Linux it was verified that the launcher reports a 200 MB grandchild (199.9 MiB) and not a 300 MB benchmark process (11.2 MiB for a trivial command). The launcher's own size, about 10 MiB, is the smallest value it can report. On macOS this is unverified.
  • Not controlled. CPU frequency scaling, other programs, and the thermal state. POV-Ray uses every core.

Results on the laptop: benchmark_render.py --quick --scale 0.5 --repeats 3, so 1 warm-up and 3 timed runs per case, at half the default image sizes. Raw data: results files.

Case Displayed atoms Bonds Image (px) Wall time, s: median (min–max) Printed render time, s (median) Peak memory, MiB (median) srtio3-1: SrTiO3 1×1×1, satin, white 15 30 400 × 300 1.68 (1.65–1.71) 1.4 71.5 srtio3-4: SrTiO3 4×4×4, satin, white 429 1,344 400 × 300 1.93 (1.91–1.98) 1.6 72.3 srtio3-8: SrTiO3 8×8×8, satin, white 2,969 9,984 400 × 300 2.57 (2.48–2.59) 2.2 79.2 srtio3-4-small: SrTiO3 4×4×4, satin, white 429 1,344 200 × 150 1.78 (1.77–1.80) 1.5 72.5 effects-plain: SrTiO3 2×2×2, satin, white 71 192 400 × 300 1.74 (1.74–1.77) 1.4 71.6 effects-studio: SrTiO3 2×2×2, satin, studio (floor, area light, soft shadows) 71 192 400 × 300 2.21 (2.19–2.27) 1.9 71.6 effects-chrome: SrTiO3 2×2×2, chrome (reflection), studio 71 192 400 × 300 3.39 (3.38–3.44) 3.1 71.4 effects-glass: SrTiO3 2×2×2, glass (refraction), studio 71 192 400 × 300 65.48 (56.21–74.95) 65.1 71.5 mgb2-style: MgB2 with --style grey-studio.ycstyle 10 1 400 × 300 2.05 (2.03–2.06) 1.1 85.0

What the numbers show, for this laptop only:

  • Atom count. From 15 to 2,969 displayed atoms (9,984 bonds), the whole command takes 1.7 to 2.6 s at 400 × 300 px. A fixed cost dominates: Python start-up, reading the input, and POV-Ray's start-up and parsing, about 1.4 s of the printed render time even for 15 atoms.
  • Image size. Halving the image size (srtio3-4-small) saves only 0.15 s at this scale.
  • Effects.
  • The studio (floor, area light, soft shadows) adds about 0.5 s to the plain scene.
  • In the same studio, chrome (reflection) instead of satin adds about 1.2 s.
  • Glass (refraction) in the studio takes about 65 s, some 30 times the satin studio scene. Its runs also vary most (56–75 s). The cause was not investigated; the laptop may lower its clock under long full load.
  • Memory. The largest process of each command used 71–85 MiB. The measurement does not say whether that was the Python process or POV-Ray.
  • Larger cases not run. The 12 × 12 × 12 case and 1600 × 1200 images were not run (too heavy for this laptop). In an interrupted trial at 800 × 600, process listings showed single renders of about 3 min for SrTiO3 12 × 12 × 12 and more than 3.5 min for the glass studio scene. These are rough observations, not recorded results.

Caveats. - Settings dominate the cost. Render time depends on the image size, the materials (glass refracts and chrome reflects, so each ray spawns more rays), area lights (5 × 5 samples with adaptive refinement), floors and shadows, and the hardware. - Not an estimate for other figures. These numbers describe these cases on this laptop, nothing more. - Not run here. The full default set at 800 × 600, with 1 + 5 runs per case, takes far longer on this laptop and was not run. The command for a faster machine: python scripts/benchmark_render.py --out bench-full.

items.title: E. Ray-traced effects
items.text:
test_validation.py::test_cast_shadows_and_soft_shadows_of_area_lights and ::test_polished_metal_reflects_and_glass_transmits render SrTiO3. Each comparison changes exactly one setting, with the same geometry and camera.

Effect Measurement Required Observed Cast shadows (studio: floor and area key light) Fraction of pixels darker by more than 15 of 255 than with shadows off > 5 % 20.4 % Soft shadows of the area light Fraction of shadow pixels between 20 % and 80 % of the full darkening, area light vs point light Area > point + 0.05 0.46 vs 0.31 Polished metal reflects a red floor Red excess (red minus the mean of green and blue) in the lower part of each grey sphere Chrome > 30; matte and satin < 5 Chrome 84–124; matte 0.0; satin 0.0 Glass transmits a blue background Blue excess in the centre of each grey sphere Glass > 20; satin < 5 Glass 49–78; satin 0.0

The existing tests add: - glass showing a background picture (test_background_image.py); - custom material parameters changing the image (test_custom_materials.py); - vector arrows (test_vectors.py).

items.title: F. Quantum ESPRESSO lattices (ibrav other than 0)
items.text:
A pw.x input with ibrav other than 0 gives its atoms in a cell that pw.x builds from celldm or A, B, C, cos…; crystal coordinates are only right if Ycrystal builds the same vectors (ycrystal.io.qe_lattice). Checks of 21 November 2026, audited for every ibrav the same day:

Check Lattices Result Vectors as written in the pw.x input documentation (tests/test_qe_lattice.py), and the conventional cell and centring vectors as whole-number combinations of them All 20 Equal within 1e-12 pw.x's own output: scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py reads the inputs of QE's test suite (test-suite/pw_lattice-ibrav, branch develop) and compares with the crystal axes and positions pw.x printed 17 (QE has no test for −9, 91, −13) Axes within 4.7e-7 alat (pw.x prints 6 decimals), positions within 1.5e-8 alat pw.x's own output for every applicable input with ibrav ≠ 0 in QE's test suite (scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py --qe-checkout) 17; 295 inputs, both parameter forms for 1, 2, 4, 6, 14 All agree within pw.x's printed precision Every lattice through the reader, celldm and A, B, C, cos… forms, against the documented vectors (tests/test_readers.py) All 20 Within 1e-9 Å Same structures as other formats: Si (ibrav = 2), MgB2 (4, from A, C), SrTiO3 (1), the triclinic cell (14, from A, B, C, cos…) against the POSCAR, CIF, and ibrav = 0 files (tests/test_readers.py) 1, 2, 4, 14 Equivalent within 1e-6 Å Independent code: ASE 3.22.1's former ibrav_to_cell in a local copy (not in the repository, so not rerunnable from it), 200 random parameter sets per lattice in both forms 19 (that code has no 91) Within 4e-15 Å

Without options the script downloads QE's 17 lattice tests (network access; QE's files are GPL and not part of Ycrystal); with --qe-checkout PATH it compares every applicable input of a local copy of QE's test suite (commands in Check it yourself). The applicable and refused cases, the dependence on the QE version (only ibrav = −13 changed, in QE 6.5), and what was not tested are described in Quantum ESPRESSO lattices.

items.title: Reproduce
items.text:
# A, B, E (and C on one machine): about 70 s on the laptop.
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_validation.py tests/test_reproducibility.py tests/test_validation_scripts.py -q
# The observed values above, as JUnit XML properties:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_validation.py -o junit_family=legacy --junitxml=validation.xml
# D and the reference set for C:
.venv/bin/python scripts/benchmark_render.py --quick --scale 0.5 --repeats 3 --out bench
.venv/bin/python scripts/replay_check.py bench/snapshots --out replay

Tests that need POV-Ray are skipped without it, unless YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 is set, which makes them fail instead.

items.title: Results files
items.text:
The raw, machine-readable results of the runs reported here, unedited (they contain no paths, user names, or host names):

  • validation-results/benchmark-linux-2026-11-17.json: benchmark_render.py --quick --scale 0.5 --repeats 3 on the laptop (every run, inputs and their SHA-256, system);
  • validation-results/replay-check-linux-2026-11-17.json: replay_check.py of that run's snapshots on the same laptop. This is the control experiment; checks between different machines are still to be run.

The images, snapshots, and generated inputs of the run stay outside Git (in artifacts/validation/, which is ignored). Rerun the commands above to regenerate them.

items.title: Limitations and unsupported input
items.text:
• Platforms. Everything here was measured on one Linux laptop. Unverified:
  • macOS (the CI job runs the tests without windows and with real POV-Ray, but not the benchmark);
  • Windows (the validation tests pass there with POV-Ray for Windows on one laptop, 18 November 2026, but the benchmark and the replay check were not run);
  • other POV-Ray builds;
  • pixel differences between machines.
  • Not checked by hand. These checks are automated and involve no window. Hands-on use of the window is listed in HANDOFF.md.
  • Unsupported input. Refused rather than drawn:
  • CIF files with partial occupancy or overlapping sites;
  • Quantum ESPRESSO input with crystal_sg positions, or with lattice parameters that pw.x would refuse.

VASP 4 files need the elements: the window asks for them, and the command line refuses the file. See supported formats. - Not vector graphics. The PDF export holds a raster image. - The test structures are small (5 to 42 atoms in the image checks). Large scenes are covered by the benchmark only, for cost, not for correctness. - Comparison with other programs. See the comparison. It rests on their documentation only; none of them was run. - Independent users. The evaluation checklist is prepared; no evaluation has taken place.

items.title: Windows installer
items.text:
The graphical Windows installer, Ycrystal-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe, installs Ycrystal without Python, Git, or PowerShell. It is the recommended installation for users (install guide). The PowerShell installation from a source folder (scripts/install-windows.ps1) stays the supported installation for developers. The two can be installed on one computer at the same time.

Requested by the user on 18 November 2026; branch feature/windows-installer.

items.title: How it is built
items.text:
Step Tool Files Freeze Ycrystal with its Python and libraries into one folder PyInstaller 6 packaging/windows/ycrystal.spec, ycrystal_gui.py, ycrystal_cli.py Wrap the folder into a setup program Inno Setup 6 packaging/windows/ycrystal.iss Both, from a clean build environment PowerShell packaging/windows/build.ps1, build tools pinned in packaging/windows/requirements.txt Check both installations side by side PowerShell packaging/windows/coexistence-check.ps1 On pull requests that change the program or its packaging GitHub Actions .github/workflows/windows-installer.yml

To build on a Windows computer, from the repository:

winget install --id JRSoftware.InnoSetup --exact      # once
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File packaging\windows\build.ps1

The build: 1. creates build\windows\venv with Python 3.12 (py -3.12, or -Python), Ycrystal installed from the folder (not editable) with the pins of constraints.txt, and PyInstaller; 2. draws build\windows\ycrystal.ico from the SVG icon with ycrystal.desktop.write_windows_icon, as the developer installation does; 3. runs PyInstaller, then checks that ycrystal-cli.exe --version reports the version; 4. compiles the installer into dist\windows.

build\ and dist\ are ignored by Git. Nothing outside them is written, and the developer installation (.venv, its Start-menu entry) is not touched.

The packaged folder holds two programs that share one copy of Python and the libraries:

  • Ycrystal.exe, the window, without a console. The Start menu and .ycrystal files start it. VTK's own window for warnings is turned off (ycrystal_gui.py).
  • ycrystal-cli.exe, the command line with a console, for --render, --check-renderer, and --batch. Without options it opens the window too.

Both run the same ycrystal.app.main as the ycrystal command of an installation from source; there is no packaged-only code path apart from the application id and the refusal of --install-desktop (below).

items.title: Coexistence with the developer installation
items.text:
The two installations must not share any identity. Then neither can redirect, replace, or remove the other's parts:

Packaged (installer) From source (--install-desktop) Start-menu shortcut Ycrystal.lnk → <app>\Ycrystal.exe, written by Inno Setup Ycrystal (development).lnk → .venv\Scripts\pythonw.exe -I -m ycrystal.app AppUserModelID (taskbar, pinning) YMatterLab.Ycrystal.App (WINDOWS_PACKAGED_APP_ID) YMatterLab.Ycrystal (WINDOWS_APP_ID) How the window picks its id windows_app_id(): sys.frozen is set by PyInstaller the same function, sys.frozen unset File type (ProgID) YMatterLab.Ycrystal.Project Ycrystal.Project Default of .ycrystal set by the installer set only if no other existing file type is the default Icon inside Ycrystal.exe %LOCALAPPDATA%\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal\ycrystal.ico Registry root HKEY_CURRENT_USER (per user) or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (all users) HKEY_CURRENT_USER Removed by its uninstaller: only its own files, shortcuts, and values; the .ycrystal default only while it names its file type --uninstall-desktop: shortcuts only if they start Python with -m ycrystal.app (is_source_shortcut), its own file type, its own default

Shared on purpose, and never deleted by either uninstallation: the settings (HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal), personal materials and their thumbnails, and POV-Ray for Windows.

Rules for later changes:

  • The packaged program must not write the developer installation's entry: in it, --install-desktop and --uninstall-desktop refuse (is_packaged, PACKAGED_MENU_MESSAGE).
  • Before this installer existed, the developer installation's shortcut was also called Ycrystal.lnk. --install-desktop replaces such a shortcut with the new name, and --uninstall-desktop removes it, only if it starts Python with -m ycrystal.app. So the installer's Ycrystal.lnk is never taken for it.
  • The installer's AppId GUID (96A7291E-332A-4D2A-ACAD-E2489153A771) must never change: Windows recognises updates and the uninstaller by it.
  • tests/test_windows_installer.py checks that the Inno Setup script's ids match the Python constants and differ from the source installation's. It also checks that the .ycrystal default has no uninstall flag (the [Code] section removes it conditionally) and that the installer never touches the settings key. tests/test_windows_desktop.py checks the source side.
  • coexistence-check.ps1 runs the whole sequence for real: installer, then source entry, then each uninstalled in turn. CI runs it on every relevant pull request.

items.title: POV-Ray
items.text: POV-Ray for Windows is not bundled: its licence (AGPL-3.0) and its own installer make it a separate program, as for the developer installation. The packaged program finds and drives it with the same code (ycrystal.render.povray): registry and Program Files search, /EXIT command line, single-instance and editor-question checks. The installer looks for it in the same places ([Code], PovrayFound) only to tell the user, and offers the download page at the end; it installs nothing of POV-Ray.

items.title: Releasing
items.text:
The installer is attached to a GitHub release by hand: build it, or take the ycrystal-windows-installer artifact of the Windows installer workflow run of the release commit, and upload Ycrystal-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe to the release (see the release checklist). Before it goes to users:

  • Code signing. The installer and the programs are not signed, so SmartScreen warns ("Windows protected your PC") until a certificate is used. Signing needs a certificate and a decision about it; build.ps1 has no signing step yet.
  • Licences. The installer bundles Python and the packages of constraints.txt (see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md); their licence texts are collected into _internal\licenses by the PyInstaller specification. ASE (LGPL) is collected as plain source files, so that users can replace it.

items.title: Results
items.text: See PROGRESS.md for what was built and checked, and on which machines.

items.title: Windows port
items.text:
Windows support was developed on branch feature/windows (PR #35): the groundwork on the Linux laptop and Windows CI (17 November 2026), the completion on a Windows 11 laptop (18 November 2026). This page records:

  • what was decided, and what is known with sources;
  • what is implemented and how it was tested;
  • the answers found on the Windows computer;
  • what is still open.

Status (18 November 2026): Ycrystal runs from a source checkout on Windows 11 with POV-Ray for Windows 3.7. On one laptop it passes every automated test (below), and the user tested it by hand there and reports that it works well. Since PR #36, Windows CI renders with the real POV-Ray for Windows too (see CI). Since PR #39, one script installs it, with a Start-menu entry (see installation); that is now the developer installation. For users, a graphical installer (PyInstaller + Inno Setup) installs it without Python, Git, or PowerShell, side by side with the developer installation (see Windows installer).

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Taken by the user on 17 November 2026: Ycrystal runs natively on Windows, and renders with the official POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 (pvengine64.exe).

The alternatives were set aside: - WSL2 only: Ycrystal and Linux POV-Ray inside WSL2. - Hybrid: native Ycrystal with wsl povray for rendering.

They remain possible later and are not implemented.

items.title: What is known, and from where
items.text: Fact Source Checked how There is no command-line POV-Ray for Windows from conda-forge conda-forge povray has builds for linux-64, linux-aarch64, osx-64, osx-arm64 only api.anaconda.org/package/conda-forge/povray, 17 Nov 2026 There is no MSYS2 package of POV-Ray packages.msys2.org search for "povray": no results 17 Nov 2026 GitHub releases of POV-Ray have Windows builds of 3.8 betas and alphas only, no 3.7 gh api repos/POV-Ray/povray/releases 17 Nov 2026 Official installer: povwin-3.7-agpl3-setup.exe, SHA-256 2B1331641B6F96113C2DBA951BE80D99EB548639480399CABB5E3A60DCE5BDC8, silent with /S, installs into %ProgramFiles%\POV-Ray\v3.7, executable bin\pvengine64.exe The Chocolatey package pov-ray 3.7.0.20161121 (its install script) Read on community.chocolatey.org. The CI job uses this URL and checksum The installer records Home (installation folder) and DocPath (user files: Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7, with include and ini) under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\POV-Ray\v3.7\Windows The registry of the Windows computer Read 18 Nov 2026 Command-line switches of POV-Ray for Windows 3.7: /EXIT (quit after the render), /NR or /NORESTORE, /RENDER FILE, /EDIT FILE, /NOEXEC, /THREADS N, /DEBUG, /DEMO, /BENCHMARK; anything else after a / is an error dialog. Other arguments (an INI file, +GA…) are ordinary POV-Ray options Its source, windows/pvtext.cpp (preparse_commandline), branch 3.7-stable of github.com/POV-Ray/povray Read 18 Nov 2026 (povray.org refuses automated access, HTTP 403) Keep Single Instance is on by default: [General] OneInstance in DocPath\ini\pvengine.ini, default 1. When a main window of class Pov37-Win64-MainWinClass (64-bit build) exists, a new copy brings it forward, shows a one-time notice ([DontShowAgain] OneInstanceSet), and passes only /EDIT and /RENDER to it; with /EXIT it shows the modal error box "Only /EDIT and /RENDER may be passed to previous instance" and exits with status 1 Source: windows/pvengine.cpp (WinMain), windows/pvtext.cpp (preparse_instance_commandline), windows/pvmisc.cpp (GetHKCU reads pvengine.ini) Read 18 Nov 2026, and observed on the Windows computer (experiment 6 below) With /EXIT, POV-Ray for Windows closes its window as soon as the render stops, before it plays the completion or error sound and before its first-time notices (render-complete sound, output file location) Source: windows/pvengine.cpp (render_stopped) Read 18 Nov 2026 Two dialogs wait for an answer even with /EXIT. (1) Without its separately licensed editor DLL (the AGPL installer does not include it), every start asks "Could not load internal editor – download it?" unless [General] UseEditors=0 (Options ▸ Other Settings ▸ Use Editor) or the editor is installed. (2) From the second start on, it shows its About box whenever [General] ItsAboutTime has passed (unset: at once), then sets it 1 day ahead the first time and 14 days ahead after that Source: windows/pvedit.cpp (LoadEditorDLL), windows/pvengine.cpp (WinMain, ShowAboutBox) Read 18 Nov 2026; both seen in screenshots of the CI runner taken by the probe Command-line renders start directly, not through POV-Ray's file queue, so the [Info] Rendering=1 flag that a killed render leaves behind does not make the next one skipped Source: windows/pvengine.cpp (WinMain, the queue code that checks Rendering) Read 18 Nov 2026

items.title: What is implemented on feature/windows
items.text:
Linux and macOS behaviour is unchanged: povray gets exactly the arguments it got before and still runs as a QProcess; every existing test passes on Linux.

  • src/ycrystal/render/povray.py (the place for renderer platform checks):
  • is_windows_engine() recognises pvengine*.exe by name.
  • windows_engine_candidates() and installed_windows_engine(platform) find POV-Ray for Windows from the registry Home values and the ProgramFiles folders (it is not on PATH); find_povray() falls back to it after povray on PATH.
  • render_arguments(): ["scene.ini"] for povray; ["/EXIT", "/NR", "+GAscene.log", "scene.ini"] for POV-Ray for Windows, which prints nothing and writes all messages to scene.log (read_log()).
  • background_startupinfo() starts it minimised (SW_SHOWMINNOACTIVE).
  • hold_foreground() / release_foreground() / foreground_held(): POV-Ray for Windows makes itself the foreground window even when started minimised or hidden. While it runs, Ycrystal calls LockSetForegroundWindow, which Windows allows only to the owner of the foreground window, so it works in the window and is refused harmlessly in a terminal. Holds are counted; every hold asks for the lock again.
  • windows_engine_conflict(): the same test POV-Ray makes at start-up (a window of its main class exists, and OneInstance is not 0 in its pvengine.ini), so that Ycrystal reports ENGINE_OPEN_MESSAGE instead of starting a copy that would show POV-Ray's modal error box and wait. keeps_single_instance() reads the setting as GetPrivateProfileInt does.
  • include_directories() also reads the user-files folder recorded in the registry (DocPath; right also when Documents was moved, for example into OneDrive), then Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7 in the home folder.
  • povray_version() never starts POV-Ray for Windows (no --version; it would open its window); it reads the executable's version resource.
  • src/ycrystal/render/jobs.py: run_job() reports a conflict without starting POV-Ray, holds the foreground while it runs, starts it minimised, and appends its log.
  • src/ycrystal/render/process.py (the window's previews, final renders, and material thumbnails): PySide6 6.12 has no QProcess.setCreateProcessArgumentsModifier, so QProcess cannot start a program minimised. POV-Ray for Windows therefore runs as a subprocess.Popen, checked every 100 ms by a QTimer. Since only one copy can render, the program's own runs take turns (a render started while another runs waits, and counts as running); whether one runs is decided by the process itself, and a waiting render checks for its turn on its own timer, so a render whose Qt object was deleted cannot hold up the others. Cancelling kills POV-Ray and reports at once. It reports no progress (POV-Ray for Windows prints none): the window shows a busy indicator, then 100 %.
  • src/ycrystal/gui/native.py: set_taskbar_identity() (an explicit AppUserModelID, so that the window has its own taskbar button and icon, not Python's; called from app.py before the application object) and executable_filter() (Render ▸ Set POV-Ray Executable… lists .exe files on Windows). That dialog now starts at the POV-Ray Ycrystal would use, not at povray on PATH.
  • Tests:
  • tests/conftest.py: python_program() makes stand-in programs work everywhere (a .cmd launcher on Windows); the povray_executable fixture also finds an installed POV-Ray for Windows.
  • tests/test_windows_povray.py checks the Windows contract on any system with stand-ins: arguments, log, version query, folder search and the recorded user folder, the Popen backend (success, failure, cancel, failure to start, preview superseding, renders taking turns, a deleted render not holding up the next), the foreground holds, the single-instance setting, and the conflict check. One test runs only on Windows, against the installed program.
  • Tests that simulate "no POV-Ray" by emptying PATH also hide an installed POV-Ray for Windows. A test that renders an exported scene by hand uses render_arguments() (with povray unchanged: povray scene.ini).
  • tests/test_preview_resolution.py compares scene files with the header's time aside (a minute could pass between two states: a flake on every system, seen first on Windows, where each preview takes longer).
  • .gitattributes: text files keep LF line endings in Windows checkouts. Several tests compare SHA-256 digests of tracked files.
  • scripts/make_examples.py writes LF on every system.
  • scripts/windows_povray_probe.py reports how POV-Ray for Windows behaves under Ycrystal; it also prints the settings file and the single-instance setting and stops when another copy is open.
  • CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml): a third test job on Windows Server 2022 with Python 3.12; experimental in PR #35, required and rendering with POV-Ray for Windows since PR #36 (see CI).
  • Documentation: a Windows section in the install guide and the README, rows in the support matrix and troubleshooting, the architecture page, and the changelog.

items.title: The Windows computer (18 November 2026)
items.text:
A laptop with Windows 11 Enterprise (build 26300), x64, a 1536 × 864 logical display at 125 % scale (device pixel ratio 1.25), and a UTF-8 system code page (65001). Python 3.12.10 from python.org (installed with winget, per user), PySide6 6.12.0, VTK 9.7.2. POV-Ray for Windows 3.7.0 (file version 3.7.0.0, VersionNo64=3.7.0.msvc10.win64), installed by the user with the official installer, user files included.

Check Result Install: py -3.12 -m venv .venv, .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev]" -c constraints.txt Installed scripts/windows_povray_probe.py Found C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe (not on PATH), version 3.7.0.0, include folder Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7\include, no include file missing. First start: no image within 90 s (see question 4); then both command lines rendered Small render (120 × 80) timing, 7 timed runs 2.3–2.8 s each after the first start (POV-Ray's start-up dominates); the second start of all took 28 s Tests without windows, real POV-Ray for Windows, before the changes of 18 November 715 passed, 3 skipped (symbolic links unavailable, execute bit, POSIX permissions), 1 failed: the test that ran pvengine64.exe scene.ini without /EXIT waited 120 s (fixed in the test) GUI tests, first run 160 passed, 12 failed: one test unexpectedly started a real render (an installed POV-Ray for Windows is found outside PATH), its window closed, and the Popen backend's "running" marker stayed set, so every later render waited for ever. Fixed (cancel reports at once; the process decides whether one runs) and covered by a new test Full suite after the fixes, YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 pytest -q -rs 898 passed, 3 skipped (see the result below)

items.title: Full suite
items.text: Check Result YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 pytest -q -rs (GUI tests with real windows at 125 % scale, all POV-Ray tests with POV-Ray for Windows) 898 passed, 3 skipped, none failed, 12 min. Skipped by design: symbolic links (need a Windows privilege), the execute bit, POSIX permissions CI's doctest module list and scripts/docs_examples.py Passed pre-commit run --all-files; zensical build --clean --strict (in .venv-docs) Passed; built without issues .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --version; --check-renderer; examples\SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render "…\SrTiO3 studio.png"; --export-pov ycrystal 0.4.0.dev0; PASS: POV-Ray 3.7.0.0 … sphere centres within 0.14 px; rendered in 4.7 s; exported (into an existing folder; a missing folder is refused, as documented) The rendering guide's command for an exported scene, Start-Process -Wait "…\pvengine64.exe" "/EXIT /NR SrTiO3.ini" Renders SrTiO3.png. PowerShell's call operator & returns at once instead (POV-Ray for Windows is a window program), hence -Wait Scripted run of the real window (as .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --sample perovskite): screen capture, 3 previews, 1 final render, foreground watched every 10 ms Draws correctly at device pixel ratio 1.25 (structure, output frame, a/b/c handles, axes, preview dock; Qt follows the Windows dark theme); previews ready in 2.6–2.7 s each; the final render saved; the foreground never left the Ycrystal window; AppUserModelID YMatterLab.Ycrystal set

items.title: Answers to the questions of the takeover
items.text:
# Question Answer (18 November 2026) 1 Does pvengine64.exe /EXIT /NR +GAscene.log scene.ini render scene.png and quit? Yes, in 2.3–2.8 s for a small scene. /EXIT /NR /RENDER scene.ini +GAscene.log behaves the same; the command line is kept 2 Exit status after success and after a parse error? 0 in both cases. After a parse error there is no image, and finish_job() already treats "status 0, no image" as a failure, explained from the log 3 Does scene.log hold POV-Ray's messages, including "Parse Error"? Yes (options, warnings, statistics, and the parse error with file and line). No progress lines 4 Does a dialog appear on the first start? Yes, two of them (found on the CI runner, see CI): the editor question on every start until the editor is installed or turned off, and the About box from the second start on, again every 14 days. On the laptop, the very first render produced no image within 90 s and the next start took 28 s: by then the user had installed the editor (its DLLs appeared in the installation folder during the session) and the About box had been shown and closed (ItsAboutTime set). POV-Ray's settings also hold [DontShowAgain] OneInstanceSet=1, the one-time Keep Single Instance notice. The completion-sound and output-file notices never appear with /EXIT (source) 5 Does the window stay minimised and not take the focus? Minimised: yes (watched in every state, "Starting" to "Done"). Focus: no — it makes itself the foreground window even when started minimised or hidden (SW_HIDE). A Qt window in the foreground that starts it took the foreground away 2 times in 2 trials without LockSetForegroundWindow, and 0 times with it (1 trial; in a second one the window had not got the foreground first, and Windows refused the lock, as documented). Implemented for the window; a terminal cannot do it, so --render loses the terminal's focus while POV-Ray runs. SW_HIDE would also keep its taskbar button away; minimised was kept, so that a POV-Ray dialog stays reachable 6 With POV-Ray for Windows already open, does a second render start a new copy? No. It shows the modal "Commandline processing error" box and waits (killed after 15 s; no image). With the new check, .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m ycrystal --check-renderer fails in 0.7 s with the explanation, and nothing appears. Ycrystal's own renders now take turns 7 Where are the include files, and are they found? Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7\include (the installation folder has none). Found; metals.inc and the others present. The folder is also read from the registry (DocPath) 8 Does povray_version() read a version starting with 3.7? Yes: 3.7.0.0 from the file version resource 9 Does the window open, draw, and render previews? Yes, in scripted runs: the 172 GUI tests open real windows at 125 % scale and pass, and a scripted run of the main window drew correctly and rendered previews without losing the focus (see the result). Not yet checked by hand 10 Do all tests pass? Yes: 898 passed, 3 skipped by design, with YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 (full suite)

Further observations:

  • Job folders whose path contains ñ, ü, or 晶体 Ω render, but this computer's system code page is UTF-8. Whether POV-Ray for Windows (an ANSI program) renders in a %TEMP% with characters outside a legacy code page (for example Chinese characters in a user name on a Western-European Windows) is unverified.
  • A clone made from main before .gitattributes existed keeps CRLF files after a switch to this branch; tests that hash tracked files would fail (see HANDOFF.md).

items.title: POV-Ray for Windows on CI
items.text:
povray.org answers GitHub's runners with a browser challenge, so CI cannot download the installer from there. Of the options considered on 17 November 2026 (a: keep the official installer as a release asset of this repository; b: a self-hosted runner; c: POV-Ray 3.8 beta; d: no POV-Ray on Windows CI), the user chose a on 18 November 2026 (PR #36):

  • The official installer, unmodified (SHA-256 above), is the asset povwin-3.7-agpl3-setup.exe of the release ci-assets (not a Ycrystal release; its notes give the licence, AGPL-3.0, and the source, github.com/POV-Ray/povray). The Windows job downloads it with its own token, refuses another checksum, and installs it silently.
  • Before POV-Ray's first start the job writes UseEditors=0 and ItsAboutTime (the latest 32-bit time) into the runner's pvengine.ini; without them, the editor question and the About box waited for an answer (screenshots of scripts/windows_povray_probe.py --screenshots, uploaded by the job).
  • The job is no longer experimental: it runs the renderer check, the documentation examples, and the tests without windows with YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1. First passing run: 727 passed, 2 skipped (POSIX-only tests), GUI tests not run (as on macOS: run them on a Windows computer).
  • Before the repository or the release becomes public, check the AGPL-3.0 obligations for passing the installer on (the release notes point to the source).

items.title: Installation in one command
items.text:
Asked by the user on 18 November 2026 ("is there a simpler method for installation?"). The manual installation had eight steps: - install Git and Python, then open a new terminal (else py is not found); - clone; create .venv; run the long pip line; - download POV-Ray for Windows from povray.org and install it; - start POV-Ray once to settle its editor question; - start Ycrystal from PowerShell every time (no Start-menu entry).

Its traps were the stale PATH and the editor question: a render then waited silently at a dialog in a minimised window.

Finding Checked how winget has the official POV-Ray installer: package PersistenceOfVisionRaytracer.POVRay 3.7, URL https://www.povray.org/ftp/pub/povray/Official/povwin-3.7-agpl3-setup.exe, the same SHA-256 as above, type nullsoft (silent with /S) winget show; winget download on the laptop fetched it from povray.org and verified the checksum (no browser challenge for a home connection); winget list recognises the installed POV-Ray as this package POV-Ray for Windows asks about its editor exactly when [General] UseEditors (in pvengine.ini, default 1) is not 0 and the editor library (cmedit64.dll for the 64-bit build) loads neither from the program's folder nor from bin of the installation folder recorded in the registry (Home) Its source: windows/pvengine.cpp (WinMain), windows/pvedit.cpp (LoadEditorDLL), windows/pvengine.h (EDITDLLNAME), windows/pvmisc.cpp (editors_enabled) Git for Windows signs in to GitHub in the browser for a private repository over HTTPS (Git Credential Manager) git config --show-origin credential.helper: manager in the installation's gitconfig The SVG icon renders without an application object (QSvgRenderer into a QImage) Run on the laptop

Implemented:

  • scripts/install-windows.ps1 (ASCII, for Windows PowerShell 5.1, which every Windows 11 has): Python 3.12 with winget --scope user unless py finds Python 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 (in this order; older ones are refused, also in an existing .venv) (it re-reads PATH from the registry, so no new terminal is needed); .venv; pip install -e . -c constraints.txt; POV-Ray for Windows with winget unless found; if POV-Ray would ask about its editor, it opens once with instructions; the Start-menu entry; --check-renderer. Idempotent; exit status 0 only when everything is ready, with a list of what is not otherwise. Options -Python, -Dev, -NoPovray, -NoStartMenu.
  • --install-desktop on Windows (desktop.py, windows_shortcut.py):
  • Ycrystal.lnk in the user's Start-menu folder (SHGetKnownFolderPath). It starts .venv\Scripts\pythonw.exe -I -m ycrystal.app, so that no console window opens; -I keeps a ycrystal module in the starting folder from shadowing the package, and is used only inside a virtual environment.
  • The shortcut carries the application id YMatterLab.Ycrystal, the one set_taskbar_identity() gives the window. It is written through IShellLinkW, IPropertyStore, and IPersistFile with ctypes, since WScript.Shell cannot set it.
  • An .ico with 8 sizes drawn from the SVG by Qt, in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal.
  • The file type Ycrystal.Project for .ycrystal under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes. The user's own Open with choice (UserChoice) is left alone, and so is an .ycrystal key that points elsewhere at uninstall.
  • --uninstall-desktop removes all three; macOS still refuses both options.
  • The editor question is reported instead of waited for: windows_engine_conflict() returns EDITOR_QUESTION_MESSAGE when editor_question_pending() holds, so --check-renderer, previews, and renders fail at once with the remedy. Stand-in programs (.cmd) are never checked.
  • Windows CI runs the script in Windows PowerShell 5.1 into a new .venv (with -Python from setup-python, POV-Ray already installed) and reads the shortcut back.

Evidence on the laptop (18 November 2026):

Check Result A copy of the checkout in a folder with a space (…\Temp\yc trial\ycrystal), no .venv, powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows.ps1 in Windows PowerShell 5.1 Found Python 3.12 through py; created .venv; installed the pinned packages; found POV-Ray; editor question settled (the editor is installed here), so no prompt; Start-menu entry and icon installed; PASS: … within 0.14 px; "Ycrystal is ready.", exit status 0 The same script again Reused .venv, reinstalled only Ycrystal, check passed; 29 s The Start-menu shortcut opened as a click does (os.startfile) One new window, "SrTiO3 (unsaved) — Ycrystal", process pythonw.exe, no console window; its own taskbar button with the Ycrystal icon; the automatic POV-Ray preview rendered (2.8 s). Get-StartApps: Ycrystal, AppID YMatterLab.Ycrystal examples\SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal opened as a double-click does Opened in Ycrystal ("SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal — Ycrystal", pythonw.exe) New tests: tests/test_windows_desktop.py (launch command, icon sizes, the shortcut's fields and application id written and read back with a non-ASCII path, Start-menu entry and file type installed and removed in a test registry key, another program's file type left alone, the two command-line options); tests/test_windows_povray.py (the editor question: settings, both library folders, other programs; reported before starting) Passed Full suite, YCRYSTAL_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 pytest -q -rs 906 passed, 3 skipped (POSIX-only), 12.4 min Python 3.13.17 and 3.14.10 (python.org, winget): the script with -Python … -Dev -NoStartMenu on fresh copies, then the full suite Both "Ycrystal is ready." (pins from wheels); 906 passed, 3 skipped on each (PROGRESS.md)

Not verified: installing Python and POV-Ray through the script (both were already on the laptop); the script's editor prompt (the editor is installed here); pinning the running window to the taskbar by hand; the entry on another Windows computer.

items.title: Still open
items.text:
1. Hands-on use. The user tested Ycrystal by hand on the Windows laptop on 18 November 2026 and reports that it works well; which items were tried was not recorded. On another Windows computer, a fuller check can follow the macOS checklist in HANDOFF.md, adapted: the window draws sharply at the display's scale; mouse and touchpad; selection; menus and Ctrl shortcuts; File Explorer dialogs; Set POV-Ray Executable… and Check Renderer; previews with Update automatically (the POV-Ray taskbar button, the keyboard focus staying in Ycrystal); a long render cancelled; closing the window during a render; a project saved on Linux or macOS renders the same on Windows and back; whether POV-Ray plays a sound (none expected with /EXIT).
  2. POV-Ray for Windows' About box for users. Every 14 days (and at the second start after installation) POV-Ray for Windows shows its About box when it starts, also when Ycrystal starts it minimised, and waits for OK; the render waits with it. This is documented (install guide, troubleshooting). Ycrystal does not change the user's POV-Ray settings; whether it should detect the box and bring it forward is undecided.
  3. The installation script on a new computer (see installation): with neither Python nor POV-Ray installed, so that the winget steps and the editor prompt run; then Pin to taskbar on the running window.
  4. Out of scope until decided:
  5. code signing of the graphical installer, which exists since branch feature/windows-installer (PyInstaller + Inno Setup; see Windows installer) but is not signed;
  6. Windows on ARM; Windows 10;
  7. progress percentages during renders with POV-Ray for Windows. It prints none, but its window title carries them (POV-Ray for Windows [Rendering scene.pov: 37%]), which a later change could read;
  8. an option to start POV-Ray hidden (SW_HIDE) instead of minimised.

items.title: Materials, backgrounds, and lighting
items.text:
The Scene ▸ Appearance tab and the two galleries (Edit ▸ Material Gallery…, Edit ▸ Environment Gallery…) control how atoms, bonds, and their surroundings look in the POV-Ray preview and the rendered PNG. Every change is undoable (Ctrl+Z) and saved in projects.

The 3D view approximates materials (colour, highlights, and transparency), gradients, and floors. Shadows, reflections, refraction, clouds, and procedural textures such as marble appear only in the POV-Ray preview (F5) and the render; use the preview to judge them.

items.title: Choosing materials
items.text: A material decides how a surface reacts to light. Colour and material are separate: the Colour column of the element table sets an element's colour, the Radius column its sphere radius in Å, and the Material column its material. The ↺ button returns an element to its default colour and radius (the covalent radius times the Atom size in the Structure tab).

items.title: Choosing colours
items.text:
Click a colour button (an element's Colour, or the background and floor colours) to open the colour dialog. Choose a colour in one of three ways:

  • Spectrum: hue from left to right, lightness from top (white) to bottom (black); the Saturation slider below it makes the colours more vivid or greyer.
  • Named colours: the 140 CSS colours (silver, steel blue, tomato, …).
  • Type a colour in any notation; all fields update together:
Field Range Example (red) Hex #RRGGBB, any case (also #RGB) #FF0000 RGB (0–255) three integers 0–255 255 0 0 RGB (0–1) three fractions, three decimals — the values stored in projects and POV-Ray scenes 1.000 0.000 0.000 HSV hue 0–359°, saturation 0–100 %, value 0–100 % 0, 100, 100 HSL hue 0–359°, saturation 0–100 %, lightness 0–100 % 0, 100, 50 Name or any notation a CSS name or any of the notations below red

In the text field, rgb(255, 0, 0), rgb(100%, 0%, 0%), hsv(0, 100%, 100%), hsl(0, 100%, 50%), and three numbers are accepted. Numbers are never reinterpreted: integers are 0–255 (1 0 0 is almost black), numbers written with a decimal point are fractions 0–1 (1.0 0 0 is red), and HSV/HSL saturation, value, and lightness are always percent, with or without %. Names ignore case and spaces; "grey" and "gray", "aqua" (= cyan), and "fuchsia" (= magenta) are accepted. A field completes names as you type.

Text that cannot be read is explained below the fields, leaves the colour unchanged, and disables OK until it is corrected; valid text that was typed but not yet confirmed with Enter is applied when you press OK. HSV and HSL show one decimal, so switching between notations does not drift (each 8-bit channel stays within one step). For a grey (no hue), the hue you typed is kept so that adding saturation continues from it. OK applies the colour as one undoable step; Cancel keeps the old one; the ↺ button in the element table returns to the default colour and radius.

The dialog works without a mouse: Tab moves between the fields and the named-colour grid; in the grid, the arrow keys move and Enter or Space chooses. Every field has an accessible name (for example "HSL lightness in percent") for screen readers.

Colour names for everyone. Rest the mouse on the spectrum or a named colour (or move the keyboard focus in the grid), and the dialog writes that colour in words with its exact values, for example Under the mouse: brown (nearest named colour: chocolate #D2691E) — #C25200 — RGB (194, 82, 0). The first part is a plain description from a small vocabulary (red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, purple, magenta, pink, brown, olive, black, grey, white, with dark, light, or greyish); the second is the closest CSS named colour by perceived difference (CIEDE2000). It says exactly the named colour … only when the colour equals it at 8-bit precision, and nearest named colour … otherwise; the hex and RGB values are always the exact ones. Hovering only identifies a colour; clicking chooses it. The chosen colour is described the same way above the fields, named-colour tooltips read like red — #FF0000 — RGB (255, 0, 0), and every colour button's tooltip and accessible name state its colour (Colour of O: red (nearest named colour: red #FF0000) with its values). This helps people with colour-vision deficiencies tell element colours apart; descriptions are approximate and supplement, not replace, the colours themselves.

The colour of an element is its base colour: it does not change its radius, material, or opacity. Materials with their own colours (gold, chrome, marble, …) hide it; the colour button's tooltip then says so, and the colour returns when you choose another material.

Materials are assigned at three levels. The most specific one wins:

  1. Selected atoms — click atoms (Ctrl+click for several), then Edit ▸ Material for Selection… (Ctrl+M) or Material for Selection… in the Appearance tab. Like hiding, this applies to the displayed balls you picked: other periodic images of the same atom keep their material.
  2. Element — the Material column of the element table, or the gallery with Apply to: Element X.
  3. Default — the Default menu, or the gallery with Apply to: All atoms.

Use Default (gallery or panel) removes the override of an element or of the selected atoms; Clear All removes every per-atom override. Each half of a bond uses the material of its atom.

items.title: The material gallery
items.text:
The gallery shows a thumbnail of every material rendered by POV-Ray in the same scene, so materials can be compared directly. Type in the search field to filter by name, description, category, POV-Ray identifier (for example T_Gold_3C), or include file (metals.inc). The category menu also offers ★ Favourites: mark a material with Add to favourites. Favourites are stored for your user account, not in projects. Double-click a thumbnail or press Apply.

Materials marked own colours use POV-Ray's built-in pigments (gold, marble, wood…) and replace the element colour; the gallery says so for each material. The others keep the element colours.

items.title: Catalog
items.text:
Material Category POV-Ray declaration Include files Colour Matte Scientific finishes finish — element colour Satin (default) Scientific finishes finish — element colour Glossy Scientific finishes finish — element colour Ceramic (glazed) Scientific finishes finish — element colour Plastic Scientific finishes finish — element colour VMD style (ASE) Scientific finishes finish — element colour Jmol style (ASE) Scientific finishes finish — element colour ASE2 style (ASE) Scientific finishes finish — element colour ASE3 style (ASE) Scientific finishes finish — element colour Intermediate (ASE) Scientific finishes finish — element colour Metallic Metals finish — element colour Polished metal (F_MetalD) Metals finish metals.inc element colour Soft metal (F_MetalB) Metals finish metals.inc element colour Gold (T_Gold_3C) Metals texture metals.inc own colour Silver (T_Silver_3C) Metals texture metals.inc own colour Copper (T_Copper_3C) Metals texture metals.inc own colour Brass (T_Brass_3C) Metals texture metals.inc own colour Bronze (Bright_Bronze) Metals texture textures.inc own colour Chrome (Polished_Chrome) Metals texture textures.inc own colour Aluminium (Aluminum) Metals texture textures.inc own colour Glass (tinted) Glass and transparent material (IOR 1.45) — element colour Frosted glass Glass and transparent material (IOR 1.5) — element colour Gem (IOR 2.4) Glass and transparent material (IOR 2.42) — element colour Clear glass (M_Glass) Glass and transparent material textures.inc own colour Ruby glass (M_Ruby_Glass) Glass and transparent material textures.inc own colour White marble (White_Marble) Decorative textures pigment textures.inc own colour Jade (Jade) Decorative textures pigment textures.inc own colour Pink granite (Pink_Granite) Decorative textures pigment textures.inc own colour Stone (T_Stone25) Decorative textures texture colors.inc, stones.inc own colour Cherry wood (Cherry_Wood) Decorative textures pigment textures.inc own colour

The ASE styles use the finish values of ASE's ase.io.pov writer. Names in parentheses are native POV-Ray identifiers. Exported scenes use them unchanged, so POV-Ray users can recognise and edit them. Scenes that use them #include the standard files listed above (shipped with POV-Ray: sudo apt install povray-includes on Linux Mint); the export says which files are needed and warns if one is missing.

Procedural textures (marble, granite, stone, wood, frosted glass, and the native metals) are scaled to each atom, so the pattern has the same size on every atom.

items.title: Customizing a material
items.text:
Customize Material… (Appearance tab, or Edit ▸ Customize Material…) starts from a material and adjusts its parameters. Choose Apply to (the default material, an element, or the selected atoms) and Start from (the material to vary). The usual precedence stays: selected atom > element > default, and each half of a bond takes the material of its atom. A selection is the one at the moment the dialog opens; selecting other atoms while the dialog is open does not change where the variant goes.

Start from Parameters you can change Matte, Satin, Glossy, Ceramic Diffuse amount, specular amount, highlight roughness, reflection amount Plastic Diffuse amount, specular amount (phong), highlight sharpness (phong size), reflection amount Glass (tinted), Gem As above, plus glass filter amount and refractive index Frosted glass As Glass, plus bump strength and bump scale of the frosted relief Marble, Jade, Granite, Stone, Wood Pattern scale (relative to each atom)

Highlight roughness changes only the size of the highlight; the bump values change the surface relief. The glass filter amount says how much light passes through, tinted by the atom colour; it is not a generic opacity or a measured optical constant. Materials that use POV-Ray's own definitions (the metals, M_Glass, M_Ruby_Glass) and the ASE styles cannot be edited; the dialog explains why and keeps Apply disabled.

While you edit, the 3D view and the POV-Ray preview show the variant (the 3D view only approximates highlight and transparency; check the preview). Reset to Base returns to the values of the material you started from. Apply assigns the variant as one undoable step; Cancel restores the previous look and leaves nothing on the undo stack. A variant leaves the built-in materials unchanged; an untouched variant renders exactly like its base.

Save as My Material keeps the variant in your user settings. It then appears in the material menus (marked ✎) and in the gallery's category My materials, with a POV-Ray thumbnail when POV-Ray is available (otherwise the base material's thumbnail with a ✎ badge). Every variant has its own id derived from its name and values, so a variant can never replace a built-in material or another variant. Projects and styles store the full definition of every variant they use, so they open on another computer without your personal list, and exported .pov files contain the variant's declaration and name.

items.title: Environments
items.text:
An environment preset sets the background, the floor, and the lighting together. Choose one from the Environment menu or the environment gallery, then adjust each part in the groups below it; the note under the menu says when the environment was modified.

Environment Background Floor Lighting Description White solid — Soft Plain white background. Transparent (PNG alpha) solid — Soft Transparent PNG; the live view shows light grey. Light grey solid — Soft Plain light grey background. Dark grey solid — Bright Dark background, light cell edges, reflection panel. Black solid — Bright Black background, light cell edges, reflection panel. White to grey gradient gradient — Soft White at the top to light grey at the bottom. Blue to white gradient gradient — Soft Soft blue at the top to white at the bottom. White studio (soft shadows) solid white Studio White matte floor with soft shadows. Grey studio with floor solid grey Studio Mid-grey floor with soft shadows. Dark studio, reflective floor solid dark, reflective Bright Floor mirrors the structure; reflection panel. Clear sky sky — Bright Pale horizon to a blue zenith. Cloudy sky sky — Bright Blue sky with white clouds.

Presets with dark backgrounds also switch the cell edges to a light colour.

items.title: Background
items.text: Type is Solid colour, Vertical gradient (top and bottom colours), or Sky (zenith and horizon colours, and Clouds from 0 to 100 %). Gradients and skies run from the bottom to the top of the output frame, whatever the orientation of the structure. Transparent PNG background gives rendered images an alpha channel; floors, gradients, and skies are then left out (transparent glass still lets the alpha through).

items.title: Background picture
items.text:
Type Image shows one of your own pictures behind the structure in the POV-Ray preview and the rendered PNG. Choose Image… imports a PNG or JPEG file (up to 64 MB, 12000 pixels per side, and 50 megapixels); the panel shows its name and pixel size. Replace… swaps the picture and keeps the framing, Remove deletes it (the background colour remains). A file that cannot be read is refused with a message, and the current background stays. Camera-phone pictures with an EXIF orientation are shown upright.

  • Framing: Fill covers the whole output frame and crops what does not fit (the default); Fit shows the whole picture, with margins in the Margin colour (the background colour). The picture keeps its proportions; it is never stretched.
  • Zoom (10–1000 %) scales the filled or fitted picture about its centre. Horizontal and Vertical move it by percentages of the output frame's width and height (positive: right and up). Brightness (0–200 %) scales its colours; 100 % shows them unchanged. Reset Framing returns to Fill, 100 %, centred.
  • The picture belongs to the output frame: orbiting or zooming the structure does not move it, and the preview and the final PNG show the same composition at any resolution. Changing the output's aspect ratio refits it.
  • Transparent pixels of a PNG show the margin colour.

The picture is a backdrop, not a light: it does not light the structure, casts no shadows, and is not seen in reflections (reflective atoms reflect its average colour). Transparent and refractive materials such as glass show the picture through the atom, bent by refraction. The 3D view shows the picture's average colour; the POV-Ray preview is authoritative. A floor covers the picture in the orthographic view: the panel then says so and offers Turn Off Floor. With Transparent PNG background the picture is left out of renders but kept for later. Choosing an environment preset changes the background type but remembers the picture, so switching back to Image restores it.

The picture is copied into the project when you save, so the original file is not needed afterwards (see Reusing the look). File ▸ Export POV-Ray… copies it next to the .pov file as bg_<digest>.png (or .jpg) and refers to it by that relative name, so the export folder can be moved as a whole.

items.title: Floor
items.text: A floor lies below the structure as seen in the frame, tilted slightly towards the viewer so that it catches shadows (and, with Reflection, mirrors the structure). Gap below atoms moves it down from the lowest atom. In the orthographic view the floor fills the whole background, so the live view simply shows its colour.

items.title: Lighting
items.text:
Lighting Description Soft (default) Upper-left key light with a soft fill; Ycrystal's lighting since the first version. Studio (soft shadows) Large area key light from the upper left: soft shadows on floors. Bright Strong key and fill point lights; for dark backgrounds and skies. Dramatic side light Hard key light from the side with a weak fill: strong shading and shadows. Top light Area light from above: shadows fall straight down onto a floor. Flat (no shadows) Two even, shadowless lights from the front: low contrast for schematic figures.

The controls below the preset adjust the Key light and Fill light intensities, the key-light direction (Key azimuth and Key elevation), Light size, Shadows, and the Reflection panel.

items.title: How the lights are placed
items.text:
Lights belong to the image, not to the crystal: they are placed relative to the output camera, so the key light always comes from the same side of the image while you orbit, roll, or pan.

  • Origin: the camera's focal point F, the point at the centre of the image.
  • Key azimuth: 0° points from F straight toward the camera (a light from the viewer's position); positive values turn to the right of the image, negative to the left; ±180° is behind the structure. The presets use −20° to −65° (upper left).
  • Key elevation: degrees above the image's horizontal, toward the top of the image; −30° to 89°. When you roll the camera, the horizontal rolls with the image.
  • Distance: both lights sit at the same distance from F: 4 R + |C − F| + 10 Å, where C and R are the centre and radius of a sphere around the displayed atoms and cell edges (boundary atoms and repeated cells included, hidden atoms left out). Zooming or changing the output size does not move the lights; panning away from the structure moves them a little further out. Light does not get weaker with distance, so the distance changes the direction of shadows slightly, not the brightness.
  • Fill light: a fixed direction at the lower right, in front of the structure (azimuth +35°, elevation −11.6° in the same convention). It never casts shadows; only its intensity can be changed.
  • Intensities are the brightness of white light (POV-Ray color rgb); 0 switches a light off.
  • Light size: 0 is a point light with sharp shadows. A larger value makes the key light a round area light whose diameter is the value times the scene radius R (0.5 on a structure with R = 4.4 Å gives a light 2.2 Å across). POV-Ray turns the round light toward each point it lights, so it behaves like a glowing ball of that size. Shadows are sampled from a 5 × 5 grid of points on the light, refined adaptively where a shadow edge needs it.
  • Reflection panel: an invisible bright disc on the key-light side of the structure that only appears in reflections, so that metals and glass do not look black on dark backgrounds. It is not a light source and does not light anything.

items.title: Lighting Setup window
items.text:
Lighting Setup… (below the lighting controls, or View ▸ Lighting Setup…) opens a 3D overview of the lights, the output camera, and a lightweight copy of the displayed structure:

  • orange sphere: the key light; blue cube: the fill light; both with labels and guide lines from F;
  • black cross: F; purple octahedron: C;
  • grey cone and line: the output camera's viewing direction (its distance does not matter for an orthographic image); blue rectangle: the output frame;
  • grey ring: the horizontal circle at the light distance, with the azimuth and elevation arcs of the key light;
  • wire sphere: the area-light diameter, when the light size is not 0; white disc: the reflection panel, when it is on.

Drag the orange key-light sphere to change azimuth and elevation together, or the flat orange disc on the ring to change only the azimuth. The angles are always measured in the output camera's frame, whichever way you have turned the overview, and they snap to whole degrees like the spin boxes. While you drag, the live view, the spin boxes, and the overview follow; releasing the button applies the change as one undoable step (and starts the automatic preview if it is on). Esc or the right mouse button cancels the drag and restores the previous direction. Elsewhere in the overview, drag to orbit, Shift-drag or middle-drag to pan, and use the wheel to zoom; this never changes the image. Reset Overview fits the overview again. The window also has azimuth and elevation spin boxes for the keyboard and a read-out of the resolved values.

items.title: What the live view shows
items.text:
The live view uses the key and fill lights at their real positions and intensities (without distance fall-off), so the shading direction matches the POV-Ray image. It does not show shadows, the softness of area lights, reflections, refraction, or the reflection panel; check those in the POV-Ray preview. The live view's shading is an approximation and is not expected to match the POV-Ray image pixel for pixel.

Area lights (Studio, Top) soften shadows at little cost for opaque materials, but make transparent materials much slower to render, because POV-Ray traces shadow rays through the glass. While composing a glass figure, use Soft or Bright lighting or switch off Update automatically in the preview dock.

items.title: Reusing the look: styles
items.text:
Materials, colours, radii, the environment, and the lighting are saved in projects (.ycrystal, schema 8) and restored exactly when the project is reopened. Projects saved by earlier versions open with their original appearance. A project or style with a background picture is saved as a ZIP package that contains the picture (the suffix stays .ycrystal or .ycstyle); others remain a single JSON file. Ycrystal recognises both forms by their content. Damaged or unsafe packages, and packages that miss their picture, are refused with a message and nothing changes. Ycrystal 0.2.0 and older cannot open schema-6 or later projects or packages.

Figures that belong together (in one paper, poster, or talk) should look alike: the same background, lighting, image size, and materials. A style keeps that look apart from any structure, so you design it once and reuse it. File ▸ Export Style… writes a .ycstyle file, and File ▸ Import Style… applies one to the open structure. The import dialog lets you choose the parts to apply:

Part Contents Materials, colours, and radii Default material; material, colour, and radius of each element; the appearance of vector arrows (never the vectors themselves); the element legend Display Atom size, repetitions, boundary atoms, cell edges, bond length, radius, and pair rules Environment Background (including a background picture), floor, lighting, transparency, and the cell-edge colour Output image size Width and height in pixels

A style never changes the structure's coordinates, and it has no camera. The import is one undoable step. Settings that refer to something the new structure does not have are left out, and a message lists them:

  • Element settings (material, colour, radius) and bond-pair rules apply to the elements the structure contains; those of other elements are left out, unless you map them (see element mapping).
  • Per-atom materials and hidden atoms refer to individual atoms of the original structure. They are applied only if the new structure has the same number of atoms with the same element at every position (for example the same structure from another file, or relaxed); otherwise they are left out.
  • Repetitions that would display more than 20,000 atoms ask for confirmation first.

A style can also be applied without a window, for example to render many structures with the same look from a script: ycrystal FILE --style STYLE.ycstyle --render OUT.png (see styles from the command line). There, the display part is left out unless you ask for it.

items.title: Element mapping: a style for another composition
items.text:
Element settings in a style are stored by element symbol. That works for the same compound, but not for a related one: a style made for SrTiO3 has settings for Sr, Ti, and O, and applied to BaZrO3 only the O settings find their element. Yet the two perovskites have the same structure, with Ba where Sr is and Zr where Ti is, and a series of figures is easiest to compare when corresponding atoms look the same. An element mapping states that correspondence for drawing: give the Ti settings (for example chrome) to Zr, and the Sr settings to Ba. Map the elements while importing:

  • In the window: the Import Style dialog lists every element the style has settings for, under Element settings go to, with the element of the open structure that receives them. Each row starts at the same symbol, or Do not transfer if the structure does not contain it, so pressing Apply without changing anything works as before. Choose another element of the structure for a row, or Do not transfer to leave its settings out. Match Symbols returns to the start. Below the rows the dialog shows what will be applied and what is left out (for example Element settings applied: O, Sr → Ba, Ti → Zr.) before you press Apply. The import stays one undoable step.
  • From the command line: --element-map Sr=Ba,Ti=Zr, with O=- to leave the settings of O out (see styles from the command line).

The mapping moves the element materials, colours, and radii, and the bond-pair rules (an O–Ti rule becomes O–Zr). Elements you do not map keep matching by symbol. The choices must be unambiguous, or Ycrystal refuses them and says why:

  • Each element of the structure receives the settings of one element at most: mapping both Sr and Ti to Ba is refused.
  • If the style also has settings for the target element itself, mapping another element onto it is refused (Ti → O when the style has O settings). Map O elsewhere, or leave its settings out, to make the choice explicit.
  • Targets must be elements of the open structure; symbols are case-sensitive (Zr, not ZR).
  • An element mapped elsewhere does not also keep its own settings: with Sr → Ti in a structure that contains Sr, the Sr atoms get no Sr settings (a note says so).

The mapping is a presentation choice: it decides which colours and materials an element is drawn with. It does not claim chemical equivalence or that the sites of the two structures correspond, and it never changes atoms, element labels, coordinates, vectors, or which bonds exist. Per-atom materials and hidden atoms still transfer only to the same structure, mapping or not. The mapping is not stored in the style file; saving the project keeps the resulting appearance.

items.title: Controls and display
items.text:
Use the mouse and view shortcuts over the 3D viewport. VTK's default keys such as q (quit) and w (wireframe) are disabled. Help ▸ Mouse Controls (F1) opens the in-app summary.
