Input Action Left drag Orbit about the view centre (or turn about the chosen axis, see below) Middle drag or Shift + left drag Pan Wheel or right drag Zoom F / toolbar Fit Fit the displayed geometry, preserving orientation View ▸ Reset View Restore the default orientation and fit Left click without dragging Select the front-most ball; empty space clears Ctrl + click Add/remove a ball from the selection Esc Clear selection (in a measurement mode: cancel the incomplete measurement) Distance / Bond angle (View along toolbar, Edit menu) Measure between clicked atoms; see Measurements Edit ▸ Vectors… Attach direction or magnetic-moment arrows to atoms; see Vectors Delete or Backspace Hide selected displayed atoms Ctrl+M Material for the selected atoms (Edit ▸ Material for Selection…) Drag an a, b, or c handle Add or remove whole cells along that axis Esc or right button during a handle drag Cancel the drag Drag a light handle in Lighting Setup Set the key-light direction (one undo step; Esc cancels) Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right Turn by the step angle about the rotation axis Ctrl+Z Undo a display-setting change Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y Redo a display-setting change Ctrl+O Open a structure or project Ctrl+S / Ctrl+Shift+S Save Project / Save Project As… F5 POV-Ray preview of the framed view Ctrl+R Render Image… as PNG, PDF, or JPEG (toolbar Cancel Render stops it) Ctrl+Q Quit (asks about unsaved changes)

On macOS, read Ctrl as ⌘ (Command) throughout: ⌘ + click toggles the selection (Control + click is a right click there), ⌘Z undoes, ⌘R renders. The function keys F1 and F5 may need the Fn key, depending on the keyboard settings. A mouse or trackpad without a middle button pans with Shift + left drag.

items.title: Boundary atoms and hiding
items.text:
View ▸ Show Boundary Atoms is on by default. Atoms are wrapped along periodic cell directions and repeated on equivalent faces, edges, and corners. A corner atom can appear eight times. Turning the option off shows each input atom once per repeated cell at its original position plus the cell translation. Repetition controls expand the display from the original structure without changing the scientific atom count.

Each ball has its own identity: the source atom (0-based internally, 1-based in the status bar) and an integer image offset (na, nb, nc). The offset is relative to the input position. A selected ball's Cartesian position is input_position + image_offset @ cell, with lattice vectors as cell rows.

Delete hides only selected balls, including from POV exports and renders. Other images of the same atom stay visible. View ▸ Show All Atoms restores all hidden IDs. Hidden IDs survive toggling boundary images off and on. Selection highlights are viewport overlays and do not appear in the figure.

Undo/redo covers every change to the figure: hiding, Show All Atoms, boundary images, repetitions (including handle drags), cell-edge modes, bond settings, atom size and element radii, materials (default, element, and atom), element colours, environments, backgrounds, floors, lighting, the output size, and style imports. A handle drag or a style import is one step; consecutive spin-box adjustments of the same value merge into one step. Camera navigation (orbit, pan, zoom, rotation, view directions) is not on the undo stack; View ▸ Reset View returns to the default orientation. File opens and saves are not undoable; opening a new file clears the undo history. A changed camera still marks the project modified. The aspect-ratio lock in the Render tab is saved in projects but is not an undo step; see lock aspect ratio.

items.title: Output framing
items.text:
The output size is set in Scene ▸ Render (width and height, 16 to 8000 pixels, with aspect presets). A blue frame in the 3D view marks the rendered area; outside it the view is dimmed. Resizing the window moves the frame on screen but does not change the image. Projection is orthographic; atoms do not shrink with distance from the camera. See output size and frame.

The structure's coordinates, occupancies, and movable flags are scientific data. Camera, radii, colours, boundary images, hiding, materials, background, and lighting are presentation state; see Materials, backgrounds, and lighting for the Scene ▸ Appearance tab and the galleries. There is no atom editor.

items.title: Supercells, bonds, and directions
items.text: The Scene dock has Structure, Bonds, Appearance, Legend (the element legend), and Render tabs. If closed, reopen it from View ▸ Scene. Under Structure, set repetitions along a, b, c (1 to 20), use + all / − all, or reset with 1 × 1 × 1. Typed counts apply on Enter or focus change. The view refits after a repetition change. Expansions above 20,000 displayable atoms ask for confirmation before building geometry. Non-periodic axes are not repeated. Hidden IDs persist across expansion and shrinking. Atom size sets the sphere radius as a multiple of the covalent radius (per-element radii are in the Appearance tab).

items.title: Supercell handles
items.text:
Coloured a (red), b (green), and c (blue) handles sit outside the repeated block, on the line through the centre of its far face along each lattice direction. Drag a handle outward to add cells along that axis, inward to remove them (at least one cell remains). While you drag, an orange outline shows the new block and a label gives the cell counts and the number of atoms; orbiting is disabled. The geometry is rebuilt when you release the button, as one undoable step; Esc or the right button cancels the drag. Handles are hidden for non-periodic axes, for structures without a cell, and for directions that point almost at the viewer (rotate the view to reach them). View ▸ Supercell Handles switches them off. Handles exist only in the live view; they never appear in exports or renders.

Cell edges offers All unit cells, Outline of the repeated block, Original cell only, or None. The boundary option applies to the repeated block.

Under Bonds, Show bonds controls visibility. Max. length ranges from 0.80 through 1.50 times the sum of covalent radii; Radius ranges from 0.02 through 0.50 Å. Element-pair checkboxes override the default rule: metal–metal pairs start off in compounds containing non-metals. The pair list reports candidates and length ranges per original cell, not the number drawn in the repeated block. A bond appears only when both endpoint atoms are displayed; hiding an atom removes its bonds. These are geometric contacts, not calculated chemical bond orders.

The View along toolbar offers a, b, c and x, y, z. The selected positive axis points toward the viewer; hold Shift when clicking to reverse it. Screen up is the first of c, b, a (for x, y, z: z, y, x) that is not parallel to the chosen axis, so looking down a or b puts c up and looking down c puts b up. a, b, c are the real-space lattice vectors, not normals of lattice planes: in a skewed cell, looking down c is not the same as looking at the (001) plane face-on, and lattice directions differ from Cartesian directions. These actions fit the view and affect the camera only; they are outside the display-setting undo stack. ycrystal --view uses exactly the same rule (see choose the view).

items.title: Rotation modes
items.text:
The Rotate menu in the View along toolbar chooses how a left drag rotates:

  • freely (default): trackball rotation in all directions.
  • about a, b, c (lattice vectors) or about x, y, z (Cartesian axes): the rotation is restricted to that axis through the view centre. The axis keeps its direction on screen while the structure turns around it. Drag across the axis as it appears on screen; when the axis points at you, move the mouse in a circle around the view centre instead.

The ⟲ and ⟳ buttons (Ctrl+Left, Ctrl+Right) turn by the angle chosen next to them (5° to 90°) about the rotation axis, or about the line of sight in free mode, for exact orientations. Clicks still select atoms, and Shift + left drag still pans. Rotation changes only the view: coordinates are unchanged, and the mode is not saved in projects. Lattice axes are unavailable for structures without a cell.

items.title: Measurements
items.text:
Distance and Bond angle in the View along toolbar (also Edit ▸ Measure Distance and Edit ▸ Measure Bond Angle) switch from selecting to measuring. The two modes exclude each other; click the active button again to return to ordinary selection. Navigation is unchanged: a drag still orbits, pans, or zooms and never picks an atom, and only a click without dragging counts.

  • Distance: click atom A, then atom B. The result is their separation in Å.
  • Bond angle: click A, then B, then C. The result is the angle A–B–C in degrees (0° to 180°) with B as the vertex, from the arms A − B and C − B. No bond needs to be drawn between the atoms.

The bold text in the status bar says which atom to click next, for example “Bond angle: select atom B — angle vertex”. The picked atoms get a teal wire cage and a boxed letter (A, B, or “B vertex”); a dashed line joins them, and an angle shows a small arc at the vertex. Esc cancels an incomplete measurement and removes these marks (a second Esc clears the ordinary selection); switching modes also cancels it. After a measurement the mode stays on, so the next click starts a new one. Clicking empty space keeps the atoms picked so far; clicking the same ball twice in one measurement is refused with an explanation.

Which atoms are measured. Each ball is one displayed instance: a source atom and its periodic image offset [na nb nc] (see Boundary atoms and hiding). Ycrystal measures exactly the instances you click, at input_position + [na nb nc] @ cell, also in supercells, with boundary images, and in non-orthogonal cells. It does not replace them by the nearest periodic image (no minimum-image convention): to measure across a cell boundary, click the image on the other side. Two images of the same atom are different balls and can be measured against each other. The values come from the structure's coordinates and cell only, so the camera, zoom, atom size, materials, and lighting never change them.

The Measurements panel opens at the bottom of the window, under the 3D view, with the first completed measurement (View ▸ Measurements shows or hides it later). Each row gives the type, the atoms (element, input label, 1-based atom number, and image, e.g. A: O #3 [0 0 0] · B (vertex): Ti #2 [0 0 0] · C: O #4 [0 1 0]), and the result, e.g. 1.9525 Å or 90.00° — vertex B. New measurements are added below the earlier ones. Distances show four decimals and angles two; the full value is in the tooltip, and the decimals do not express an uncertainty. Copy Selected (or Ctrl+C in the table) copies the selected rows as text with atoms, units, and the vertex, for example Angle A–B–C: 90.00° — vertex B (A = O #3 [0 0 0], B = Ti #2 [0 0 0], C = O #4 [0 0 0]). Remove Selected and Clear All delete rows.

Measurements are inspection data for the current session: they are not saved in projects, styles, or exports, and the marks never appear in the POV-Ray preview, the rendered PNG, or the .pov file; they do not affect Fit, the lights, or picking. Opening another structure or project clears all measurements. When a measured ball disappears from the display (boundary atoms off, fewer repetitions, hiding), the measurements that use it are removed and the panel says so; the others stay, because each identity still denotes the same position in the same structure. Undoing the change does not bring removed measurements back.

items.title: Vectors (arrows on atoms)
items.text:
Edit ▸ Vectors… (or Vectors… in the Appearance tab) attaches arrows to atoms, for example to illustrate a magnetic structure. You enter the vectors yourself; Ycrystal does not compute, read, or infer magnetic moments.

What a vector is. Three Cartesian components in the structure's own right-handed frame, the frame of the atom positions (not fractional or lattice coordinates, and not a DFT code's spin axes). The camera never changes them. Each vector has a meaning:

  • Magnetic moment: components in Bohr magnetons (μB);
  • Direction: a dimensionless illustration, never presented as a measured moment.

The table shows the components and the modulus. A zero vector is kept as data (modulus 0) and draws no arrow; vectors with a modulus up to 10⁻⁹ count as zero.

Attaching. Select atoms in the 3D view, then Add/Set for Selection…. The editor asks where the vector goes:

  • Selected displayed atom(s) only: exactly those balls (source atom and periodic image), as an image override;
  • All periodic images of their source atom(s): a source default that every image of the atom shows, with the same components in every cell.

An image override takes precedence over its source default, and Suppress on Selected Images removes the arrow from chosen balls even if their source has a default. Each ball shows at most one vector. Atoms of the same element are never grouped: two iron atoms can carry opposite moments. Ycrystal infers no alternating signs, propagation vector, or magnetic symmetry, so an antiferromagnetic pattern has to be assigned explicitly (per source atom, per image, or with a magnetic repeat cell as the structure).

While the editor is open, the 3D view and the POV-Ray preview show the new vector without an undo step; selecting other atoms does not change the editor's targets. Apply is one undo step (also for many atoms at once), Cancel restores the previous state.

The table lists every source default, image override, and suppression with its atom, image, components, meaning, modulus, and how many displayed balls show it. Choosing rows selects their balls in the 3D view. Edit… changes the components of the chosen rows, Reverse negates them, Show/Hide hides arrows without deleting the data, and Remove deletes rows (removing an image override brings back the source default). Each action is one undo step.

Arrow appearance (all arrows): Placement Centred on atom (the default; the arrow runs from r − L u/2 to r + L u/2) or Tail at atom centre (r to r + L u), where u is the unit direction and L the total length, head included. Length is either uniform (L in Å for every arrow) or proportional (L = scale × modulus, with scale in Å per μB for moments and Å per unit for directions). Switching never changes the components. Shaft radius, head length and radius, colour, and material (built-in or one of your custom materials) are separate from the atoms; materials with their own colours ignore the arrow colour. On short arrows the head takes at most 60 % of the length and the whole arrow gets thinner in proportion; the length itself is never changed. A short arrow can be hidden inside its atom: make it longer or the atom smaller.

In figures. Arrows are part of the figure: the POV-Ray preview, the PNG, and the .pov file contain them (as a cylinder and a cone each, with a comment naming the atom and the components), lit and shadowed like the atoms. Fit and the render keep whole arrows in view, including their heads; adding or editing a vector does not move the camera by itself. The lights stay where they are (they depend on the atoms and cell only). Arrows are never picked by clicks and do not change measurements, bonds, or atom counts.

What happens when the display changes. Hiding an atom hides its arrow. Fewer repetitions hide the arrows of images that are no longer displayed, without deleting their overrides; more repetitions bring them back. Changing atom radii does not change arrows. Opening another structure starts without vectors.

Saving. Projects store all vectors at full precision (since project schema 7), including suppressions and the arrow appearance, and the definition of a custom arrow material. Styles carry only the arrow appearance (with the Materials, colours, and radii part); they never transfer vectors to another structure, and importing a style keeps the current structure's vectors. examples/vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal shows a small synthetic two-site cell with opposite moments assigned by hand.

items.title: Examples and the command line
items.text:
The checkout's examples/ directory contains ready-made projects and a style. They are ordinary .ycrystal files with the structure embedded, so they open anywhere:

File Shows examples/SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal SrTiO3 2 × 2 × 1, chrome Ti and ceramic O, grey studio with floor shadows, 800 × 600 examples/MgB2-gradient.ycrystal MgB2 3 × 3 × 1 (from tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif), glossy B, blue gradient, 700 × 700 examples/triclinic-transparent.ycrystal Low-symmetry triclinic cell, matte, transparent PNG background, 900 × 600 examples/vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal Synthetic two-site cubic cell (not a real material) with opposite magnetic-moment arrows (±2.2 μB along z) assigned by hand, 800 × 600 examples/grey-studio.ycstyle The style of the SrTiO3 example (chrome Ti, ceramic O, grey studio, 800 × 600, 2 × 2 × 1 cells), to apply to other structures in the window or with --style examples/batch-series.json A batch manifest: the grey studio style for SrTiO3, BaZrO3 (Ti → Zr), MgB2 (down c), a triclinic cell, and the vector example, all 600 × 450; see render a series examples/publication/ The publication gallery: two styles (paper and cover), a manifest with snapshots, and structure inputs including kyanite from the Crystallography Open Database; see the figure gallery

Open one with File ▸ Open…, or .venv/bin/ycrystal examples/MgB2-gradient.ycrystal. python scripts/make_examples.py regenerates them.

items.title: Render without a window
items.text:
.venv/bin/ycrystal examples/SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render SrTiO3.png
.venv/bin/ycrystal examples/SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render small.png --width 400 --height 300
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --render MgB2.png
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --export-pov out/MgB2.pov

--render draws a project exactly as saved (camera, output size, materials, environment) or a structure file with the default settings and view, runs POV-Ray, and writes the PNG; --width/--height override the size (the image keeps its centre and height, as in the window). --export-pov writes NAME.pov and NAME.ini and needs no POV-Ray; the directory must exist. Both need no display, so they also work over SSH or in scripts. --povray PATH chooses the POV-Ray executable. Errors print ERROR: … and exit with status 1. Files that need a question answered (format, CIF data block, VASP 4 elements) must be opened in the window first and saved as a project.

A project (or a style applied with --style) whose element legend is on gets the legend in the PNG as well; Ycrystal paints it after POV-Ray, without a window. A fitted view (a structure file, --view, --camera-policy fit) keeps the structure beside a legend at an edge; a saved camera is used as it is. --export-pov notes that the .pov scene does not contain the legend.

On the development laptop (Intel Core Ultra 5 135U), each example renders at 400 × 300 in about 1–2 seconds.

items.title: Reuse the example style
items.text:
Open your own structure, choose File ▸ Import Style…, and pick examples/grey-studio.ycstyle. Element settings apply to the elements your structure contains; see styles.

For a structure with other elements, map them in the same dialog. For example, to give BaZrO3 the chrome that the style gives Ti:

  1. Open tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif (File ▸ Open…).
  2. Choose File ▸ Import Style… and pick examples/grey-studio.ycstyle.
  3. Under Element settings go to, the row O → shows O (matching symbol) and the row Ti → shows Do not transfer (BaZrO3 has no Ti). The text below reads Element settings applied: O. and Left out: Ti.
  4. Set the Ti → row to Zr. The text changes to Element settings applied: O, Ti → Zr.
  5. Press Apply. Zr is now chrome and O ceramic, in the grey studio; Edit ▸ Undo removes the whole import in one step.

Setting the Ti → row to O instead is refused before Apply: the dialog explains that O would receive the settings of both O and Ti, and Apply stays disabled until you choose differently (or set the O → row to Do not transfer).

items.title: Apply a style from the command line
items.text:
Why. Figures in one paper or talk usually share a look: the same background, lighting, floor, image size, and materials. Design that look once in the window, save it as a style (File ▸ Export Style…), and give it to every other structure from the command line, for example from a script that renders a whole series. The figures stay consistent, and nobody has to repeat the same clicks for each structure.

--style applies a .ycstyle file to FILE before --render or --export-pov, without a window. A style has two kinds of settings:

  • settings that suit any structure: the environment (background, floor, lighting), the output size, and the default material;
  • settings for particular elements: element materials, colours, and radii, and bond-pair rules (for example "Ti is chrome").

The first kind always applies. The second kind applies to the elements the structure contains. The style designed for SrTiO3 therefore gives MgB2 the same grey studio, even though MgB2 has neither Ti nor O (a warning says that those settings were not used):

.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --render MgB2.png
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --export-pov out/MgB2.pov
.venv/bin/ycrystal examples/vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --render afm.png

The first command prints WARNING: Element overrides for O, Ti were not applied: the structure has no O, Ti. on standard error and renders an 800 × 600 PNG (the style's size).

  • Parts. By default the command line applies appearance (default material, element materials, colours, and radii, arrow appearance), environment (background including a background picture, floor, lighting, transparency), and output (image size). display (atom size, repetitions, cell edges, bonds, hidden atoms) is left out, because the repetitions and hidden atoms of the style's structure rarely suit another one. Choose the parts with --style-parts, a comma-separated list, for example --style-parts appearance,display,environment,output for everything, or --style-parts environment for the studio only. In the window, File ▸ Import Style… offers all four parts as before.
  • Transfer rules. The same as in the window: element settings apply to the elements the structure contains; per-atom materials and hidden atoms only to the same structure (same atoms in the same order). What is left out is printed as WARNING: … lines; the command still succeeds.
  • What is kept. The coordinates, the cell, and the vectors of FILE are never changed, and neither FILE nor the style file is written. A saved project keeps its camera (with display, a warning says if the style's repetitions may not fit in it); a structure file gets the default view, fitted to the styled structure.
  • Size. --width and --height override the style's size, each on its own: --width 400 with the 800 × 600 style gives 400 × 600.
  • Large displays. With display, a style may not raise the number of displayed atoms above 20,000; the command stops with an error before writing anything. Apply such a style in the window (which asks) and save a project, or leave out display.
  • Errors. A missing or damaged style file prints ERROR: …, writes nothing, and exits with status 1. --style without --render or --export-pov, or an unknown part in --style-parts, is a usage error (status 2) and opens no window.
  • A style package with a background picture or custom materials carries them, so it works on a machine where the picture and the personal materials do not exist.

--render still writes PNG only; PDF and JPEG come from Render Image… in the window.

items.title: Map elements to another composition
items.text:
Why. Element settings are stored by element symbol, so they are lost when the composition changes, even when the figures should match. SrTiO3 and BaZrO3 are both ABO3 perovskites: Zr sits where Ti sits, at the centre of the oxygen octahedron. In a series of perovskite figures you will usually want the B-site atom drawn the same way in every figure, so readers can compare them at a glance. A mapping says which element of the new structure takes over which element's look. You decide the correspondence; Ycrystal never guesses it.

The grey studio style has settings for Ti (chrome) and O (ceramic). BaZrO3 (tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif, an illustrative cubic perovskite) has O but no Ti, so without a mapping its Zr atoms keep the default material. --element-map gives the Ti settings to Zr:

.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --element-map Ti=Zr --render BaZrO3.png

This renders chrome Zr and ceramic O in the grey studio, with no warning. Two more examples, with the messages they print:

# A deliberately partial mapping: Ti's chrome goes to Mg; MgB2 has no O.
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --element-map Ti=Mg --render MgB2-chrome.png
# WARNING: Element overrides for O were not applied: the structure has no O.

# Ti's chrome to Zr, and leave the style's O settings out (O keeps its default look).
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --element-map Ti=Zr,O=- --render BaZrO3-no-O.png
# WARNING: Element settings for O were left out by the element mapping.

Nothing is guessed: B in MgB2 gets no settings, because no element is mapped to it.

  • Syntax. SOURCE=TARGET pairs separated by commas: --element-map Sr=Ba,Ti=Zr. SOURCE=- leaves the style's settings for SOURCE out: --element-map O=-. Symbols are case-sensitive; spaces around them are ignored. Elements that are not listed keep matching by symbol. --element-map needs --style.
  • What moves. The element materials, colours, and radii of the appearance part, and the bond-pair rules of the display part (when requested with --style-parts). Atoms, element labels, coordinates, vectors, and which bonds exist are never changed, and per-atom settings still transfer only to the same structure.
  • Warnings. A source element the style has no settings for is reported (with --element-map Sr=Ba the grey studio prints WARNING: The style has no element settings for Sr; its mapping changes nothing.), as are settings left out with =-.
  • Errors. A malformed entry, an unknown or wrongly capitalised symbol (ti), or an element mapped twice is a usage error (status 2). A target the structure does not contain (Ti=Mg for BaZrO3), two elements mapped to one target, or a mapping onto an element that keeps its own settings (Ti=O, while the style also has O settings) is an error (status 1). In every case nothing is written and POV-Ray does not start.

The mapping is a presentation choice, not a statement of chemical equivalence or site correspondence; see element mapping.

items.title: Choose the view and framing
items.text:
Why. Without options, --render and --export-pov draw a project with its saved camera and a structure file with the default view. That suits one figure. For a series, or for figures made by a script, you usually want every structure seen along the same crystallographic direction, framed so that nothing is cut off, and sometimes drawn at the same physical scale so that sizes can be compared. These options choose the camera without opening the window; the structure itself is never rotated or moved.

# Look down the c axis of MgB2 (the hexagonal cell seen from above):
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif --view c --render MgB2-c.png
# Two perovskites along a, at the same scale: 9 Å of height in both images.
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/SrTiO3.cif --view a --view-height 9 --width 600 --height 600 --render SrTiO3-a.png
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif --view a --view-height 9 --width 600 --height 600 --render BaZrO3-a.png
# A saved project after a style changed its cells: keep its orientation, refit the frame.
.venv/bin/ycrystal examples/MgB2-gradient.ycrystal --style examples/grey-studio.ycstyle --style-parts display --camera-policy fit --render MgB2-refit.png

In the second pair the BaZrO3 cell (a = 4.19 Å) is visibly larger than the SrTiO3 cell (a = 3.905 Å), because both images show 9 Å of height.

  • --view default, a, b, c, x, y, or z: the named axis points toward the viewer, as with the window's View along buttons (same rule, same camera). a, b, c are the real-space lattice vectors, not normals of lattice planes (hkl); for skewed cells they differ from each other and from x, y, z. Screen up is the first of c, b, a (z, y, x) that is not parallel to the axis: down a or b, c is up; down c, b is up. A structure without a cell has no a, b, c views (an error says so); x, y, z, and default always work.
  • --camera-policy saved or fit. saved (the default without --view) uses a project's saved camera exactly as saved; a structure file, which has none, gets the default view. fit keeps the saved orientation but refits the centre and scale to what is drawn now, useful after a style changed the repetitions. --view and --view-height imply fit; combining them with --camera-policy saved is a usage error.
  • Fitting includes everything drawn: atoms, cell edges, and whole vector arrows. Nothing is clipped at any output shape, portrait or landscape. --fit-margin sets the space around it as a fraction of the half-height, 0–1 (default 0.06).
  • --view-height ANGSTROM shows a fixed height of the scene (in Å) instead of fitting the scale, centred on the scene; the width follows the image's shape. If the scene does not fit, the command stops with an error that gives the height needed (for example it needs at least 5.85 Å for SrTiO3 along a at 1200 × 800) instead of cutting the figure.
  • Without these options nothing changes: the camera is chosen exactly as before.
  • Errors. An unknown view, a margin outside 0–1, a non-positive height, or --camera-policy saved with --view is a usage error (status 2); these options without --render or --export-pov are a usage error too, and open no window. A lattice view without a cell, or a scene too large for --view-height, is an error (status 1). Nothing is written in either case.

Orthographic projection is used throughout, so atoms at the back are as large as atoms at the front, and the visible height in Å is a true scale of the structure.

items.title: Render a series from a manifest
items.text:
Why. A paper often needs the same kind of figure for many structures: one style, one orientation, one size, perhaps with an element mapping for some of them. Running one command per structure works, but the settings end up scattered over a shell script. A batch manifest states them once, in a small JSON file that you can keep next to the data, check in, and rerun later. Ycrystal checks the whole manifest before it renders anything, renders the figures one after the other, and writes a report of what happened.

.venv/bin/ycrystal --batch examples/batch-series.json --output-dir renders --dry-run
.venv/bin/ycrystal --batch examples/batch-series.json --output-dir renders

The first command checks everything and lists what would be rendered, without rendering or writing anything:

WARNING: MgB2: Element overrides for O, Ti were not applied: the structure has no O, Ti.
WARNING: afm-vectors: Element overrides for O, Ti were not applied: the structure has no O, Ti.
SrTiO3: would render SrTiO3.png (600 × 450, 15 atoms)
BaZrO3: would render BaZrO3.png (600 × 450, 15 atoms)
MgB2: would render MgB2.png (600 × 450, 10 atoms)
triclinic: would render triclinic.png (600 × 450, 5 atoms)
afm-vectors: would render vectors/afm.png (600 × 450, 22 atoms)
Checked 5 job(s); nothing was rendered (--dry-run).

The second renders the five PNGs into renders/ (about 6 s on the development Mac) and writes renders/ycrystal-batch-report.json.

items.title: The manifest
items.text:
examples/batch-series.json, shortened:

{
 "format": "ycrystal-batch",
 "schema_version": 1,
 "defaults": {"style": "grey-studio.ycstyle", "view": "a", "width": 600, "height": 450},
 "jobs": [
  {"id": "SrTiO3", "input": "../tests/fixtures/SrTiO3.cif"},
  {"id": "BaZrO3", "input": "../tests/fixtures/BaZrO3.cif", "element_map": {"Ti": "Zr"}},
  {"id": "MgB2", "input": "../tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif", "view": "c"},
  {"id": "triclinic", "input": "../tests/fixtures/triclinic.cif",
   "style_parts": ["environment", "output"]},
  {"id": "afm-vectors", "input": "vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal",
   "output": "vectors/afm.png", "camera_policy": "fit"}
 ]
}
  • format and schema_version identify the file. jobs lists the figures, rendered in this order. Each job needs an id (letters, digits, ., _, -; unique) and an input: a structure file or a .ycrystal project.
  • defaults holds settings for every job; a job can set any of them for itself, which replaces the default. The settings are those of the single-figure options:
Setting Meaning Command-line equivalent output PNG file in the output folder (default <id>.png); subfolders allowed --render format poscar, cif, qe, or project (default: detected) --format style .ycstyle file, or null for none --style style_parts List of parts, default ["appearance", "environment", "output"] --style-parts element_map {"Ti": "Zr"}; null as a value leaves an element's settings out --element-map Ti=Zr (O=-) view default, a, b, c, x, y, z --view camera_policy saved or fit --camera-policy fit_margin 0–1, default 0.06 --fit-margin view_height Fixed visible height in Å --view-height width, height Image size, 16–8000 px (default: the input's, or the style's) --width, --height max_atoms Largest number of displayed atoms allowed, default 20,000 (none)
  • Paths are relative to the manifest's folder, so a manifest works wherever the folder is copied with its data. Absolute input and style paths are accepted too; outputs must stay inside the output folder (no .., no absolute paths).
  • Unknown keys are refused (a misspelt "veiw" is an error, not silently ignored). A "comment" key at the top level is allowed for notes.
  • "save_projects": true at the top level also saves, next to each image, the figure's self-contained snapshot (SrTiO3.ycrystal) and its provenance record (SrTiO3.provenance.json); see reproducible figures.

items.title: What happens
items.text:
1. Everything is checked first. Ycrystal reads every input and style, applies the styles and element mappings, chooses every camera, and checks every output name. It reports all problems of all jobs at once (for example a missing input, an unknown element, two jobs writing the same file, ../ in an output, a scene larger than max_atoms or than view_height) and then stops with status 2, before rendering or writing anything.
  2. Existing images are not replaced unless you add --overwrite; without it, an existing image or report is one of the problems of step 1.
  3. Jobs run one after the other, in manifest order. POV-Ray already uses all processor cores for one image, so jobs are not run in parallel. A job that fails (for example a POV-Ray error) is recorded and the others continue; an image is written only when its render succeeded, never half-written.
  4. The report ycrystal-batch-report.json lists every job in order with its status (rendered or failed), time, size, number of atoms, warnings, and error message, plus the Ycrystal and POV-Ray versions. Paths are written as given in the manifest. With save_projects, project and provenance name each job's snapshot and record (otherwise they are null).
  5. Exit status: 0 when every job was rendered; 1 when any job failed (or POV-Ray is missing, then nothing is rendered); 2 when the manifest is invalid.

--batch takes all settings from the manifest: combining it with FILE, --render, --style, --view, or the other single-figure options is a usage error. Batch rendering writes PNG files; PDF and JPEG come from Render Image… in the window.

items.title: Your first crystal figure
items.text: Prerequisites: install Ycrystal, use an X11 desktop with working OpenGL, and install POV-Ray for the PNG step. Commands below start in the checkout root. The built-in sample works without importing a file.

items.title: Start and arrange the sample
items.text:
1. Create an output directory and launch:

    mkdir -p artifacts/first-figure
.venv/bin/ycrystal --sample perovskite

  2. The window shows SrTiO3 and reports 15 atoms and 30 bonds shown, with 1 × 1 × 1 cells. The default view also draws bonds. Eight Sr corner balls and six O face balls are periodic images of the 5 input atoms; the Ti ball is at the centre. Use the Scene ▸ Structure tab to change repetitions; leave them at 1 × 1 × 1 for this tutorial.

  3. Drag with the left mouse button to orbit. Shift + left drag pans; the wheel zooms. Press F over the 3D view to fit everything while keeping the current orientation. View ▸ Reset View restores the initial orientation and fits it.
  4. Click a visible corner ball without dragging. It gets an orange highlight and the status bar reports the element, source atom number, image offset, and fractional/Cartesian coordinates. Press Delete: just that ball disappears and the status shows 14 atoms with 1 hidden (the status also includes bond and cell counts). Press Ctrl+Z to restore it. Press Esc to clear the selection. Hiding changes the figure, not the structure.

items.title: Save the project and export the scene
items.text:
1. Choose File ▸ Save Project (Ctrl+S). Navigate to the checkout's artifacts/first-figure/ directory and save as SrTiO3.ycrystal. The title loses its modified marker (*). The project embeds the structure, view, and display settings, so reopening it does not need a source structure file.
  2. In the Scene dock, open the Render tab and set Width to 640 and Height to 400 (or Width 640 and Aspect 16:10). The toolbar shows 640 × 400 px, and a blue frame in the 3D view marks the image area. Press F to fit the structure into the frame. In the Appearance tab, keep the Satin default material and the White environment (see Materials, backgrounds, and lighting for the other choices).
  3. Choose File ▸ Export POV-Ray… and save as artifacts/first-figure/SrTiO3.pov. Ycrystal writes SrTiO3.pov and SrTiO3.ini in that directory. This step runs no renderer and creates no PNG. Both text files replace existing files of the same name; use a new name to preserve earlier work.

items.title: Render the PNG
items.text:
1. Press F5 for a preview: the POV-Ray preview dock shows a small POV-Ray image of the framed view after a moment. With Update automatically checked, it refreshes shortly after each change.
  2. Choose Render ▸ Check Renderer. Expect a pass message naming POV-Ray and a sphere-centre error below 1 pixel. The check briefly blocks the window. If it fails, follow renderer setup.
  3. Choose Render ▸ Render Image… (Ctrl+R). Keep PNG and Output size (Render panel), set Save as to artifacts/first-figure/SrTiO3.png, and press Render. (The same dialog writes PDF and JPEG files and publication sizes; see rendering.) The status bar shows Rendering … with the progress, and the window stays responsive. Cancel Render would stop it without writing the file.
  4. When complete, a dialog shows the PNG and its path. The image is 640 × 400 pixels. It shows exactly the area inside the blue frame, with the same hidden atoms as the live view and POV-Ray lighting. Orientation axes, the frame, and selection highlights are omitted. See the example render for the default view at 640 × 400.
  5. Press Ctrl+S again to save the output settings. Close the window, relaunch, and use File ▸ Open… to reopen SrTiO3.ycrystal. Coordinates, hidden atoms, output size, and camera are restored, with the same framing in a window of any shape.

Optional: an element legend. Open the Scene ▸ Legend tab and check Show the element legend: ● Sr ● Ti ● O appears at the bottom of the frame. Press Fit View Beside Legend so that the structure sits above it, then render again. See element legend for the layout, font, marker, and order choices.

Your chosen directory now contains the project, two editable scene files, and the PNG. GUI renders use a separate temporary job directory and remove it after completion. They do not render the exported .pov file; editing that file requires running its .ini directly.

items.title: Figure gallery
items.text:
Seven figures made by Ycrystal and POV-Ray 3.7 from the inputs in examples/publication/, all by the command line. They show:

  • a restrained style for a journal page;
  • the same figure with ray-traced lighting and materials;
  • one style applied to several compositions with an explicit element mapping;
  • a low-symmetry mineral;
  • a synthetic magnetic-moment illustration.

The thumbnails below are 480 px wide JPEG copies, downscaled from the 1600 × 1200 PNG renders of the run recorded at the end of this page. They are not mock-ups.

items.title: Lighting and materials, with geometry and camera fixed
items.text:
Paper style Cover environment only Cover environment and materials

The left image is rendered from SrTiO3.cif with styles/paper.ycstyle. Its snapshot srtio3.ycrystal is then rendered with styles/cover.ycstyle:

  • the middle image applies only the cover's environment: a dark studio, a reflective floor, and hard shadows;
  • the right image also applies its materials: ceramic Sr, chrome Ti, ruby-glass O.

A snapshot keeps its camera and image size, so the structure, camera, and size are exactly the same in all three; tests/test_gallery.py checks this. Reflections and refraction are computed by POV-Ray. The materials are a presentation choice, not physical properties of the atoms.

items.title: One style, several structures
items.text:
SrTiO3 BaZrO3, Sr → Ba, Ti → Zr MgB2 Kyanite, Al₂SiO₅ (P-1, COD 1008755) Synthetic antiferromagnet (not a real material)

All five come from one batch manifest, gallery.json, with the paper style:

  • SrTiO3 and BaZrO3 share a visible height of 9 Å, so the larger BaZrO3 cell (a = 4.19 Å against 3.905 Å) appears larger. BaZrO3 keeps the A and B site colours through the explicit mapping "element_map": {"Sr": "Ba", "Ti": "Zr"}. The mapping is a presentation choice, not chemical equivalence.
  • MgB2 (3 × 3 × 1 cells, looking down c, showing the boron honeycomb) and kyanite receive the style's background, lighting, size, and default material. Their elements keep their default colours, except kyanite's O, which matches the style's O. The run prints a warning for each element setting it could not use.
  • The antiferromagnet is synthetic: moments of ±2.2 μB assigned by hand. It illustrates atom-attached vectors, not a real material.

Sources and licences of the structures are listed in examples/publication/README.md.

items.title: Make the figures yourself
items.text:
python scripts/make_gallery.py --out artifacts/gallery

The script copies the inputs to a temporary folder and runs the batch manifest there. It renders the two cover variants from the SrTiO3 snapshot and then deletes the inputs. Next it renders every snapshot again with scripts/replay_check.py and compares the pixels. Finally it writes the figure-methods table below (figure-methods.md) and the list of commands it ran (commands.txt).

  • On the development laptop (Linux, POV-Ray 3.7.0.10), the whole run at 1600 × 1200 took well under a minute of rendering: 9.7 s for the five batch figures, 2.6 s and 9.2 s for the two variants. All 7 replays had identical pixels.
  • --scale 0.25 makes the same figures at a quarter of the size, for a quick check.
  • --thumbnails docs/assets/gallery also writes the thumbnails of this page.

To render one figure again from its snapshot, for example on another computer:

ycrystal artifacts/gallery/figures/kyanite.ycrystal --render kyanite-again.png

items.title: Figure methods
items.text:
Written by scripts/make_gallery.py from the provenance records and snapshots of the run on 17 November 2026 (Linux Mint 22.1 laptop, Ycrystal 0.4.0.dev0, POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial), unedited. Atoms counts the atoms of the structure, displayed those drawn (with periodic images and repetitions). The two variants have the snapshot srtio3.ycrystal as their input; saved means the snapshot's camera was used as it is.

Figure Input Atoms (displayed) Size, px Style (parts; mapping) Camera Key settings Renderer srtio3.png: SrTiO3, paper style SrTiO3.cif 5 (15) 1600 × 1200 paper.ycstyle (appearance, environment, output) fit: default, fixed height 9 Å white background, soft lighting; default material satin; element colours O, Sr, Ti POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial srtio3-cover-light.png: SrTiO3, same snapshot: cover environment only srtio3.ycrystal 5 (15) 1600 × 1200 cover.ycstyle (environment) saved: saved orientation studio_dark background, bright lighting; floor (reflection 0.35); default material satin; element colours O, Sr, Ti POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial srtio3-cover.png: SrTiO3, same snapshot: cover environment and materials srtio3.ycrystal 5 (15) 1600 × 1200 cover.ycstyle (appearance, environment) saved: saved orientation studio_dark background, bright lighting; floor (reflection 0.35); default material satin; O glass_ruby, Sr ceramic, Ti chrome; element colours O, Sr, Ti POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial bazro3-mapped.png: BaZrO3, paper style mapped Sr → Ba, Ti → Zr BaZrO3.cif 5 (15) 1600 × 1200 paper.ycstyle (appearance, environment, output; Sr → Ba, Ti → Zr) fit: default, fixed height 9 Å white background, soft lighting; default material satin; element colours Ba, O, Zr POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial mgb2.png: MgB2 3 × 3 × 1 down c, paper style (no settings for Mg, B) MgB2-gradient.ycrystal 3 (50) 1600 × 1200 paper.ycstyle (appearance, environment, output) fit: c white background, soft lighting; default material satin POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial kyanite.png: Kyanite Al2SiO5 (COD 1008755), paper style kyanite-COD-1008755.cif 32 (34) 1600 × 1200 paper.ycstyle (appearance, environment, output) fit: default white background, soft lighting; default material satin; element colours O POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial afm-synthetic.png: Synthetic antiferromagnet (not a real material), paper style vectors-synthetic-afm.ycrystal 2 (22) 1600 × 1200 paper.ycstyle (appearance, environment, output) fit: a white background, soft lighting; default material satin; 2 source vectors POV-Ray 3.7.0.10.unofficial

The scenes need the standard POV-Ray include file textures.inc for chrome and ruby glass. It belongs to the POV-Ray installation and is not part of the inputs.

items.title: Install and launch
items.text: The integration baseline is Linux Mint 22.1 / Ubuntu 24.04 with the system Python 3.12, an X11 desktop, and working OpenGL. macOS 15 on Apple silicon is supported from the same source and passes the same automated tests. Windows 11 with POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 is supported from the same source too: it passes the automated tests and was tested by hand on one computer; there, a graphical installer is the recommended way (Windows). Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14 are supported; where each was tested is in the support matrix. Ycrystal is installed from its source folder into its own virtual environment; no sudo is needed except for the system packages.

items.title: Without Git
items.text:
The sections below get the source with git clone, which makes updating a git pull. Git is not needed otherwise: download the source as a ZIP file (also under the green Code button on GitHub), unpack it, and run the remaining commands of your system in the unpacked folder ycrystal-main instead of ycrystal:

curl -L -o ycrystal.zip https://github.com/ymatterlab/ycrystal/archive/refs/heads/main.zip
unzip ycrystal.zip && cd ycrystal-main

On Windows, in PowerShell (or unpack with File Explorer's Extract All):

Invoke-WebRequest https://github.com/ymatterlab/ycrystal/archive/refs/heads/main.zip -OutFile ycrystal.zip
Expand-Archive ycrystal.zip . ; cd ycrystal-main

To update without Git, download and unpack the new ZIP file, install again in the new folder (on Linux also --install-desktop again if you use the menu launcher; on Windows run the installation script there, which also moves the Start-menu entry to it), and delete the old folder.

items.title: Linux Mint
items.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git povray povray-includes libxcb-cursor0 python3.12-venv
git clone https://github.com/ymatterlab/ycrystal.git
cd ycrystal
/usr/bin/python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . -c constraints.txt
.venv/bin/ycrystal

Use /usr/bin/python3: Miniconda/Anaconda's bundled libstdc++ can prevent Mesa from loading and cause “Could not initialize GLX”. libxcb-cursor0 is needed by Qt on X11. POV-Ray is optional for opening structures and exporting scenes, and required for previews and rendering PNGs; povray-includes provides the standard include files that native POV-Ray materials (gold, marble, M_Glass, …) need. The pip install step downloads about 300 MB of wheels (Qt, VTK) the first time. To install developer tools, use -e ".[dev]" instead of -e ..

If using uv, the equivalent environment setup is:

uv venv --python /usr/bin/python3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e . -c constraints.txt

items.title: macOS
items.text:
With Homebrew on macOS 15 (Apple silicon):

xcode-select --install            # Git and the command-line tools, if missing
brew install python@3.12 povray
git clone https://github.com/ymatterlab/ycrystal.git
cd ycrystal
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . -c constraints.txt
.venv/bin/ycrystal

Homebrew's povray is POV-Ray 3.7 and contains the standard include files; Ycrystal finds it on PATH (/opt/homebrew/bin/povray). The window is started from the terminal: there is no application bundle or Dock launcher yet, so the Dock and the menu bar show “Python”, and --install-desktop (below) applies to Linux and Windows only. Shortcuts use ⌘ where this guide says Ctrl. A virtual environment cannot be copied between Linux and macOS: create it on each machine.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
There are two installations for Windows 11 (x64). Most users want the first:

  • the installer (recommended): a graphical setup program that installs Ycrystal with everything it needs except POV-Ray; no Python, Git, or PowerShell;
  • the developer installation: Ycrystal from its source folder, set up by a PowerShell script, for working on Ycrystal or running its newest source.

Both can be on one computer: they have separate Start-menu entries (Ycrystal and Ycrystal (development)), and uninstalling one leaves the other working (see both installations). Both need POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 for previews and images (below).

items.title: Windows: the installer (recommended)
items.text:
1. Download Ycrystal-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe from the Releases page (version 0.4.0 is the first with it). The installer of the newest source, between releases, can be downloaded with a GitHub account from the latest run of the Windows installer workflow (artifact ycrystal-windows-installer: a ZIP file with the installer inside).
  2. Run it. The installer is not signed yet, so Windows may show "Windows protected your PC": choose More info, then Run anyway.
  3. Follow the wizard. By default it installs for you alone, without administrator rights, into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Ycrystal; an administrator can choose an installation for all users (Program Files). It adds Ycrystal to the Start menu and, unless you untick it, opens .ycrystal projects with Ycrystal from File Explorer. If it does not find POV-Ray for Windows, it says so and offers its download page at the end.
  4. Start Ycrystal from the Start menu.

The installed folder also holds ycrystal-cli.exe, the command line (the ycrystal command of the other installations), for example in PowerShell: & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Ycrystal\ycrystal-cli.exe" --check-renderer. To update, run the installer of the new version: it replaces the old one. To uninstall, use Settings ▸ Apps ▸ Installed apps ▸ Ycrystal ▸ Uninstall. Settings, favourites, and personal materials are kept in both cases.

items.title: Windows: developer installation (PowerShell)
items.text:
In PowerShell. Install Git for Windows first if it is missing (winget install --id Git.Git --exact, then open a new PowerShell window), or get the source without Git and skip the first two lines:

git clone https://github.com/ymatterlab/ycrystal.git
cd ycrystal
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows.ps1

The script installs what is missing and checks the result:

  1. Python 3.12 with winget, for the current user, unless py finds Python 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 (in this order);
  2. the virtual environment .venv in the checkout, with Ycrystal and the tested package versions of constraints.txt (about 300 MB the first time);
  3. POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 with winget, unless it is installed: its official installer from povray.org, which asks Windows for administrator permission;
  4. if POV-Ray for Windows would ask at every start whether to download its editor, it opens once so that you can answer for good: No, then untick Options ▸ Other Settings ▸ Use Editor, and close it (details below);
  5. Ycrystal (development) in the Start menu, and .ycrystal projects opening with it from File Explorer unless the installed Ycrystal already opens them (menu entry);
  6. the renderer check (--check-renderer).

Then start Ycrystal (development) from the Start menu. The script can run again at any time: after git pull it updates the installation. It ends with "Ycrystal is ready." (exit status 0), or with a list of what is not ready yet. Its options: -Python C:\path\to\python.exe (another Python, 3.12 or newer, for .venv; newer than 3.14 with a warning; ignored once .venv exists, so delete .venv to change it), -Dev (also the developer tools), -NoPovray, and -NoStartMenu; Get-Help .\scripts\install-windows.ps1 -Detailed describes them. -ExecutionPolicy Bypass lets this one PowerShell run the script, which Windows' default policy refuses otherwise; it changes no setting.

POV-Ray for Windows is a window program. For each preview and render, Ycrystal starts it minimised (its button appears on the taskbar while it runs) and it closes by itself. It cannot render for Ycrystal while you have POV-Ray for Windows open yourself: close it first, or turn off Options ▸ Keep Single Instance in POV-Ray (see troubleshooting).

items.title: Developer installation, step by step
items.text:
The same installation without the script:

winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 --exact --scope user       # or python.org's installer
winget install --id PersistenceOfVisionRaytracer.POVRay --exact   # or povray.org's installer
# Then open a NEW PowerShell window (restart VS Code for its terminal), so that py is found.
cd ycrystal
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e . -c constraints.txt
.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --install-desktop
.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe

py is the Python launcher that python.org's installer (and winget) puts on PATH. A terminal that was open before the installation keeps its old PATH, also VS Code's integrated terminal until VS Code is restarted; there PowerShell answers "The term 'py' is not recognized". In a new terminal, py --list shows the installed versions. Once .venv exists, use its own programs (.venv\Scripts\python.exe, .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe); they need nothing on PATH. The Windows Store python command (an alias that opens the Store) is not used.

items.title: POV-Ray for Windows
items.text:
Both installations render with POV-Ray for Windows 3.7, installed separately. The developer script installs it with winget if it is missing; for the installer version, install it yourself:

winget install --id PersistenceOfVisionRaytracer.POVRay --exact   # or povray.org's installer

The winget package of POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 runs its official installer from povray.org (povwin-3.7-agpl3-setup.exe, the same file and checksum), which can also be run by hand; keep its user files: they include the standard include files, which go to Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7\include. Ycrystal finds pvengine64.exe in POV-Ray's installation folder by itself (POV-Ray for Windows has no povray command and is not on PATH); Render ▸ Set POV-Ray Executable… or YCRYSTAL_POVRAY choose another one.

After installing it, start POV-Ray for Windows once from the Start menu. It asks whether to download its editor ("Could not load internal editor – download it?"): the AGPL installer does not include it. Either install the editor from the page that Yes opens, or answer No and untick Options ▸ Other Settings ▸ Use Editor. Otherwise it asks at every start; Ycrystal then refuses to render and says so, because each render would wait for that answer. Then close POV-Ray.

items.title: Both installations on one computer
items.text:
Installer version Developer installation Start-menu entry Ycrystal (Ycrystal.exe in the installation folder) Ycrystal (development) (the checkout's .venv\Scripts\pythonw.exe) Taskbar its own button and identity its own: the windows of the two never group together .ycrystal file type registered by the installer, which opens projects added to Open with; opens projects only if no other program does Removed by Settings ▸ Apps (its uninstaller) .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --uninstall-desktop POV-Ray, settings, personal materials shared shared

Each removes only what it added, so uninstalling one leaves the other working. --install-desktop belongs to the developer installation; the installed ycrystal-cli.exe refuses it. A Start-menu entry named Ycrystal made by an earlier developer installation is renamed Ycrystal (development) when the script or --install-desktop runs again.

items.title: Check the installation
items.text:
.venv/bin/ycrystal --version          # ycrystal 0.5.0
.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer   # PASS: POV-Ray 3.7… passed
.venv/bin/ycrystal examples/SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render SrTiO3.png

On Windows, in PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --version          # ycrystal 0.5.0
.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --check-renderer   # PASS: POV-Ray 3.7.0.0 at C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe passed…
.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe examples\SrTiO3-studio.ycrystal --render SrTiO3.png

The last command renders an example project without opening a window. The other commands of this guide work the same way on Windows, with .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe for .venv/bin/ycrystal, .venv\Scripts\python.exe for .venv/bin/python, and backslashes in paths.

items.title: Menu entry
items.text:
On Linux,

.venv/bin/ycrystal --install-desktop

adds Ycrystal to the Linux Mint menu (category Science), with an icon, and makes .ycrystal projects open in Ycrystal from the file manager. It writes three files for the current user only, under ~/.local/share (applications/ycrystal.desktop, icons/hicolor/scalable/apps/ycrystal.svg, mime/packages/ycrystal.xml). The launcher starts this checkout's .venv/bin/ycrystal by absolute path: run the command again if you move the checkout. .venv/bin/ycrystal --uninstall-desktop removes the files. The menu may need a moment (or a new login) to show the entry.

On Windows, in the developer installation, .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --install-desktop (the installation script runs it) adds Ycrystal (development) to the Start menu, for the current user, without administrator rights. The installer version has its own entry, Ycrystal, made by its installer (see both installations).

  • the shortcut Ycrystal (development).lnk in the user's Start-menu folder. It starts this checkout's .venv\Scripts\pythonw.exe with -I -m ycrystal.app, so that no console window opens, and it carries the application id that this installation's window uses on the taskbar (YMatterLab.Ycrystal; the installer version uses another one);
  • its icon, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal\ycrystal.ico, drawn from the application's SVG icon;
  • the file type Ycrystal.Project of .ycrystal projects, under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes. It is added to the Open with list, and opens projects from File Explorer if no other program does: when the installer version is installed, it keeps opening them. A program that you chose for .ycrystal files in Windows' Open with dialog stays your choice.

Run the command again if you move the checkout. --uninstall-desktop removes the shortcut, the icon, and the file type, and nothing of the installer version. Started this way, Ycrystal has no console for messages; to see them, start it from PowerShell with .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe.

items.title: Update and uninstall
items.text:
cd ycrystal
git pull
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . -c constraints.txt

On Linux, if you installed the menu launcher, refresh it after updating:

.venv/bin/ycrystal --install-desktop

The launcher uses a separate copy of the application icon under ~/.local/share; git pull updates the source SVG but does not replace that installed copy.

The installer version on Windows is updated by running the installer of the new version, and uninstalled in Settings ▸ Apps; the rest of this section is about installations from source.

On Windows, update with git pull, then run the installation script again (powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows.ps1): it updates .venv and the Start-menu entry. Without the script, run the pip install line with .venv\Scripts\python.exe, then .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --install-desktop.

Projects and styles from earlier versions keep opening; newer project files are refused by older versions with a message to update. To uninstall, run .venv/bin/ycrystal --uninstall-desktop (Linux; on Windows .venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --uninstall-desktop), then delete the checkout directory. On Windows, Python and POV-Ray for Windows stay installed; remove them in Settings ▸ Apps if nothing else needs them. Settings (POV-Ray path, favourites, last folder) are in ~/.config/Y-Matter Lab/Ycrystal.conf on Linux and in ~/Library/Preferences/com.y-matter-lab.Ycrystal.plist on macOS, where the thumbnails of personal materials are in ~/Library/Application Support/Y-Matter Lab/Ycrystal. On Windows the settings are in the registry (HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal) and the thumbnails in %APPDATA%\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal, for both Windows installations; neither uninstallation deletes them.

items.title: Launch options
items.text:
Run these from the checkout root:

.venv/bin/ycrystal --sample perovskite
.venv/bin/ycrystal --sample triclinic
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif
.venv/bin/ycrystal tests/fixtures/Si.pw.in --format qe
.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer
.venv/bin/ycrystal --help

The default sample is cubic SrTiO3: 5 scientific atoms, displayed as 15 balls with boundary images. The triclinic sample contains O, Fe, S, Cl, and N at general positions in a skewed cell, so it shows 5 balls. Both are synthetic and require no downloaded data. There is no sample chooser in the current GUI; choose one at launch.

A file argument opens after the window appears. If import fails, a message explains why and the sample stays. File ▸ Open… (Ctrl+O) opens structures or projects; File ▸ Open As… overrides format detection. The checkout's tests/fixtures/ contains small valid inputs and deliberate rejection cases; see supported formats.

--check-renderer runs without a window or display and exits with status 0 for PASS, 1 for FAIL. See renderer setup. For documentation-only installation, see the documentation workflow.

items.title: Quantum ESPRESSO lattices (ibrav)
items.text:
In a pw.x input, the ibrav variable of &SYSTEM chooses how the cell is given:

  • ibrav = 0: the lattice vectors are written out in a CELL_PARAMETERS card;
  • any other value: ibrav names a Bravais lattice, and pw.x builds the lattice vectors itself from a few parameters, celldm(1) … celldm(6) or A, B, C, cosAB, cosAC, cosBC.

Ycrystal reads both. For ibrav other than 0 it builds the same lattice vectors as pw.x, with pw.x's orientation and choice of primitive vectors. This matters because ATOMIC_POSITIONS {crystal} gives fractions of exactly those vectors: another choice of vectors for the same lattice would put the atoms elsewhere. ASE, which Ycrystal uses for the rest of the file, does not read ibrav other than 0 (ASE 3.29), so the lattice is built by Ycrystal's own module, ycrystal.io.qe_lattice, following the pw.x input documentation (INPUT_PW, variable ibrav) and pw.x's lattice generator (Modules/latgen.f90).

items.title: Applicable cases
items.text:
Every ibrav that pw.x accepts is read. In the table, a, b, c are the lattice parameters, α the angle between b and c, β between a and c, γ between a and b. The vectors v1, v2, v3 are the rows of the cell that Ycrystal shows and exports.

ibrav Lattice Parameters needed v1, v2, v3 1 cubic P (simple cubic) a (a, 0, 0), (0, a, 0), (0, 0, a) 2 cubic F (fcc) a (a/2)(−1, 0, 1), (a/2)(0, 1, 1), (a/2)(−1, 1, 0) 3 cubic I (bcc) a (a/2)(1, 1, 1), (a/2)(−1, 1, 1), (a/2)(−1, −1, 1) −3 cubic I (bcc), more symmetric axes a (a/2)(−1, 1, 1), (a/2)(1, −1, 1), (a/2)(1, 1, −1) 4 hexagonal and trigonal P a, c (a, 0, 0), (−a/2, a√3/2, 0), (0, 0, c) 5 trigonal R, threefold axis along z a, cos α (a·tx, −a·ty, a·tz), (0, 2a·ty, a·tz), (−a·tx, −a·ty, a·tz) −5 trigonal R, threefold axis along (111) a, cos α (a′u, a′v, a′v), (a′v, a′u, a′v), (a′v, a′v, a′u) 6 tetragonal P a, c (a, 0, 0), (0, a, 0), (0, 0, c) 7 tetragonal I (bct) a, c (a/2, −a/2, c/2), (a/2, a/2, c/2), (−a/2, −a/2, c/2) 8 orthorhombic P a, b, c (a, 0, 0), (0, b, 0), (0, 0, c) 9 orthorhombic base-centred (C) a, b, c (a/2, b/2, 0), (−a/2, b/2, 0), (0, 0, c) −9 orthorhombic base-centred (C), alternate axes a, b, c (a/2, −b/2, 0), (a/2, b/2, 0), (0, 0, c) 91 orthorhombic one-face base-centred (A) a, b, c (a, 0, 0), (0, b/2, −c/2), (0, b/2, c/2) 10 orthorhombic face-centred a, b, c (a/2, 0, c/2), (a/2, b/2, 0), (0, b/2, c/2) 11 orthorhombic body-centred a, b, c (a/2, b/2, c/2), (−a/2, b/2, c/2), (−a/2, −b/2, c/2) 12 monoclinic P, unique axis c a, b, c, cos γ (a, 0, 0), (b cos γ, b sin γ, 0), (0, 0, c) −12 monoclinic P, unique axis b a, b, c, cos β (a, 0, 0), (0, b, 0), (c cos β, 0, c sin β) 13 monoclinic base-centred, unique axis c a, b, c, cos γ (a/2, 0, −c/2), (b cos γ, b sin γ, 0), (a/2, 0, c/2) −13 monoclinic base-centred, unique axis b a, b, c, cos β (a/2, b/2, 0), (−a/2, b/2, 0), (c cos β, 0, c sin β) — see QE versions 14 triclinic a, b, c, cos α, cos β, cos γ (a, 0, 0), (b cos γ, b sin γ, 0), (c cos β, c (cos α − cos β cos γ)/sin γ, c √(1 + 2 cos α cos β cos γ − cos²α − cos²β − cos²γ)/sin γ)

For ibrav = 5: tx = √((1 − cos α)/2), ty = √((1 − cos α)/6), tz = √((1 + 2 cos α)/3). For ibrav = −5: a′ = a/√3, u = tz − 2√2·ty, v = tz + √2·ty. In both, a is the length of each vector and α the angle between any two of them.

items.title: Two ways to give the parameters
items.text:
Either form works, but not both in one file (pw.x refuses that too):

Parameter celldm form (lengths in bohr) Crystallographic form (lengths in Å) a celldm(1) A b celldm(2) = b/a B c celldm(3) = c/a C cos α of ibrav 5, −5 (rhombohedral angle) celldm(4) cosAB cos γ of ibrav 12, 13 celldm(4) cosAB cos β of ibrav −12, −13 celldm(5) cosAC cos α, cos β, cos γ of ibrav 14 celldm(4), celldm(5), celldm(6) cosBC, cosAC, cosAB

This is pw.x's own mapping (its routine abc2celldm). Note the one surprise it contains: for the rhombohedral lattices (5, −5) the angle α is given as cosAB. Parameters a lattice does not use are ignored, as in pw.x (for example celldm(4) with ibrav = 8).

items.title: Atom positions
items.text:
• crystal: fractions of v1, v2, v3 above.
  • alat: multiples of a (celldm(1) or A), as in pw.x — not of b or c.
  • bohr and angstrom: Cartesian coordinates, as for ibrav = 0.
  • if_pos flags (0/1) are kept, as for ibrav = 0.
  • As in pw.x, each coordinate may be simple arithmetic (1/4, 2*(1/8), 1/(2/(1/2))), and numbers may be written in Fortran notation (0.25d0, and 16.D0 for a mass); see structure files for the rules. This holds for every ibrav, 0 included.

items.title: What Ycrystal records
items.text: The structure's source record (metadata["source"], saved in projects) keeps qe_ibrav and qe_celldm (celldm(1) in bohr, then the five other values; from the crystallographic form after pw.x's mapping), next to the file's name and checksum.

items.title: Cases that are not applicable
items.text:
Ycrystal refuses these files with a message that names the file and the problem. pw.x refuses them too, with two exceptions: crystal_sg positions, which pw.x supports and Ycrystal does not, and a triclinic cell of zero volume, which passes pw.x's lattice check but cannot be used.

Input Message (shortened) An ibrav pw.x does not know (for example 15 or −4) ibrav = 15 is not a pw.x Bravais lattice (known: 0, 1, 2, …) No lattice parameters ibrav = 1 needs the lattice parameters: celldm(1)…celldm(6) or A, B, C, … Both celldm and A, B, C, cos… the lattice is given twice … A parameter the lattice needs is missing, zero, or negative (for example C for ibrav = 4) ibrav = 4 needs celldm(3) or C > 0. A cosine outside −1 … 1, or exactly ±1 for an angle the lattice uses ibrav = 12 needs celldm(4) = cos(gamma) strictly between −1 and 1, … A rhombohedral angle with cos α ≤ −1/2 or ≥ 1 (ibrav 5, −5) ibrav = 5 needs −1/2 < celldm(4) = cos(alpha) < 1 … Triclinic angles that do not close a cell the angles of this triclinic cell … do not make a cell with a volume. A CELL_PARAMETERS card together with ibrav other than 0 … pw.x refuses this (redundant cell) … ATOMIC_POSITIONS {crystal_sg} (positions reduced by a space group; supported by pw.x, not by Ycrystal) … crystal_sg (symmetry-reduced) form, which Ycrystal does not support … A triclinic cell whose angles give exactly zero volume (passes pw.x's lattice check) the angles of this triclinic cell … do not make a cell with a volume. A coordinate pw.x's arithmetic cannot evaluate (1/0, an unbalanced parenthesis, a letter) ATOMIC_POSITIONS line 'Mg 1/0 0 0': division by zero in '1/0'.

Not detected, and therefore not refused: a file with ibrav = −13 and crystal positions written for QE 6.4.1 or older opens with the current axes, which puts the atoms in other places (see the next section). Ycrystal cannot tell from the file which version of QE it was written for.

items.title: Quantum ESPRESSO versions
items.text:
Ycrystal follows current QE (6.5 and later). For all lattices except one, that is also every older version: the lattice code of each ibrav in latgen.f90 was compared, as text, in 23 releases from QE 4.3.2 to the current development branch, and only ibrav = −13 changed. In detail:

What Depends on the QE version? Vectors of ibrav 1–14, −3, −5, −9, −12, 91 No: unchanged since each value appeared Vectors of ibrav = −13 Yes. QE 5.2.0 to 6.4.1 used other axes: v1(old) = −v2(new), v2(old) = v1(new). QE 6.5 changed them ("crystal axis converted to a more standard orientation", release notes of 6.5), and pw.x prints BEWARE: axis for ibrav=-13 changed. The lattice is the same, so alat, bohr, and angstrom positions are unaffected; crystal positions written for the old axes must be converted with (x, y, z) → (y, −x, z), as QE's release notes say. Ycrystal reads them as new-axes positions. A, B, C, cos… for ibrav = −13 Yes. QE 6.2.x did not read cosAC for −13 (fixed in 6.3, release notes). Ycrystal follows 6.3 and later. Versions before 6.2.0 were not checked for this mapping. Which ibrav values exist 1–14, −5, −12 in every version checked (4.3.2 onwards); −9 since 5.0; 91 and −13 since 5.2.0; −3 since 6.2.0. A file with a newer value does not run on an older pw.x, but Ycrystal reads it. Length of the bohr (for celldm(1) and bohr units) Slightly. Ycrystal uses ASE's value, 0.5291772083535 Å (CODATA 2006), as it already did for ibrav = 0. QE used 0.52917720859 Å (CODATA 2006) up to 6.5, and uses 0.529177210903 Å (CODATA 2018) since 6.6. The relative differences, 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ and 4.8 × 10⁻⁹, are below 5 × 10⁻⁸ Å for a 10 Å cell. Lengths given in Å (A, B, C, angstrom) are not affected.

items.title: How this was verified, and what was not
items.text:
Audited on 21 November 2026. Each lattice is checked in up to five independent ways:

  1. Documented vectors: the vectors Ycrystal builds equal those written in INPUT_PW (typed into the test from the documentation, not from the code), within 1e-12 (tests/test_qe_lattice.py).
  2. Through the reader, in both forms: a pw.x input with celldm and one with A, B, C, cos… are read with read_structure and give the documented vectors and the right Cartesian positions for crystal coordinates, within 1e-9 Å (tests/test_readers.py).
  3. Lattice geometry: the conventional cell and its centring vectors are whole-number combinations of v1, v2, v3, and the volumes differ by the number of lattice points; for the rhombohedral lattices the lengths, the angle, and the threefold axis; for the triclinic lattice the lengths and the three angles (tests/test_qe_lattice.py).
  4. pw.x's own output: every input with ibrav other than 0 in QE's test suite that has a stored pw.x output, read with Ycrystal and compared with the crystal axes, celldm(1), and atom positions pw.x printed (scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py --qe-checkout, QE development branch). Agreement means within pw.x's printed precision: axes 2e-6 alat (6 decimals), positions 2e-7 alat (7 decimals), celldm(1) 2e-7 relative.
  5. Independent code: ASE 3.22.1's former ibrav_to_cell, in a copy with its ibrav = 11 typo fixed and −13 added (not part of Ycrystal), on 200 random parameter sets per lattice in both forms; largest difference 4e-15 Å.
ibrav 1 Documented 2 Reader, both forms 3 Geometry 4 pw.x output: inputs (forms) 5 Independent code 1 Yes Yes Yes 63 (celldm, A) Yes 2 Yes Yes Yes 140 (celldm, A) Yes 3 Yes Yes Yes 13 (celldm) Yes −3 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes 4 Yes Yes Yes 27 (celldm, A) Yes 5 Yes Yes Yes (rhombohedral) 8 (celldm) Yes −5 Yes Yes Yes (rhombohedral) 4 (celldm) Yes 6 Yes Yes Yes 10 (celldm, A) Yes 7 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes 8 Yes Yes Yes 4 (celldm) Yes 9 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes −9 Yes Yes Yes none: no such input in QE Yes 91 Yes Yes Yes none: no such input in QE No (that code has no 91) 10 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes 11 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes 12 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes −12 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes 13 Yes Yes Yes 2 (celldm) Yes −13 Yes Yes Yes none: no such input in QE Yes 14 Yes Yes Yes (lengths, angles) 10 (celldm, A) Yes

In total 295 QE inputs were compared and all agree (for 8 of them, QEHeat inputs whose atom positions come from a trajectory, only the axes). The tests run every statement of ycrystal.io.qe_lattice and of the reader's ibrav branch. Refused inputs and their messages are tested too (tests/test_readers.py, tests/test_qe_lattice.py), and the existing equivalence tests read Si (ibrav = 2), MgB2 (4, from A, C), SrTiO3 (1), and a triclinic cell (14, from A, B, C, cos…) as the same structures as their POSCAR, CIF, and ibrav = 0 files.

Where the comparison with pw.x's output does not apply, the script says why. In QE's test suite these are inputs whose structure pw.x read from an earlier run (a restart: the printed cell is not the input's) and inputs with no stored pw.x output (for example CP inputs): 106 in all. Six inputs that Ycrystal could not read at first, for reasons unrelated to ibrav, are read since the same day and agree: five give atomic masses as Fortran numbers such as 16.D0, and one gives positions as arithmetic (1/4, 2*(1/8)); pw.x accepts both. A separate check of the same kind on QE's 37 applicable ibrav = 0 inputs found all of them read and in agreement too.

items.title: Check it yourself
items.text:
The comparison with pw.x's output needs no QE installation and no pw.x run:

# QE's 17 lattice tests, downloaded from GitHub (network access needed):
.venv/bin/python scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py
# Every applicable input of QE's test suite, from a local copy (about 200 MB):
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/QEF/q-e.git q-e
git -C q-e sparse-checkout set test-suite
.venv/bin/python scripts/check_qe_ibrav.py --qe-checkout q-e

The script prints, per ibrav, the number of inputs and the largest differences, then the inputs where the comparison does not apply and why; it exits with status 1 if any input differs. QE's files are GPL and stay outside Ycrystal's repository.

Not tested:

  • ibrav −9, 91, and −13 against pw.x itself: no input in QE's test suite or examples uses them, and pw.x was not run here. They rest on checks 1–3, and −9 and −13 also on 5. ibrav = 91 is the least checked lattice: its vectors are confirmed only against the documentation and by its geometry.
  • The A, B, C, cos… form against pw.x for the lattices with angles (5, −5, 12, −12, 13, −13): QE's tests give these only with celldm. The mapping follows pw.x's routine abc2celldm, read from its source, and is checked by the tests' own table.
  • Older QE versions by running them: the version comparison above reads QE's source and release notes; no older pw.x was run.
  • macOS and Windows: the tests run there in continuous integration once the change is merged; the comparison with pw.x's output was run on Linux.

items.title: Configure and check POV-Ray
items.text:
On Linux Mint, install the distribution renderer with sudo apt install povray; on macOS, brew install povray; on Windows, POV-Ray for Windows 3.7 with its official installer, which the installation script installs with winget (see installation). The tested baseline is POV-Ray 3.7. In the GUI, discovery uses the first source that is set:

  1. Render ▸ Set POV-Ray Executable… (saved on this machine).
  2. The YCRYSTAL_POVRAY environment variable.
  3. povray on PATH.
  4. On Windows, POV-Ray for Windows in its installation folder (from the registry, or Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe); it is not on PATH.

An invalid configured path fails immediately; discovery does not fall back. Choose the executable in the menu to replace a stale setting (/usr/bin/povray on Linux Mint, /opt/homebrew/bin/povray with Homebrew on Apple silicon, where command -v povray prints it; C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe on Windows). GUI settings are separate from projects. On Linux they normally live in ~/.config/Y-Matter Lab/Ycrystal.conf, on macOS in ~/Library/Preferences/com.y-matter-lab.Ycrystal.plist, and on Windows in the registry under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Y-Matter Lab\Ycrystal.

Render ▸ Check Renderer renders a small known scene, verifies dimensions, positions, and colours, and shows a verdict. It runs synchronously and briefly blocks the window. The command-line check needs no display:

.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer
.venv/bin/ycrystal --check-renderer --povray /usr/bin/povray

On Windows, in PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --check-renderer
.venv\Scripts\ycrystal.exe --check-renderer --povray "C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe"

--povray applies only to --check-renderer; that command does not read the path saved by the GUI. Without the option it uses the environment, then PATH, then (on Windows) the installation of POV-Ray for Windows. A pass prints PASS: …; a renderer failure prints FAIL: … and exits 1. The check creates temporary files and removes the completed job. It launches POV-Ray, but no Qt window. On Windows it fails at once, with the remedy, if POV-Ray for Windows is open or would ask about its missing editor (see troubleshooting).

items.title: Export an editable scene
items.text:
