set_output_size(width: int, height: int, ratio: float | None = None) -> None

Set the output image size in pixels as an undoable step; the camera is kept.

The frame in the 3D view takes the new aspect ratio; the image keeps its centre and visible height in Å, so a new resolution at the same ratio keeps the composition. Values are clamped to 16–8000 pixels. Consecutive size changes merge into one undo step.

Parameters:

  • height (int) –

request_preview() -> bool

items.title: export_pov
items.text:
export_pov(path: str | Path | None = None) -> Path | None

Write the current view as an editable POV-Ray scene (File ▸ Export POV-Ray…).

Writes NAME.pov and NAME.ini next to each other; the .ini file names NAME.png as output. POV-Ray is not needed and not started.

Parameters:

  • path (str | Path | None, default: None ) –

    Scene file; None shows a file dialog. The suffix is replaced by .pov.

Returns:

    Path of the .pov file, or None if the dialog was cancelled.

Raises:

Notes

Existing files are replaced. The file dialog asks before replacing the .pov file; the .ini file is replaced without asking. The scene header records the POV-Ray version found at export time, if any, and the standard include files the materials need. If an include file is not found on this computer, an error message says so (the files are still written). A background picture is copied next to the scene (bg_<digest>.png or .jpg) and named relatively, so the folder can be moved as a whole.

Returns:

items.title: render_image
items.text:
render_image(path: str | Path, options: ExportOptions, show_result: bool = True) -> bool

Start a POV-Ray render of the current view and write it as PNG, PDF, or JPEG.

POV-Ray renders options.width × options.height pixels with the current camera, geometry, and environment; a size of another shape than the output frame shows a wider or narrower area at the same scale (never stretched). The scene, the Render panel's output size, and the project are not changed.

After a synchronous version query (up to 15 seconds) and job preparation, POV-Ray runs in the background in a temporary job directory. The method returns once that process has been requested; the toolbar's Cancel stops it and the status bar shows its progress. When it finishes, the image is written to the destination by write_export (replacing an existing file only once the new one is complete), the job directory is deleted, and the image is shown or an error message explains the failure. A cancelled render leaves the destination untouched and shows no error.

Parameters:

  • path (str | Path) –

    Destination file; its suffix is made to match options.format.

  • options (ExportOptions) –

    Format, pixel size, resolution, and JPEG quality.

  • show_result (bool, default: True ) –

    Whether to show the finished image in a dialog.

Returns:

  • bool –

    Whether a render started. False if one is already running or POV-Ray is not found (a message explains how to set it up).

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If the temporary job directory or scene files cannot be created.

items.title: check_renderer

check_renderer() -> None

Run the renderer self-test and show the verdict (Render ▸ Check Renderer).

Runs synchronously: the window does not respond until the test finishes, normally within a few seconds.

items.title: PreviewRequest
items.text:

items.title: export_dialog
items.text:
The Render Image dialog: format, figure size, resolution, and file (FR-EXPORT-01).

The dialog only collects choices; the main window renders with POV-Ray and writes the file (see ycrystal.render.formats). Sizes are entered in pixels or millimetres; the pixel size POV-Ray renders follows from them and the resolution (figure_pixels). With the shape kept (the default), the height follows the blue output frame of the 3D view, so the image shows exactly the framed area at any size.

items.title: style_dialog
items.text:
The File ▸ Import Style… dialog: style parts and the optional element mapping.

The dialog only collects a choice; the main window applies it with apply_style as one undoable step. The element mapping (FR-STYLE-MAP-01) sends the style's settings for one element to another element of the open structure, or leaves them out. Every row starts at the transfer by matching symbols, so pressing Apply without changing a row behaves as before. What will be applied and left out is shown before Apply, from resolve_element_map; an ambiguous mapping disables Apply and says why.

items.title: StructureViewport
items.text:
StructureViewport(parent: QWidget | None = None)

Bases: QWidget

Interactive 3D view of a DisplayGeometry.

The only place where VTK objects live. It draws exactly the geometry it is given, exchanges views as Camera objects, and reports clicks as indices into that geometry. It never changes the structure or the geometry. The orientation axes in the corner and the selection highlight exist only in this live view. Sphere and bond tessellation drops above 2,000 and 8,000 displayed atoms; POV-Ray continues to use exact spheres and cylinders.

    Qt parent widget.

items.title: set_scene
items.text:
set_scene(geometry: DisplayGeometry, environment: Environment) -> None

Replace drawn atoms, bonds, cell edges, and vector arrows; keep the camera.

Parameters:

  • geometry (DisplayGeometry) –

    Geometry to draw. A reference is kept for picking and fitting; it is not copied or modified.

  • environment (Environment) –

    Background, floor, and transparency are approximated (see Notes); the key and fill lights are taken from the shared lighting rig (see set_lighting).

Raises:

  • PresetError –

    If a material of the geometry is not a known material preset.

Notes

The selection highlight is removed; call set_highlight again if needed. Atoms and half-bonds are grouped by material, one actor per material (atom_actors and bond_actors), each with the material's live approximation (Phong coefficients and opacity); POV-Ray renders the real material. The background is Environment.live_background: the floor colour when there is a floor, a vertical gradient for gradients and skies. Shadows, area-light softness, reflections, refraction, the reflection panel, clouds, and procedural patterns appear only in the POV-Ray preview and render.

items.title: set_lighting
items.text:
set_lighting(environment: Environment) -> None

Use the lights of environment without rebuilding the scene.

The key and fill lights become VTK scene lights at the world positions of resolve_lighting for the output camera and the current geometry: positional, white, with the environment's intensities, no distance attenuation (constant attenuation 1), and no spotlight cone. A light with non-positive intensity is switched off. The positions are resolved again before every redraw, so they follow the camera; they are already in world coordinates and get no further camera-relative transformation.

Parameters:

  • environment (Environment) –

    Environment whose lighting values are shown; background and floor are not changed (use set_scene for those).

items.title: set_measurement
items.text:
set_measurement(points: ndarray, radii: ndarray, kind: str | None) -> None

Show the helpers of a measurement: picked atoms and a guide.

Parameters:

  • points (ndarray) –

    Positions in Å of the picked atoms in order (A, B, C), shape (n, 3); empty removes the helpers.

  • radii (ndarray) –

    Drawn radii of those atoms (for the cage size).

  • kind (str | None) –

    "distance" (dashed line A–B) or "angle" (dashed arms B–A and B–C, and a solid arc at the vertex B once all three atoms are picked). The lines are drawn in front of the atoms.

Notes

Each picked atom gets a wire cage and a boxed letter label (A, B, C; "B vertex" for angles) that stays readable in front of the atoms. The helpers are separate, non-pickable VTK actors: they are not part of the geometry, so exports, bounds, Fit, the lights, and picking ignore them, and the camera does not change.

items.title: RenderProcess
items.text:
RenderProcess(job: RenderJob, executable: str, parent: QObject | None = None)

Bases: QObject

Run POV-Ray for one job without blocking the Qt event loop.

start returns immediately; the render runs in a separate process. A running Qt event loop (QCoreApplication is sufficient; no window or display is needed) delivers the result through finished.

povray runs as a QProcess, whose output gives the progress. POV-Ray for Windows prints nothing and must start minimised, which QProcess cannot ask for in PySide6: it runs as a subprocess.Popen that a timer checks every WINDOWS_ENGINE_POLL_MS (100 ms) for its exit, with the foreground held (see hold_foreground). It reports no progress until the final 100. Only one copy of it can run at a time, so this program's renders with it take turns: one started while another runs waits (and counts as running) until that one has finished. An open POV-Ray for Windows that keeps a single instance makes the render fail at once with an explanation (see windows_engine_conflict).

Parameters:

  • job (RenderJob) –

    Prepared job; POV-Ray runs with job.directory as its working directory.

  • executable (str) –

    POV-Ray executable.

  • parent (QObject | None, default: None ) –

    Qt parent object.

Attributes:

  • job –

    The job being rendered. Its directory is not removed by this class; call job.cleanup() after finished.

  • executable –

    The POV-Ray executable.

items.title: readers
items.text:
Read POSCAR/CONTCAR, CIF, and Quantum ESPRESSO pw.x input into a Structure.

ASE does the parsing; this module adds format detection, provenance, and the checks that keep Ycrystal from drawing something different from what the file means:

  • VASP 4 files (no element line) need an explicit element mapping. ASE would guess elements from words in the free-text comment line, which can be silently wrong.
  • CIF sites with partial occupancy, or distinct sites at the same position, are rejected instead of being drawn as an ordered structure.
  • QE input with ibrav = 0 needs a CELL_PARAMETERS card. Other ibrav values (ASE does not read them) are converted here with pw.x's own conventions (ycrystal.io.qe_lattice); crystal_sg positions are rejected. Card values that pw.x reads but ASE does not are rewritten first: Fortran reals such as 16.D0, and arithmetic in coordinates such as 1/4. Species labels are kept separately from elements; labels that do not name an element unambiguously need a mapping.

Interactive questions are raised as exceptions (FormatChoiceRequired, BlockChoiceRequired, ElementMappingRequired) so that the GUI can ask and call again with the answer. The readers never modify the input file and never open a window.

All readers return Cartesian positions in Å with periodic boundary conditions along a, b, and c. POSCAR and QE cells keep the lattice vectors as written in the file (converted to Å); CIF cells are built from the cell parameters with a along x and b in the xy plane.

items.text:

items.title: read_structure
items.text:
read_structure(path: str | Path, fmt: str | None = None, *, block: str | None = None, element_map: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> Structure

Read a POSCAR/CONTCAR, CIF, or Quantum ESPRESSO input file.

Parameters:

  • path (str | Path) –

    Structure file. It is read once as bytes and never modified.

  • fmt (str | None, default: None ) –

    "poscar", "cif", or "qe" to skip detection; None detects the format with detect_format.

  • block (str | None, default: None ) –

    CIF data block to read; required when a CIF file contains several structures.

  • element_map (dict[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    Element symbol for each species key of an earlier ElementMappingRequired.

Returns:

  • Structure –

    The structure in Cartesian Å, periodic along a, b, and c. Its metadata["source"] holds the provenance: path (absolute), name, format, sha256 and size_bytes of the file, imported_at (UTC, ISO 8601), reader (the ASE version), and element_map if one was given. Format-specific entries are comment and vasp_version (POSCAR), block and, if known, spacegroup (CIF), qe_species (QE label to element), and qe_ibrav and qe_celldm (QE input with ibrav other than 0).

Raises:

  • FormatChoiceRequired –

    If fmt is None and the format cannot be detected.

  • BlockChoiceRequired –

    If a CIF file has several structures and block is None.

  • ElementMappingRequired –

    If elements are needed for VASP 4 species or ambiguous QE labels.

  • UnsupportedStructureError –

    If the file uses a construct that Ycrystal does not draw (see the module description).

  • StructureImportError –

    If the file cannot be read, is a project file, is malformed, or contains no atoms. str(error) explains the problem.

Examples:

Paths are relative to a source checkout:

>>> from ycrystal.io.readers import read_structure
>>> mgb2 = read_structure("tests/fixtures/MgB2.cif")
>>> mgb2.composition(), mgb2.labels
('MgB2', ('Mg1', 'B1', 'B1'))
>>> mgb2.metadata["source"]["spacegroup"]
{'number': 191, 'symbol': 'P 6/m m m'}

items.title: evaluate_qe_expression
items.text:
evaluate_qe_expression(expression: str) -> float

Evaluate a coordinate of ATOMIC_POSITIONS as pw.x does.

pw.x accepts simple arithmetic for each coordinate (its eval_infix): numbers (also .5 and exponents with e, E, d, or D), +, -, *, /, ^ (power), and parentheses, without spaces. ^ and the signs + and - bind tightest and group from the right (-2^2 is −4, 2^3^2 is 512, and 2^-1 is 0.5); then * and /; then + and -, which group from the left.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    For anything else, an unbalanced parenthesis, or a division by zero.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.io.readers import evaluate_qe_expression
>>> evaluate_qe_expression("1/4"), evaluate_qe_expression("2*(1/8)")
(0.25, 0.25)
>>> evaluate_qe_expression("1/(2/(1/2))"), evaluate_qe_expression("-2^2")
(0.25, -4.0)
>>> evaluate_qe_expression("0.5d0")
0.5

items.title: fortran_real
items.text:
fortran_real(token: str) -> str

Return a Fortran real with a D exponent in the E notation Python reads.

pw.x reads masses and cell vectors with Fortran, which accepts 16.D0 or 1.5d-3; other text is returned unchanged.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.io.readers import fortran_real
>>> fortran_real("16.D0"), fortran_real("-1.5d-3"), fortran_real("Si.pbe-d.UPF")
('16.E0', '-1.5e-3', 'Si.pbe-d.UPF')

items.title: qe_lattice
items.text:
Bravais lattices of Quantum ESPRESSO input with ibrav other than 0 (FR-QE-IBRAV-01).

In a pw.x input, ibrav names a Bravais lattice and its parameters are given either as celldm(1) … celldm(6) (celldm(1) = a in bohr, the others ratios and cosines) or as A, B, C, cosAB, cosAC, cosBC (lengths in Å). pw.x builds the lattice vectors from them with fixed conventions; this module builds the same vectors, so that a structure opens with exactly the cell pw.x uses.

The vectors follow the definitions in the pw.x input documentation (INPUT_PW, the ibrav variable) and pw.x's lattice generator (Modules/latgen.f90), including its checks of the parameters, and the mapping of A, B, C, cosAB… onto celldm (abc2celldm). Every ibrav value pw.x accepts is supported:

========== ========================================================= ibrav Lattice ========== ========================================================= 1 cubic P (sc) 2 cubic F (fcc) 3, -3 cubic I (bcc); -3 is the more symmetric axis choice 4 hexagonal and trigonal P 5, -5 trigonal R, threefold axis along z (5) or along (111) (-5) 6 tetragonal P (st) 7 tetragonal I (bct) 8 orthorhombic P 9, -9 orthorhombic base-centred, C type (two axis choices) 91 orthorhombic one-face base-centred, A type 10 orthorhombic face-centred 11 orthorhombic body-centred 12, -12 monoclinic P, unique axis c (12) or b (-12) 13, -13 monoclinic base-centred, unique axis c (13) or b (-13) 14 triclinic ========== =========================================================

The vectors are those of QE 6.5 and later. They are the same in every older version, except for ibrav = -13: QE 5.2.0 to 6.4.1 used other axes, v1(old) = −v2 and v2(old) = v1 (pw.x warns about this change). crystal positions written for the old axes therefore describe other atom places here; QE's release notes convert them with (x, y, z) → (y, −x, z). The mapping of A, B, C, cos… onto celldm is that of QE 6.3 and later (6.2 ignored cosAC for ibrav = -13). Details, and how this was checked, are in the user guide (Quantum ESPRESSO lattices).

Examples:

Silicon in the fcc lattice of pw.x (ibrav = 2, celldm(1) in bohr):

>>> from ycrystal.io.qe_lattice import ibrav_cell
>>> ibrav_cell(2, (10.2631026323, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), bohr=0.529177).round(4)
array([[-2.7155,  0.    ,  2.7155],
       [ 0.    ,  2.7155,  2.7155],
       [-2.7155,  2.7155,  0.    ]])

MgB2, hexagonal, from crystallographic parameters in Å:

>>> from ycrystal.io.qe_lattice import celldm_from_input
>>> celldm = celldm_from_input(4, {"a": 3.086, "c": 3.524}, bohr=0.529177)
>>> ibrav_cell(4, celldm, bohr=0.529177).round(4)
array([[ 3.086 ,  0.    ,  0.    ],
       [-1.543 ,  2.6726,  0.    ],
       [ 0.    ,  0.    ,  3.524 ]])

items.title: project
items.text:
The .ycrystal project file: versioned JSON with the embedded structure.

A project that uses a background picture is saved as a ZIP package instead: the same JSON document as project.json plus the picture under assets/ (see ycrystal.io.package). Both forms are recognised by content, so the suffix stays .ycrystal.

A project reopens without the original structure file: the canonical structure (cell, positions, elements, labels, occupancy, movable flags) is stored in full, together with its import provenance, the display settings (including hidden atoms), environment, camera, and output settings. Floats are written with Python's shortest round-trip representation, so reopening reproduces every coordinate exactly.

The top-level JSON object has the keys format (always "ycrystal-project"), schema_version, generator, saved_at, structure, scene, environment, camera, and output. Machine-specific settings such as the POV-Ray path are not stored in projects.

Schema history: 1 — first version (M1); 2 — repetitions, cell mode, and bonds (M2); 3 — material and background presets, explicit output size (M3); 4 — element and atom material overrides, element colours, and the full environment: background type, floor, lighting, and reflection panel (M4); 5 — element radii (M5); 6 — background pictures (environment.background.image, ZIP packages with assets; FR-BGIMAGE-01) and custom material variants (top-level materials list with the full definition of every variant the scene uses; FR-MATERIAL-01); 7 — atom-attached vectors (scene.vectors with source defaults and image overrides at full precision, scene.vector_style; FR-VECTOR-01); 8 — the element legend (scene.legend; FR-LEGEND-01), absent and so disabled in older files. Projects without a picture are still single JSON files. Older files open with the M3 appearance: no overrides, plain background, no floor, and the "soft" lighting. Schema-1 files load with bonds disabled to preserve their original appearance. In every schema the saved camera describes the output image of output.width × output.height pixels (schemas 1 and 2 recorded the output size the camera was rendered at), so reopening reproduces the framing exactly, whatever the window size. Schema-1/2 files get the "satin" material they were drawn with, and the "transparent" background preset if their output had a transparent background.

The optional output.aspect_locked and output.aspect_ratio keys store the Render panel's aspect-ratio lock (FR-RENDER-01). They do not change the stored contract, so the schema version stays 5: files without them open locked to their own width / height, and Ycrystal 0.1.0 ignores them.

items.title: Project dataclass
items.text:
Project(structure: Structure, scene: SceneSettings = SceneSettings(), environment: Environment = Environment(), camera: Camera | None = None, output: RenderSettings = RenderSettings())

Everything a project file stores, independent of any window.

Attributes:

  • structure (Structure) –

    The scientific structure, stored in full.

  • scene (SceneSettings) –

    Display settings, including hidden atoms and the boundary policy.

  • environment (Environment) –

    Background, floor, transparency, and lighting.

  • camera (Camera | None) –

    Camera of the output image (output.width × output.height), or None to use the default view when the project is opened.

  • output (RenderSettings) –

    Output image size and antialiasing. transparent_background mirrors environment.transparent, which is authoritative.

Notes

This container is mutable. Its scene, environment, camera, and output objects are frozen dataclasses. Structure arrays are read-only, but structure metadata remains mutable.

Validate a project document and convert it to a Project.

Parameters:

items.title: save_project
items.text:
save_project(path: str | Path, project: Project) -> Path

Write a project file atomically.

A project whose environment refers to a background picture is written as a ZIP package with the picture (see ycrystal.io.package); others as plain JSON. The JSON text is written to a temporary file .ycrystal-*.tmp in the target directory, which then replaces path with a single rename. An existing file at path is overwritten without asking; if writing fails, it is left unchanged.

Parameters:

  • path (str | Path) –

    Destination, used as given: no suffix is added. Missing parent directories are created.

  • project (Project) –

    Project to save.

Returns:

  • Path –

    path as a Path.

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If the directory or file cannot be written; the temporary file is removed.

  • ValueError –

    If a value cannot be written as JSON, for example a non-finite coordinate.

  • ImageError –

    If the background picture is not registered in this session.

items.title: load_project
items.text:
load_project(path: str | Path) -> Project

Read a project file.

Parameters:

  • path (str | Path) –

    Project file: UTF-8 JSON or a ZIP package with pictures (recognised by content). The original structure and picture files are not needed; the package's pictures are registered for this session.

Returns:

  • Project –

    The restored project; coordinates are identical to the saved ones.

Raises:

  • ProjectError –

    If the file cannot be read, is not UTF-8 text or valid JSON (the message gives the line), is a damaged or unsafe package, misses a referenced picture, or fails the checks of project_from_dict.

Examples:

>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from ycrystal.core.samples import perovskite_srtio3
>>> from ycrystal.io.project import Project, load_project, save_project
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
...     path = save_project(Path(tmp) / "SrTiO3.ycrystal", Project(perovskite_srtio3()))
...     reopened = load_project(path)
>>> reopened.structure.composition(), reopened.camera is None
('SrTiO3', True)

items.title: images
items.text:
Imported pictures: validation, normalisation, and content-addressed storage.

Background pictures (FR-BGIMAGE-01) are imported once and then referred to by content identity: the SHA-256 digest of the stored bytes. Renders, projects, styles, and exports use the stored bytes, never the original path, so moving or deleting the original file changes nothing.

Import rules: PNG and JPEG files are decoded with Pillow to check them. A file is stored unchanged when POV-Ray 3.7 can read it as it is (RGB or greyscale PNG, with or without alpha; RGB or greyscale JPEG) and has normal orientation; otherwise (EXIF rotation, CMYK, palette, or other modes) the decoded, upright pixels are stored as PNG. The size limits are MAX_IMAGE_BYTES, MAX_IMAGE_SIDE, and MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS.

Stored pictures are kept in a process-wide registry (register_image, get_image). Entries are immutable and keyed by their content, so registering the same picture twice is harmless, and undo/redo steps that still refer to a replaced or removed picture keep working for the whole session.

items.title: package
items.text:
ZIP packages for projects and styles that carry pictures (FR-BGIMAGE-01).

A package is a ZIP archive with one JSON document (project.json or style.json, the same document a plain JSON file holds) and the pictures it refers to under assets/, each named by its content identity: assets/<sha256>.png or .jpg. Files without pictures stay plain JSON. Readers recognise the two forms by content (the ZIP signature), not by the file-name suffix.

Reading is defensive: entry names must be relative, without .., backslashes, or drive letters; sizes are limited (see the constants); every referenced picture must be present, decode as a picture in stored form, and match its digest. Anything else is refused with a message, and nothing is changed.

items.title: style
items.text:
Reusable figure styles (.ycstyle files).

A style is the presentation of a project without its structure and camera: materials, colours, radii, display settings, the environment, and the output size. It can be applied to another structure; the structure's scientific data are never changed.

A style whose environment has a background picture is saved as a ZIP package with the picture (style.json plus assets/, see ycrystal.io.package), so it works after the original picture file is moved or deleted; other styles stay plain JSON. Style schema 2 adds the picture record and the definitions of the custom materials the style uses (FR-MATERIAL-01); schema 3 adds the element legend (FR-LEGEND-01). Older styles still load, with the legend disabled.

Transfer rules

A style has four parts; apply_style applies any subset of them (see STYLE_PARTS):

appearance Default material. Material, colour, and radius overrides of elements are applied to the elements the target structure contains; overrides of other elements are left out and listed in the notes. The vector arrow appearance (placement, length mode, sizes, colour, material) and the element legend (FR-LEGEND-01) are applied too; the legend's custom element order follows the element mapping. display Atom size, repetitions, boundary atoms, cell edges, bond settings. Bond-pair rules apply when the target contains both elements. environment Background, floor, lighting, transparency, and the cell-edge colour. output Output image size in pixels.

Vectors themselves (components and atom attachments, FR-VECTOR-01) are a property of one structure, not of a look: styles never store or transfer them, and importing a style keeps the target's vectors unchanged.

Per-atom material overrides and hidden atoms refer to individual atoms of the source structure. They transfer only if the target is compatible: the same number of atoms with the same element at every position in the input order (for example the same structure read from another file or relaxed). Otherwise they are left out, and the notes explain why.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.core.samples import perovskite_srtio3, triclinic_marker
>>> from ycrystal.core.scene import Environment, SceneSettings
>>> from ycrystal.io.style import Style, apply_style
>>> source = perovskite_srtio3()
>>> scene = (
...     SceneSettings(material="glossy")
...     .with_element_material("O", "glass")
...     .with_element_material("Ti", "gold")
...     .with_atom_materials([(0, (0, 0, 0))], "chrome")
... )
>>> style = Style.from_state(source, scene, Environment(), (800, 600))
>>> target = triclinic_marker()
>>> sorted(set(target.symbols))
['Cl', 'Fe', 'N', 'O', 'S']
>>> result = apply_style(style, target, SceneSettings(), Environment(), (1200, 800))
>>> result.scene.material, result.scene.element_materials, result.scene.atom_materials
('glossy', (('O', 'glass'),), ())
>>> result.output_size
(800, 600)
>>> print(result.notes[0])
Element overrides for Ti were not applied: the structure has no Ti.
>>> print(result.notes[1][:52])
1 per-atom material override was not applied: it ref

items.title: apply_style
items.text:
apply_style(style: Style, structure: Structure, scene: SceneSettings, environment: Environment, output_size: tuple[int, int], parts: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = STYLE_PARTS, element_map: dict[str, str | None] | None = None) -> StyleResult

Apply a style to a structure's current presentation.

Parameters:

  • style (Style) –

    Style to apply.

  • structure (Structure) –

    Target structure; it is read, never modified.

  • scene (SceneSettings) –

    Current presentation of the target; parts that are not applied stay as they are.

  • environment (SceneSettings) –

    Current presentation of the target; parts that are not applied stay as they are.

  • output_size (SceneSettings) –

    Current presentation of the target; parts that are not applied stay as they are.

  • parts (tuple[str, ...] | list[str], default: STYLE_PARTS ) –

    Parts to apply, a subset of STYLE_PARTS.

  • element_map (dict[str, str | None] | None, default: None ) –

    Optional {source element: target element or None} that sends the element materials, colours, and radii, and the bond-pair rules, of a source element to another element of the structure, or leaves them out (None); see resolve_element_map. None (the default) transfers by matching symbols, as before. Atoms, coordinates, vectors, and bonds themselves are never mapped, and per-atom settings still transfer only to the same structure.

Returns:

  • StyleResult –

    New settings and notes on what was left out (see the module's transfer rules).

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If parts contains an unknown name.

  • ElementMapError –

    If element_map is invalid or ambiguous (a subclass of ValueError).

check_element("Ti") 'Ti'

items.title: style_elements
items.text:
style_elements(style: Style, parts: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = STYLE_PARTS) -> tuple[str, ...]

appearance contributes the element materials, colours, and radii; display the elements of bond-pair rules. Other parts have no element settings.

items.title: resolve_element_map
items.text:
resolve_element_map(style: Style, structure: Structure, element_map: dict[str, str | None] | None = None, parts: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = STYLE_PARTS) -> ElementTransfer

Decide where each of a style's element settings goes in a structure.

Without a mapping every element keeps its symbol: its settings apply if the structure contains it (the transfer rule of earlier versions). A mapping sends the settings of a source element to another element of the structure, or leaves them out (None); the mapping is a presentation choice, not a statement of chemical or crystallographic equivalence.

Parameters:

  • style (Style) –

    Style whose element settings are transferred.

  • structure (Structure) –

    Target structure; it is read, never modified.

  • element_map (dict[str, str | None] | None, default: None ) –

    {source element: target element or None}. Elements that are not keys keep their symbol. {"Ti": "Ti"} is allowed and changes nothing.

  • parts (tuple[str, ...] | list[str], default: STYLE_PARTS ) –

    Parts that will be applied (decides which element settings count).

Returns:

  • ElementTransfer –

Raises:

  • ElementMapError –

    If a key or value is not an element symbol, a target element is not in the structure, two source elements are mapped to the same target, or a mapped element would land on an element that keeps its own settings by symbol. Ambiguity is an error, never resolved by order.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.core.samples import perovskite_srtio3
>>> from ycrystal.core.scene import Environment, SceneSettings
>>> source = perovskite_srtio3()
>>> scene = (
...     SceneSettings()
...     .with_element_material("Ti", "gold")
...     .with_element_color("O", (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))
... )
>>> style = Style.from_state(source, scene, Environment(), (800, 600))
>>> resolve_element_map(style, source, {"Ti": None}).targets
(('O', 'O'),)
>>> try:
...     resolve_element_map(style, source, {"Ti": "O"})
... except ElementMapError as error:
...     print(str(error)[:45])
O would receive the settings of both O and Ti

items.title: presets
items.text:
Material, environment, and lighting presets.

Every preset is a small JSON manifest shipped with the package: one file per material in presets/materials/, one per environment in presets/environments/, and the lighting presets in presets/lighting.json. Each material and environment also has a thumbnail rendered by POV-Ray (presets/thumbnails/, regenerated with scripts/render_thumbnails.py).

A material records how POV-Ray draws it (one of four declaration kinds, see Material), the native POV-Ray identifiers it uses, the standard include files they need, whether it keeps the element colour, and an approximation for the live VTK view. An environment preset initialises the background, the floor, and the lighting of an Environment; the user can change each of them afterwards.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.presets import DEFAULT_MATERIAL, get_material, materials
>>> DEFAULT_MATERIAL
'satin'
>>> len(materials()) >= 20
True
>>> gold = get_material("gold")
>>> gold.kind, gold.native, gold.includes, gold.keeps_element_color
('texture', ('T_Gold_3C',), ('metals.inc',), False)
>>> [m.id for m in materials() if m.matches("marble")]
['marble']

"texture" A complete native texture (own colours), for example T_Gold_3C. "material" A material with an interior: either the native identifier in material (own colours) or, without it, the element colour with filter, finish, optional normal, and interior.

items.title: custom
items.text:
Custom material variants made from Ycrystal's own recipes (FR-MATERIAL-01).

A variant starts from a built-in material whose recipe Ycrystal writes itself and changes some of its parameters. The parameters are typed numbers with explicit ranges (see SCHEMAS); the POV-Ray 3.7 recipe text is generated from them, never edited as text. Built-in presets stay unchanged.

Editable bases:

  • Opaque finishes (Matte, Satin, Glossy, Ceramic, Plastic): diffuse, specular highlight amount and roughness (Plastic: phong highlight amount and size), reflection.
  • Glass (tinted), Frosted glass, Gem: as above plus the pigment filter amount and the index of refraction; Frosted glass also the bump strength and scale of its surface relief.
  • Decorative textures (Marble, Jade, Granite, Stone, Wood): the pattern scale, in the material's unit texture space (relative to each atom).

Native POV-Ray definitions (metals, M_Glass, M_Ruby_Glass) and the ASE styles are not editable.

A MaterialDefinition stores the base id, a name, the definition version, and every parameter value (also those not shown in the dialog), so a saved figure does not change if a built-in default changes later. Its id is derived from that content (custom_<base>_<digest>): two different definitions can never share an id, and a variant cannot replace a built-in or another variant.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.presets.custom import base_definition, schema_for
>>> satin = base_definition("satin")
>>> satin.parameter("specular"), satin.parameter("roughness")
(0.35, 0.02)
>>> shiny = satin.with_values(specular=0.7, roughness=0.005).renamed("Shiny satin")
>>> shiny.id.startswith("custom_satin_"), shiny.material().finish
(True, 'ambient 0.08 diffuse 0.75 specular 0.7 roughness 0.005')
>>> [p.key for p in schema_for("glass_frosted").visible()]
['diffuse', 'specular', 'roughness', 'reflection', 'filter', 'ior', 'bump_strength', 'bump_scale']

items.title: thumbnails
items.text:
Gallery thumbnails rendered by POV-Ray with fixed scenes.

Every material is shown on the same three bonded spheres (strontium, titanium, and oxygen colours) in one fixed environment (MATERIAL_ENVIRONMENT), and every environment on the same SrTiO3 unit cell with the satin material, so thumbnails can be compared with each other. The scenes are written by the ordinary scene_to_pov; the thumbnails are genuine POV-Ray images, not approximations.

The thumbnails are shipped in ycrystal/presets/thumbnails/ together with index.json, which records a digest of each scene. When a preset recipe or the scene writer changes, the digest no longer matches (the test suite checks this), and scripts/render_thumbnails.py renders the affected thumbnails again.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.render.thumbnails import material_scene, scene_digest
>>> text = material_scene("gold")
>>> "texture { T_Gold_3C" in text and '#include "metals.inc"' in text
True
>>> len(scene_digest(text))
64

items.title: pov_writer
items.text:
Write a POV-Ray 3.7 scene (.pov) and render settings (.ini) from the shared scene.

The camera is written with explicit location/direction/right/up vectors taken from Camera; look_at and sky are not used, so POV-Ray does not re-derive the basis or flip handedness. Coordinates are the original right-handed world coordinates in ångström, which keeps the scene readable and editable.

Scenes use only POV-Ray 3.7 language features (#version 3.7;). Materials that use native POV-Ray identifiers (for example T_Gold_3C) #include the standard files that declare them; other scenes are self-contained. Colours are written as sRGB values and converted to linear light inside the scene (assumed_gamma 1.0); the .ini file writes the PNG with sRGB gamma. The writer produces text only; running POV-Ray is the job of ycrystal.render.jobs.

items.title: scene_to_pov
items.text:
scene_to_pov(geometry: DisplayGeometry, camera: Camera, environment: Environment, settings: RenderSettings, *, title: str = 'Ycrystal scene', renderer_note: str | None = None) -> str

Return the text of a POV-Ray scene.

Parameters:

  • geometry (DisplayGeometry) –

    Atoms and cell edges to draw; hidden atoms are already absent from it.

  • camera (Camera) –

    View to reproduce.

  • environment (Environment) –

    Background, floor, transparency, and lighting.

  • settings (RenderSettings) –

    Output size and background transparency. The size sets the camera's visible width and height; it should match the size in the .ini file. The background is transparent if either settings.transparent_background or environment.transparent is set.

  • title (str, default: 'Ycrystal scene' ) –

    Text of the first comment line.

  • renderer_note (str | None, default: None ) –

    Optional comment naming the renderer the scene was written for.

Returns:

  • str –

    The scene text. Its header lists the standard #include files the materials need (see required_includes); a scene without them is self-contained.

Raises:

  • PresetError –

    If a material of the geometry is not a known preset.

Notes

The camera is orthographic, with direction set to the unit viewing direction and right and up set to the screen vectors scaled to the visible width and height in Å. Its location lies on the line through the focal point along the viewing direction, far enough back to keep everything drawn (and, with a floor, the whole frame) in front of the eye; under orthographic projection this does not change the image.

Lights come from resolve_lighting: they are placed around the camera's focal point at 4 R + |C - F| + 10 Å (R and C from the geometry's bounding sphere), the key light in the environment's direction (a circular, oriented area light without jitter when light_size > 0, so renders are deterministic) and a shadowless fill light at the lower right; a light with non-positive intensity is omitted. There is no distance attenuation.

A floor is a plane below the drawn spheres as seen in the frame, tilted by FLOOR_TILT_DEG towards the viewer; in an orthographic view it fills the background. Gradients and skies are painted on a backdrop plane behind the scene, aligned with the frame (a sky_sphere would be a single colour in an orthographic view); it sits in a light_group without lights because it needs no lighting. Transparent backgrounds leave out floor and backdrop. The optional reflection panel is a bright disc on the key-light side of the structure (3 R from C) marked no_image: invisible to the camera, it appears only in reflections.

Each material is declared once per element colour (once in total for materials with their own pigment), as a texture or a material. Materials in unit texture space are applied to a unit sphere that is scaled and moved to each atom. Each atom is a sphere with a comment giving its 1-based source atom number, element, and image offset; a comment states how many atoms are hidden. Bonds are two half cylinders with the material of their endpoint atoms, using geometry.bond_radius. Cell edges are cylinders with spheres at the corners, marked no_shadow.

The header records the generation time (UTC), so two exports of the same scene differ in that line.

items.text:
write_scene_files(directory: Path, basename: str, geometry: DisplayGeometry, camera: Camera, environment: Environment, settings: RenderSettings, **kwargs: str) -> tuple[Path, Path, Path]

Write a scene file and its .ini file into a directory.

Parameters:

  • directory (Path) –

    Existing directory for both files.

  • basename (str) –

    File name without suffix. Spaces and non-ASCII characters are supported; avoid double quotes because the INI writer removes them from file names.

  • geometry (DisplayGeometry) –

    Atoms and cell edges to draw.

  • camera (Camera) –

    View to reproduce.

  • environment (Environment) –

    Background, transparency, and light intensities. A transparent environment also switches on Output_Alpha in the .ini file.

  • settings (RenderSettings) –

    Output image settings.

  • **kwargs (str, default: {} ) –

    Passed to scene_to_pov (title, renderer_note).

Returns:

  • pov_path ( Path ) –

    directory / f"{basename}.pov".

  • ini_path ( Path ) –

    directory / f"{basename}.ini".

  • image_path ( Path ) –

    directory / f"{basename}.png", the output named in the .ini file. It is not created here.

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If a file cannot be written, for example because directory does not exist.

Notes

Both files are written as UTF-8 and replace existing files of the same name without asking. The .ini file refers to the scene and the image by relative names, so run povray basename.ini with directory as the working directory (POV-Ray for Windows: pvengine64.exe /EXIT /NR basename.ini, see render_arguments). The I/O restrictions of the Ubuntu and Linux Mint povray package also allow writing the image only there (or under /tmp). A background picture is copied next to the scene (stage_assets) and named relatively, so the directory can be moved as a whole.

Only the background picture of an "image" environment is drawn (not with a transparent background). Files are named by content (asset_filename); an existing file with that name is replaced.

items.title: lighting
items.text:
Resolved lighting rig shared by the POV-Ray writer and the live views (FR-LIGHT-01).

The lighting controls of an Environment are relative values: angles in the output camera's screen basis and a size in units of the scene radius. resolve_lighting turns them into world-space positions in Å for a given output camera and displayed geometry. The POV-Ray writer, the live view's light approximation, and the Lighting Setup window all use this one result, so they cannot disagree. Nothing here depends on Qt, VTK, or POV-Ray syntax, and nothing is stored: the rig is derived from the environment, the camera, and the geometry whenever it is needed.

Conventions

The basis is the output camera's (right, up, direction) from Camera.basis; direction points from the eye into the scene, so -direction points toward the viewer.

  • Origin: the camera's focal point F (the point at the image centre).
  • Distance: D = 4 R + |C - F| + 10 Å, with C and R the centre and radius of DisplayGeometry.bounding_sphere (displayed atoms including boundary images and repetitions, plus cell edges; hidden atoms excluded).
  • Key light: F + D (cos(el) (sin(az) right - cos(az) direction) + sin(el) up). Azimuth 0 and elevation 0 point from F toward the viewer; positive azimuth turns toward screen right, positive elevation toward screen up. Orbiting or rolling the camera turns the whole rig with the image.
  • Fill light: fixed direction normalize(0.70 right - 0.25 up - 1.0 direction) (lower right, toward the viewer: azimuth +35.0°, elevation -11.6°) at the same distance, always shadowless.
  • Intensities are white light in linear units; there is no distance attenuation.
  • Light size: the key light becomes a circular area light whose diameter is light_size × R Å, sampled on a 5 × 5 grid with adaptive refinement and no jitter; orient turns the disc toward each shaded point, so it acts like a sphere of that diameter rather than a fixed panel.
  • Reflection panel: a disc of radius 1.6 R at C + 3 R × key direction, facing back along the key direction (anchored on C, not F).

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.core.camera import Camera
>>> from ycrystal.core.lighting import resolve_lighting_for_bounds
>>> from ycrystal.core.scene import Environment
>>> camera = Camera((0, 0, 30), (0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), parallel_scale=5.0)
>>> env = Environment(key_azimuth=-65, key_elevation=25, key_light=1.3, fill_light=0.12)
>>> rig = resolve_lighting_for_bounds(env, camera, center=(0, 0, 0), radius=4.0)
>>> rig.distance
26.0
>>> [round(float(v), 3) for v in rig.key.position]
[-21.356, 10.988, 9.959]
>>> rig.key.is_area, rig.fill.shadows
(False, False)

items.title: aspect
items.text:
Output-size arithmetic with an optional locked aspect ratio (FR-RENDER-01).

The Render panel keeps a target ratio r = width / height. While the ratio is locked, editing one dimension computes the other from r in whole pixels; r itself is kept across edits and never recomputed from the rounded dimensions, so repeated edits do not drift. These functions hold that arithmetic without Qt, so the panel, the window, and the tests share one implementation.

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.core.aspect import linked_size, swapped
>>> ratio = 2400 / 1600
>>> linked_size("height", 1920, (2400, 1600), ratio, locked=True)
(2880, 1920)
>>> linked_size("width", 3000, (2400, 1600), ratio, locked=True)
(3000, 2000)
>>> linked_size("height", 1920, (2400, 1600), ratio, locked=False)
(2400, 1920)
>>> swapped((2400, 1600), ratio)
((1600, 2400), 0.6666666666666666)

The POV-Ray preview has its own size (FR-PREVIEW-01): a chosen width, and the height that keeps the output's shape.

>>> from ycrystal.core.aspect import preview_size
>>> [preview_size((2400, 1600), width)[:2] for width in (480, 800, 1200)]
[(480, 320), (800, 533), (1200, 800)]
>>> preview_size((1600, 2400), 480)[:2]
(480, 720)
>>> preview_size((640, 480), 1200)
PreviewSize(width=640, height=480, requested=1200, limit='output')

items.title: preview_size
items.text:
preview_size(output: Size, requested_width: int) -> PreviewSize

Return the preview size for a requested width and the output image's shape.

The height is round(width × output height / output width), half up, so the preview shows the same frame as the final image (rounding moves its edges by less than half a preview pixel). The result is never larger than the output. A portrait output whose height would exceed MAX_PREVIEW_PIXELS is scaled down to that height, and an extreme shape whose short side would be under MIN_PREVIEW_PIXELS is scaled up to it (at most to the output size), so the shape is never distorted.

Parameters:

    Output image (width, height) in pixels.

  • requested_width (int) –

    Preview width in pixels, MIN_PREVIEW_PIXELS to MAX_PREVIEW_PIXELS.

items.title: export
items.text:
Image export: formats, figure sizes, and resolution arithmetic (FR-EXPORT-01).

POV-Ray renders a raster image; Ycrystal writes it as PNG, PDF, or JPEG. This module holds the arithmetic shared by the export dialog, the window, and the tests, without Qt. Writing the files is ycrystal.render.formats.

Four quantities are kept apart:

  • the pixel size POV-Ray renders (width × height), which is the size of the PNG and JPEG and of the image embedded in the PDF;
  • the resolution in dots per inch, stored as metadata in PNG and JPEG files and used to compute the PDF page size;
  • the physical size, pixels / dpi × 25.4 mm;
  • the size the user entered, in pixels or millimetres (figure_pixels converts it).

Examples:

>>> from ycrystal.core.export import pixels_from_mm, mm_from_pixels
>>> pixels_from_mm(85, 600)  # single column at 600 dpi
2008
>>> pixels_from_mm(180, 600)  # double column at 600 dpi
4252
>>> round(mm_from_pixels(2008, 600), 2)
85.01
>>> figure_pixels("mm", 85, 85 / 1.5, 600)
(2008, 1339)
>>> [round(mm, 2) for mm in ExportOptions("pdf", 2008, 1339, dpi=600).physical_size_mm()]
[85.01, 56.68]

items.title: formats
items.text:
Write a rendered POV-Ray image as PNG, PDF, or JPEG (FR-EXPORT-01).

POV-Ray always writes an 8-bit PNG at the requested pixel size (with an element legend, Ycrystal has already painted it onto that PNG, see ycrystal.render.legend). This module turns that image into the file the user asked for, without resampling it:

  • PNG: the rendered file byte for byte; with a resolution, a pHYs chunk is inserted after the header (the image data are not decoded or re-encoded).
  • JPEG: decoded once and encoded once with the chosen quality. JPEG has no alpha channel, so a transparent background is composited over white first. The JFIF header carries the resolution.
  • PDF: one page whose size is the physical size of the image at the chosen resolution, with the image embedded losslessly (Flate) at its full pixel size and any alpha channel kept as a soft mask. The PDF contains a raster image: it is not a vector drawing and does not become sharper when enlarged. PDF page sizes are whole PostScript points (1/72 inch), so the page may differ from the exact physical size by up to half a point (0.18 mm); the image is centred on it without distortion.

Every format is written to <destination>.part, checked, and then renamed over the destination, so a failed export never leaves a truncated file under the final name. Uses Qt's image classes (QImage, QPdfWriter), which need no window or display.

items.title: JPEG_MATTE module-attribute

items.title: povray
items.text:
Locate the POV-Ray executable and explain its failures in plain language.

Two kinds of POV-Ray are supported:

  • the command-line program povray of Linux and macOS (distribution packages, Homebrew), which prints its messages and progress;
  • POV-Ray for Windows, a window program (pvengine64.exe) without a povray command. It renders an INI file given on its command line with /EXIT and quits; its messages go to a log file in the job directory (see render_arguments).

items.title: find_povray
items.text:
find_povray(configured: str | PathLike[str] | None = None) -> str

Return the POV-Ray executable to use.

The first source that is set decides, in this order: configured, the environment variable YCRYSTAL_POVRAY (ignored if empty), then povray on PATH, and on Windows an installed POV-Ray for Windows (installed_windows_engine).

Parameters:

  • configured (str | PathLike[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Explicit executable, for example the GUI setting (Render ▸ Set POV-Ray Executable…) or ycrystal --check-renderer --povray PATH. ~ is expanded.

Returns:

  • str –

    Path of an existing executable file. Whether it is a working POV-Ray is not checked; use run_self_test.

Raises:

  • PovrayNotFoundError –

    If the deciding source names a missing or non-executable file, or if no source is set and no POV-Ray is found.

Notes

A configured or environment path that is invalid raises immediately; the search does not fall back to the next source. Nothing is executed.

items.title: povray_version
items.text:
povray_version(executable: str, timeout: float = 15.0) -> str | None

Return the version that povray --version reports.

Runs the executable synchronously. POV-Ray for Windows has no --version (it would open its window); its version is read from the executable's version resource instead, without running it.

Parameters:

  • executable (str) –

    POV-Ray executable.

  • timeout (float, default: 15.0 ) –

    Seconds to wait for the process.

Returns:

  • str or None –

    Version string such as "3.7.0.10"; None if the program cannot be run, times out, or prints no recognizable version.

items.title: explain_failure
items.text:
explain_failure(returncode: int | None, log: str) -> str

Turn POV-Ray's exit status and output into a readable message.

Parameters:

  • returncode (int | None) –

    Exit status, or None if the process was stopped or crashed.

  • log (str) –

    POV-Ray's output.

Returns:

  • str –

    An explanation for known problems (a miscompiled build that rejects cameras without angle, I/O restrictions, a missing include file); otherwise the exit status and the last 12 lines of output.

items.title: include_directories
items.text:
include_directories(executable: str | PathLike[str] | None = None) -> list[Path]

Return the directories where POV-Ray looks for standard include files.

POV-Ray is installed under a prefix (/usr, /usr/local, Homebrew's /opt/homebrew, a Conda environment, …) with its settings in PREFIX/etc/povray/VERSION/povray.ini and its include files in PREFIX/share/povray-VERSION/include. This function reads the Library_Path entries of the povray.ini files of the system (/etc/povray/3.7), of the executable's prefix, and of the user (~/.povray/3.7), and adds the prefix's include directories and INCLUDE_FALLBACK_DIRS.

Parameters:

  • executable (str | PathLike[str] | None, default: None ) –

    POV-Ray executable whose installation is searched; None uses the one that find_povray returns without a configured path ($YCRYSTAL_POVRAY, then PATH), if any.

Returns:

  • list of pathlib.Path –

    Existing directories, without duplicates. Nothing is executed.

Return the include files of names that none of the include directories has.

Parameters:

  • names (tuple[str, ...] | list[str]) –

    Include file names, for example from required_includes.

  • executable (str | PathLike[str] | None, default: None ) –

    POV-Ray executable whose installation is searched; see include_directories.

Returns:

  • list of str –

    The missing names, in the given order; empty when all are found.

items.title: is_windows_engine
items.text:
is_windows_engine(executable: str | PathLike[str]) -> bool

Return whether an executable is POV-Ray for Windows (pvengine*.exe).

is_windows_engine(r"C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe") True is_windows_engine("/usr/bin/povray") False

items.title: windows_engine_candidates
items.text:
windows_engine_candidates(environ: Mapping[str, str], registry_homes: Iterable[str] = ()) -> list[Path]

Return where POV-Ray for Windows may be installed, most likely first.

POV-Ray for Windows does not put itself on PATH. Its installer writes its folder to the registry (Software\POV-Ray\v3.7\Windows, value Home) and installs into %ProgramFiles%\POV-Ray\v3.7 by default; the executables are in its bin folder. Nothing is hard-coded but that layout: the folders come from registry_homes and the ProgramFiles variables of environ.

paths = windows_engine_candidates({"ProgramFiles": "C:/PF"}, ["D:/POV"]) names = [p.as_posix() for p in paths] names[0], names[3] ('D:/POV/bin/pvengine64.exe', 'C:/PF/POV-Ray/v3.7/bin/pvengine64.exe')

items.title: installed_windows_engine
items.text:
installed_windows_engine(platform: str = sys.platform) -> str | None

Return an installed POV-Ray for Windows, or None (always None elsewhere).

Looks on PATH first, then in the folders of windows_engine_candidates.

items.title: render_arguments
items.text:
render_arguments(executable: str | PathLike[str], ini_name: str) -> list[str]

Return the command-line arguments that render an INI file, without the executable.

povray takes the INI file alone. POV-Ray for Windows is a window program: it gets /EXIT (quit when the render is done), /NR (do not reopen the files of its last session), and +GA with LOG_NAME (write all messages to that file, because it prints nothing).

render_arguments("/usr/bin/povray", "scene.ini") ['scene.ini'] render_arguments("C:/POV-Ray/v3.7/bin/pvengine64.exe", "scene.ini") ['/EXIT', '/NR', '+GAscene.log', 'scene.ini']

items.title: background_startupinfo
items.text:
background_startupinfo(executable: str | PathLike[str]) -> Any

Return subprocess start-up information that keeps POV-Ray for Windows minimised.

Its window would otherwise open at full size for every render. Minimised (not hidden), it stays reachable from the taskbar, should it ever wait for an answer in a dialog. None for other executables and on other systems.

Minimising does not stop POV-Ray for Windows from making itself the foreground window; see hold_foreground.

items.title: hold_foreground
items.text:
hold_foreground(executable: str | PathLike[str], platform: str = sys.platform) -> bool

Keep POV-Ray for Windows from taking the keyboard focus while it renders.

POV-Ray for Windows brings its window to the foreground when it starts, even when started minimised, which takes the keyboard focus from the window the user works in, for example during every automatic preview. While a hold is active, Ycrystal asks Windows to refuse such requests of other programs (LockSetForegroundWindow). Windows grants this only to the program that owns the foreground window: Ycrystal's window when the user works there, not a terminal that runs ycrystal --render. It lifts the lock by itself when the user presses Alt or clicks another window.

Every hold asks for the lock again (Windows may have lifted it since), and holds are counted, so that renders that overlap keep the lock until the last one ends.

Parameters:

  • executable (str | PathLike[str]) –

    The POV-Ray that is about to start; only POV-Ray for Windows needs a hold.

  • platform (str, default: platform ) –

    sys.platform value to decide for; the default is the running system.

Returns:

  • bool –

    Whether a hold was taken; then call release_foreground once when POV-Ray has exited.

items.title: release_foreground
items.text:
release_foreground() -> None

End one hold of hold_foreground.

items.title: foreground_held
items.text:
foreground_held(executable: str | PathLike[str]) -> Iterator[None]

Hold the foreground for the duration of a with block.

See hold_foreground.

items.title: keeps_single_instance
items.text:
keeps_single_instance(settings_file: str | PathLike[str]) -> bool

Return whether POV-Ray for Windows keeps a single instance, from its settings file.

The option Options ▸ Keep Single Instance is stored as OneInstance in the [General] section of pvengine.ini (in Documents\POV-Ray\v3.7\ini). It is read as POV-Ray reads it (GetPrivateProfileInt): absent means on (the default), and a value counts by its leading integer, so that 0 or a value without one means off. A missing or unreadable file counts as on.

items.title: editor_library
items.text:
editor_library(executable: str | PathLike[str]) -> str

Return the file name of the editor library that POV-Ray for Windows loads.

The editor is a separately licensed library, not included in the AGPL installer. Each build of the program loads its own (EDITDLLNAME in POV-Ray's source).

editor_library(r"C:\Program Files\POV-Ray\v3.7\bin\pvengine64.exe") 'cmedit64.dll' editor_library("pvengine32-sse2.exe"), editor_library("pvengine.exe") ('cmedit32-sse2.dll', 'cmedit32.dll')

items.title: editor_question_pending
items.text:
editor_question_pending(executable: str | PathLike[str], settings_file: str | PathLike[str] | None, homes: Iterable[str] = ()) -> bool

Return whether POV-Ray for Windows will ask about its editor when it starts.

At every start, also with /EXIT, POV-Ray for Windows loads its editor library (editor_library) from its own folder, then from the bin folder of its installation (Home in the registry). If both fail and Options ▸ Other Settings ▸ Use Editor is on (UseEditors in the [General] section of pvengine.ini, on by default), it asks whether to download the editor and waits for the answer: a render started by Ycrystal would wait too.

Only program files (pvengine*.exe) are checked; other programs never ask.

Parameters:

  • executable (str | PathLike[str]) –

    The POV-Ray for Windows program.

  • settings_file (str | PathLike[str] | None) –

    Its pvengine.ini; None if it has none yet (it has never run), which leaves the option on.

  • homes (Iterable[str], default: () ) –

    Installation folders recorded in the registry.

items.title: windows_engine_conflict
items.text:
windows_engine_conflict(executable: str | PathLike[str], platform: str = sys.platform) -> str | None

Return why POV-Ray for Windows cannot start a render now, or None.

Two reasons are checked before POV-Ray starts, so that a render fails at once with an explanation instead of waiting for a dialog in a minimised window:

  • its question about a missing editor (editor_question_pending): EDITOR_QUESTION_MESSAGE;
  • with Keep Single Instance on (its default), POV-Ray for Windows does not render when another copy is open: it brings that copy forward, shows an error dialog for the switch /EXIT, and exits without an image: ENGINE_OPEN_MESSAGE.

Parameters:

  • executable (str | PathLike[str]) –

    The POV-Ray about to start; None is returned for other programs than POV-Ray for Windows.

  • platform (str, default: platform ) –

    sys.platform value to decide for; the default is the running system.

items.title: read_log
items.text:
read_log(directory: str | PathLike[str]) -> str

Return the log POV-Ray for Windows wrote into a job directory (empty if none).

items.title: windows_file_version
items.text:
windows_file_version(path: str | PathLike[str]) -> str | None

Return the file version of a Windows executable ("3.7.0.0"), or None.

Reads the fixed version information of the file with the Windows version API; None on other systems, for files without version information, and on errors.

items.title: jobs
items.text:
Render jobs: isolated temporary directories with short ASCII file names.

POV-Ray runs with the job directory as its working directory and writes only there. This avoids problems with spaces/non-ASCII characters in user paths and works within POV-Ray's I/O restrictions (povray.conf normally permits the working directory). The finished image is copied to the user's destination by Python afterwards.

A job goes through these steps; the caller owns the job directory throughout:

  1. prepare_job creates a new directory ycrystal-job-* (in the system temporary directory by default) containing scene.pov and scene.ini.
  2. POV-Ray runs with that directory as its working directory, either synchronously with run_job or asynchronously with RenderProcess. It writes scene.png.
  3. finish_job turns the exit status and log into a RenderResult; renderer failures are reported in the result, not raised. If the job has an enabled element legend, it is painted onto the image now (ycrystal.render.legend), so that every use of the image (preview, export, command line) has it.
  4. copy_result copies the image to its destination.
  5. RenderJob.cleanup deletes the directory. Nothing in this module does that automatically.

items.title: RenderResult dataclass
items.text:
RenderResult(ok: bool, returncode: int | None, log: str, image_path: Path | None, message: str = '', cancelled: bool = False, elapsed: float = 0.0)

Outcome of one POV-Ray run.

Attributes:

  • ok (bool) –

    Whether POV-Ray exited with status 0 and wrote a non-empty image.

  • returncode (int | None) –

    Exit status, or None if POV-Ray could not be started, timed out, crashed, or was stopped.

  • log (str) –

    POV-Ray's combined standard output and standard error.

  • image_path (Path | None) –

    The rendered PNG inside the job directory when ok is true, else None. It disappears when the job is cleaned up.

  • message (str) –

    Readable explanation of a failure; empty when ok is true.

  • cancelled (bool) –

    Whether the run was stopped on request (then ok is false and the message says so; it is not an error to report).

  • elapsed (float) –

    Wall-clock seconds the process ran, when measured (0 otherwise).

items.title: parse_progress
items.text:
parse_progress(output: str) -> int | None

Return the latest render progress in percent from POV-Ray output.

POV-Ray prints Rendered N of M pixels lines when Verbose=on, which the .ini files written by Ycrystal set.

Parameters:

  • output (str) –

    A chunk of POV-Ray's output (lines may be separated by carriage returns).

Returns:

  • int or None –

    Percentage between 0 and 100 from the last progress line, or None if the chunk contains none.

Examples:

>>> parse_progress("Rendered 1024 of 480000 pixels (0%)\rRendered 240000 of 480000 pixels")
50
>>> parse_progress("Parsing...") is None
True

items.title: prepare_job
items.text:
prepare_job(geometry: DisplayGeometry, camera: Camera, environment: Environment, settings: RenderSettings, parent: Path | None = None, legend: LegendSettings | None = None, **writer_kwargs: str) -> RenderJob

Create a job directory and write the scene and settings into it.

Parameters:

  • geometry (DisplayGeometry) –

    Atoms and cell edges to draw.

  • camera (Camera) –

    View to reproduce.

  • environment (Environment) –

    Background colour and light intensities.

  • settings (RenderSettings) –

    Output image settings.

  • parent (Path | None, default: None ) –

    Directory in which to create the job directory; None uses the system temporary directory ($TMPDIR, usually /tmp).

  • legend (LegendSettings | None, default: None ) –

    Element legend to paint onto the finished image (SceneSettings.legend); None or a disabled legend leaves the image exactly as POV-Ray renders it. The scene files do not contain it.

  • **writer_kwargs (str, default: {} ) –

    Passed to scene_to_pov.

Returns:

  • RenderJob –

    The prepared job. Call RenderJob.cleanup when it is no longer needed.

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If the directory or the files cannot be created.

Notes

If writing fails after directory creation, the partial directory is retained and no job is returned; the caller may need to remove it manually.

items.title: finish_job
items.text:
finish_job(job: RenderJob, returncode: int | None, log: str) -> RenderResult

Interpret the exit status and output of a finished POV-Ray process.

Parameters:

  • job (RenderJob) –

    The job that was rendered.

  • returncode (int | None) –

    Exit status, or None if the process crashed or was stopped.

  • log (str) –

    Combined output of the process.

Returns:

  • RenderResult –

    Success if returncode is 0 and job.image_path is a non-empty file; otherwise a failure whose message comes from explain_failure. A job with an enabled legend has it painted onto the image first; if that fails, the result is a failure that says so.

items.title: run_job
items.text:
run_job(job: RenderJob, executable: str, timeout: float | None = 600.0) -> RenderResult

Run POV-Ray for a job and wait until it finishes.

The calling thread blocks for the whole render. The command line interface, the tests, and the renderer check use this function; the GUI uses RenderProcess so that the window stays responsive.

Parameters:

  • job (RenderJob) –

    Prepared job; POV-Ray runs with job.directory as its working directory.

  • executable (str) –

    POV-Ray executable, for example from find_povray.

  • timeout (float | None, default: 600.0 ) –

    Seconds after which POV-Ray is killed; None waits indefinitely.

Returns:

  • RenderResult –

    The outcome. A failure to start, a timeout, or a failed render gives ok=False with an explanation instead of an exception.

Notes

The job directory is not removed; call RenderJob.cleanup afterwards.

POV-Ray for Windows is not started while another copy of it that keeps a single instance is open (see windows_engine_conflict); the result then explains why.

items.title: copy_result
items.text:
copy_result(image: Path, destination: Path) -> Path

Copy a finished image to its destination.

Parameters:

  • image (Path) –

    Rendered image, usually RenderResult.image_path.

  • destination (Path) –

    Target path; any characters are allowed. Missing parent directories are created.

Returns:

  • Path –

    destination as a Path.

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If the image cannot be read or the destination cannot be written.

Notes

The image is first copied to <destination>.part in the same directory and then renamed, which replaces an existing file without asking. If copying fails, the .part file is not removed.

items.title: RenderJob dataclass

RenderJob(directory: Path, pov_path: Path, ini_path: Path, image_path: Path, settings: RenderSettings, legend: LegendSettings | None = None, legend_entries: tuple[LegendEntry, ...] = ())

Files of one render, in a private directory.

    Element legend painted onto the image after the render, or None.

  • legend_entries (tuple[LegendEntry, ...]) –

    The legend's entries, resolved from the rendered geometry.

items.title: arguments
items.text:
arguments(executable: str | None = None) -> list[str]

Return the POV-Ray command-line arguments, without the executable.

Parameters:

  • executable (str | None, default: None ) –

    The POV-Ray that will run: POV-Ray for Windows needs more arguments (see render_arguments). None means povray.

Returns:

    ["scene.ini"] for povray. The names are relative, so the process must run with directory as its working directory.

items.title: cleanup
items.text:
cleanup() -> None

Delete the job directory and everything in it, ignoring errors.

This also deletes the rendered image, so copy it first.

items.title: selftest
items.text:
Renderer self-test: render a tiny known scene and check its geometry.

The scene uses a rotated, panned camera and a non-square image. Three spheres of different colours must appear at the analytically projected pixels (within one pixel), with the expected colours (detects mirroring) and the requested dimensions.

items.title: TOLERANCE_PX module-attribute
items.text:
TOLERANCE_PX = 1.0

Largest accepted distance in pixels between rendered and predicted sphere centres.

items.title: SelfTestResult dataclass
items.text:
SelfTestResult(ok: bool, executable: str | None, version: str | None, message: str, max_error_px: float | None = None, matches: list[Match] = list())

Outcome of run_self_test.

Attributes:

  • ok (bool) –

    Whether the renderer passed.

  • executable (str | None) –

    Executable that was tested; None if none was found.

  • version (str | None) –

    Version reported by the executable, if any.

  • message (str) –

    Readable verdict, printed by ycrystal --check-renderer.

  • max_error_px (float | None) –

    Largest centre error in pixels, if the image could be measured.

  • matches (list[Match]) –

    Per-sphere measurements, if the image could be measured.

items.title: run_self_test
items.text:
run_self_test(configured: str | None = None, timeout: float = 60.0) -> SelfTestResult

Check that a POV-Ray executable reproduces Ycrystal's camera.

Finds the executable like find_povray, asks for its version, and renders a 120 × 80 pixel image with a transparent background in a temporary job directory. The image passes if it has the requested size and each sphere is within TOLERANCE_PX of its predicted pixel position, with the expected dominant colour channel (which detects mirroring).

Parameters:

  • configured (str | None, default: None ) –

    Executable to test first; see find_povray. The GUI passes its stored setting; ycrystal --check-renderer passes --povray.

  • timeout (float, default: 60.0 ) –

    Seconds allowed for the render.

Returns:

  • SelfTestResult –

    The verdict. A missing or failing renderer gives ok=False with an explanation.

Raises:

  • OSError –

    If the temporary job cannot be prepared or its image cannot be read. Other image-decoding or measurement errors may also propagate.

Notes

Runs synchronously: the caller waits for the version query (up to 15 s) and the render (up to timeout). Once preparation succeeds, the job directory is removed in finally, including on image-reading or measurement failures.

items.title: legend
items.text:
Paint the element legend onto images (FR-LEGEND-01).

The legend is drawn in two dimensions with Qt's QPainter and is independent of the three-dimensional scene: POV-Ray renders the structure exactly as without a legend, and draw_legend_on_file then paints the legend onto the rendered PNG at its full pixel size (in finish_job). PNG, PDF, and JPEG exports, the preview, and the command line all start from that image. The live view draws the same legend with legend_overlay, so what the frame shows is what the image gets.

To stay sharp and identical at every size, the layout is computed once at a reference text size and scaled to the image: the text height is a fixed fraction of the image height (see LegendSettings). Symbols are drawn as the outlines of their glyphs, antialiased, without font hinting or subpixel (coloured) antialiasing, so they look the same in a 480-pixel preview and a 6000-pixel export, and the edges carry no colour fringes in print.

Painting text needs a QGuiApplication. In the window there is one; the command line creates one without windows when the first legend is drawn (ensure_gui_application).

items.title: DEFAULT_FONT_FAMILIES module-attribute
items.text:
DEFAULT_FONT_FAMILIES = ('Arial', 'Helvetica', 'Liberation Sans', 'Nimbus Sans', 'DejaVu Sans')

Families tried in turn for the default font (an empty font_family): Arial or Helvetica, as many journals ask for in figures, or a metric-compatible free family. If none is installed, Qt's default sans-serif family is used.

items.title: REFERENCE_SIZE module-attribute
items.text:
REFERENCE_SIZE = 100.0

Text pixel size at which the layout is computed before it is scaled to the image.

items.title: LABEL_GAP module-attribute
items.text:
LABEL_GAP = 0.35

Gap between a marker and its symbol, in multiples of the text height.

items.title: PADDING module-attribute
items.text:
PADDING = 0.45

Space between the legend and the edge of its background box (text heights).

items.title: CORNER_RADIUS module-attribute
items.text:
CORNER_RADIUS = 0.3

Corner radius of the background box (text heights).

items.title: OUTLINE module-attribute
items.text:
OUTLINE = 0.04

Width of a marker's outline, as a fraction of the marker diameter.

items.title: MIN_FREE_FRACTION module-attribute
items.text:
MIN_FREE_FRACTION = 0.2

Smallest share of the frame width or height left for the structure by legend_fit_region; a legend that leaves less reserves nothing.

items.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

The legend could not be drawn; str() explains why.

The legend laid out for one image size.

Markers and labels are in reference units (text height REFERENCE_SIZE); rect is where the legend's box lands in the image, in image pixels.

Attributes:

    Box of the legend in image pixels (top-left origin), including the background padding when there is a background.

    Image pixels per reference unit.

Map a point from reference units to image pixels.

items.title: ensure_gui_application
items.text:
ensure_gui_application() -> None

Make sure a QGuiApplication exists, as text drawing needs one.

In the window, the application exists and nothing happens. Otherwise (the command line, scripts) one is created without windows, with the platform plug-in chosen by ycrystal.gui.native.painting_platform (offscreen on Linux and macOS, the native one on Windows) unless QT_QPA_PLATFORM names one.

items.title: resolved_font_family
items.text:
resolved_font_family(name: str = '') -> str

Return the font family that draws the legend for the setting name.

An empty name selects the first installed family of DEFAULT_FONT_FAMILIES. A name that is not installed is returned as it is: Qt then draws with a similar family.

items.title: legend_font
items.text:
legend_font(name: str = '') -> QFont

Return the legend's font at REFERENCE_SIZE.

Hinting and subpixel antialiasing are off, so that the glyph outlines scale exactly.

items.title: legend_layout
items.text:
legend_layout(entries: Sequence[LegendEntry], settings: LegendSettings, width: float, height: float) -> LegendLayout | None

Lay out the legend for an image of width × height pixels.

Returns None when there is nothing to draw (no entries). The legend is not clipped here: a legend larger than the image extends beyond it.

items.title: legend_fit_region
items.text:
legend_fit_region(entries: Sequence[LegendEntry], settings: LegendSettings, aspect: float) -> tuple[float, float, float, float] | None

Return the part of the frame that a legend at an edge leaves for the structure.

The region is (left, top, right, bottom) in fractions of the frame (top-left origin), as Camera.fitted takes it: the frame without the legend and, towards the structure, a gap as wide as the legend's margin. Fitting into it puts the structure beside the legend instead of under it.

Returns:

  • tuple or None –

    None (the whole frame) when the legend is disabled, has no entries, is at a custom position, or would leave less than MIN_FREE_FRACTION of the frame.

items.text:
